hypothesis: If we generate a large volume of raw name candidates and defer judgement to a scheduled evaluation, then the shortlist is not anchored on the first few names that came to mind.

signal.check: Naming discussion has stalled on 5 to 10 candidates with no larger raw list generated first, and ideas are being judged as soon as they are said.

expected_effect.size: clients typically stall at 50 to 100 names; an agency working list runs toward about 2,000 raw candidates (1 agency's practice)

risk.note: A generation exercise.

steps: Set a target raw candidate count appropriate to the brand's scale (a small brand can scale down from an agency's 2,000).
Ban judgement or elimination during the generation session.
Keep groups small (roughly 4 to 10 people) since larger groups are reported to degrade brainstorm output.
Schedule a separate session for evaluation after generation is done.

test.method: Count the raw candidate list length before the evaluation session starts.
test.measure: other:raw_candidate_count.

title: Shortlist names from the tension zone, not the safest consensus pick
hypothesis: If we keep at least 1 polarising name on the shortlist instead of defaulting to consensus comfort, then the brand avoids a comprehensible but forgettable name, because comprehension is not the same as differentiation.

signal.check: The naming shortlist contains only names everyone mildly likes, with no candidate that splits opinion.

risk.note: A polarising name still needs to pass legal and believability checks before launch.

prerequisites: A raw candidate list
steps: Poll 5 to 10 people on each finalist with a no sevens rule (force a like or dislike, not a neutral score).
Keep at least 1 candidate with strong like and strong dislike on the shortlist.
Do not eliminate the polarising candidate for lacking full consensus; carry it to the believability and legal gate instead.

test.method: Score the shortlist for polarisation using the no sevens poll.
test.measure: Whether at least 1 shortlisted name shows a split vote.

title: Test candidate name sound and syllable count before finalising
hypothesis: If we count syllables and read each finalist name aloud, then the chosen name is easy to say and remember, because the mind processes a name aurally before it processes the spelling.

signal.check: Name finalists have not been read aloud or checked for syllable count and initial letter before selection.

expected_effect.size: unknown; practitioner opinion, no controlled study cited

risk.note: A quick check.

prerequisites: A naming shortlist
steps: Read each finalist aloud to 3 or more people.
Count syllables and note the initial letter.
Prefer shorter, more sayable names, and check any abbreviation really shortens the spoken name.

test.method: Record reactions and ease of pronunciation for each finalist read aloud.
test.measure: Syllable count and pronunciation ease score.

title: Avoid initials and acronyms as a brand name until the brand is already famous
hypothesis: If we avoid launching with an acronym or initials, then the brand avoids a name shoppers cannot yet decode, because initials only work once the full name is already known.

signal.check: A naming shortlist includes an acronym or initials for a brand that is not yet a household name.

risk.note: A naming rule check.

steps: Flag any acronym or initials candidate on the shortlist.
Check if the brand is already a household name; if not, drop the acronym candidate.
If the brand truly needs a short form later, plan for it after the full name is established.

test.method: Review the shortlist for acronym candidates before finalists are chosen.
test.measure: Number of acronym candidates removed.

title: Watch for a successful descriptive name becoming generic and guard the trademark
hypothesis: If we watch for the public shortening a descriptive name into a category word, then we can act before losing exclusive rights to it, because a name the public turns generic can be legally lost.

signal.check: Customers or press are shortening the brand's descriptive name into a general category term (for example, calling any product in the category by the brand's own descriptor).

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named historical case only (Miller Lite)

risk.note: Once a name goes generic in legal terms, trademark protection can be lost permanently.

steps: Search press and social mentions for the brand name used as a generic category term.
If found, use the brand name consistently with its full descriptor in official copy.
Consult trademark counsel if generic use is spreading.

test.method: Run a quarterly search for generic use of the brand name in press and social mentions.
test.measure: Number of generic-use mentions found.

title: Do not hide a product's plain nature behind a euphemism where trust matters
hypothesis: If a category has a trust problem, then naming the product plainly, even if the plain name polarises, builds more pride and trust than a euphemism, because hiding the nature of the product reads as evasive once discovered.

signal.check: The product name uses a euphemism to soften a plain fact about the product in a category where customers already distrust vague labelling.

expected_effect.size: unknown; sources are dated examples only

risk.note: A name change to be more plain-spoken may need a rename process; check R84 triggers first.

steps: Check if the category has a known trust or transparency problem.
List any euphemisms in the current product name or description.
Test a plainer, more direct alternative with a small customer panel before committing.

test.method: Survey a small panel on trust perception for the euphemistic name versus a plain alternative.
test.measure: Trust perception score.
test.read_point: Before any naming decision is finalised

title: Avoid naming the brand after the founder if it must outlive the founder's visibility
hypothesis: If the brand is meant to outlive the founder's public visibility, then avoiding a founder name protects the brand's future, because a founder name ties the brand's meaning to 1 person's continued presence.
does_not_apply_when: The founder has committed to remain the public face of the brand long term

signal.check: A new brand or product name candidate uses the founder's own name, with no explicit plan for the founder to stay the face long term.

risk.note: Renaming a brand built on the founder's name later is a costly, low-reversibility move.

prerequisites: Founder's stated horizon as the public face
steps: Ask the founder directly how long they plan to remain the public face of the brand.
If the answer is indefinite, a founder name is a valid choice.
If the brand should outlive that visibility, choose a non-founder name instead.

test.method: Document the founder's stated horizon before the naming decision is finalised.
test.measure: Whether the naming choice matches the stated horizon.

title: Run trademark, domain and language checks on every name finalist before it is presented
hypothesis: If we run trademark, domain and pronunciation checks on every finalist before presenting it, then a name is never launched only to be blocked or embarrassing in another market.

signal.check: A name finalist is being presented for a launch decision with no trademark register search, domain check, or pronunciation and connotation test done in each selling country.

risk.note: Skipping the legal screen risks a costly rename after launch or a market-specific embarrassment.

prerequisites: A list of finalist names
A list of every selling country and language
steps: Search trademark registers in every selling country for each finalist.
Check domain and social handle availability for each finalist.
Test pronunciation and connotation in every selling language, including dialect readings for markets like China.
Drop any finalist that fails a check with no appeal.
Narrow the surviving list to 10 to 15 finalists.

test.method: Complete the legal and language screen for every finalist before any is presented to a decision maker.
test.measure: Number of finalists cleared versus dropped.

title: Present name finalists in realistic mock-ups, not a spreadsheet list
hypothesis: If we show name finalists in a PDP header, an ad in placement, and a pack mock-up, then a decision maker can judge believability at a glance, because names are hard to judge as plain text on a spreadsheet.

signal.check: Name finalists are being presented as a plain text list or spreadsheet with no in-context mock-up.

risk.note: Mock-ups are a presentation step, not a live commitment.

prerequisites: 2 to 3 finalist names that passed the legal screen
steps: Build a PDP header mock-up for each finalist.
Build an ad mock-up in its real placement, and a pack or search result mock-up.
Label every mock-up clearly so it does not imply real coverage, endorsements or claims.
Present the mock-ups, not a list, to the decision maker.

test.method: Show each mock-up for under 1 second and ask if it feels like a real existing brand.
test.measure: Pass or fail on the sub-second believability read.

title: Use AI to bulk-generate raw name candidates, keep judgement and category knowledge in-house
hypothesis: If we use an AI assistant only to bulk-generate raw name candidates and keep the judging framework in-house, then generation scales without the scarce skill of judging candidates being outsourced.

signal.check: Naming generation is slow or thin, and no AI assistant has been used to add raw candidate volume before the human judging pass.

expected_effect.size: an assistant can generate 200 to 300 raw candidates quickly (1 practitioner's estimate)

risk.note: A generation aid; judgement still happens with the human-defined criteria.

prerequisites: The naming audit and screening criteria written before generation starts
steps: Define the judging criteria (BRD-070's 7 qualities) before generating any candidates.
Ask an AI assistant to bulk-generate 200 to 300 raw candidates from the product facts and audit.
Apply the in-house judging framework to the AI-generated list exactly as with human-generated names.

test.method: Compare the quality and hit rate of AI-assisted candidates against a human-only generation session.
test.measure: Number of AI-generated candidates surviving the first screening pass.

title: Deliver nomenclature, a positioning line and a short story with any finalised name
hypothesis: If a naming decision ships with nomenclature, a positioning line and a short brand story attached, then the team downstream can use the name correctly from day 1, instead of guessing how to talk about it.

signal.check: A name has been finalised with no accompanying nomenclature guide, positioning line, or short brand story for the team to use.

risk.note: A documentation step.

prerequisites: A finalised, cleared name
steps: Write the nomenclature: how the product should be described alongside the name.
Write a 1-sentence positioning line for the name.
Write a short brand story (a few sentences) explaining the name's meaning.
Plan to track recall and correct category association at 90 to 120 days.

test.method: Track branded search, recall, and spelling or search errors at 90 to 120 days post-launch.
test.measure: Recall and correct category association.

title: Type and test any tagline against the strip test before it earns a place
hypothesis: If a tagline still communicates the category or the claim once the product image is removed, then it earns its place; if not, it should be cut, because a tagline that only works with the image beside it is not doing the work of language.

signal.check: A tagline is in use or proposed with no check of whether it survives with the product image removed.

risk.note: A copy check.

steps: Classify the tagline's job: imperative, descriptive, superlative, provocative, or specific.
Remove the product image and read the tagline alone.
Check it still communicates the category or the claim, is short, differentiated, and legible at small size.
Cut the tagline if it fails the strip test.

test.method: Run the strip test with the tagline alone on 3 to 5 people unfamiliar with the brand.
test.measure: Share who correctly infer the category or claim.

title: Rename rather than force a name into a tier it cannot carry
hypothesis: If a name cannot credibly hold the tier the brand wants to move into, then a rename is needed rather than forcing the old name to stretch, because words are empty containers that only carry what buyers already believe about them.

signal.check: A repositioning into a higher or different tier is being planned while keeping a name that reads as belonging to the old, lower or different tier.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases only (Volkswagen, Eastern Airlines)

risk.note: A diagnostic check; the rename decision itself carries its own risk, see R84 to R88.

steps: State the new tier the brand wants to occupy.
Ask a sample of shoppers unfamiliar with the plan what tier the current name implies.
If the name implies the wrong tier, run the rename decision process (BRD-089) instead of forcing the repositioning.

test.method: Survey a small panel on perceived tier from the name alone.
test.measure: Match rate between perceived tier and target tier.

title: Run the name screen checklist on every finalist before it is shown as a finalist
hypothesis: If every naming finalist passes the full 16-point name screen (meaningful, distinctive, tension zone, believable, sound, not initials, budget-matched type, future-proof, non-generic, trademark clear, domain clear, market-positive, founder-name check, visual, shopping-list and bartender tests, search anchor), then weak or risky names get caught before launch spend.

signal.check: A naming finalist is about to be presented or launched without a full, structured run through the name screen checklist.

risk.note: A review step.

prerequisites: A naming shortlist that has passed initial legal screening
steps: Run each finalist through every row of checklist 5.2.
Score the shopping-list test (does the brand name alone say 1 clear product) and the bartender test (is it ambiguous spoken aloud).
Confirm no invented claim is embedded in the name itself.
Only present names that pass the full checklist.

test.method: Complete the checklist for each finalist with a second reviewer.
test.measure: Number of checklist rows passed per finalist.

title: Run the full naming project when the brand needs a real shortlist with screens
hypothesis: If we run the full naming sequence (audits, type-driven generation, volume, tension-zone shortlisting, sound and legal screens, mock-ups, tracking) in order, then the final name choice rests on evidence instead of the first idea someone liked.

signal.check: A naming decision is being made without following a structured sequence: audits, generation, screening, legal clearance, and post-launch tracking.

risk.note: A finalised, launched name is costly to change later.

prerequisites: Brand brief (BRD-065) or at least product facts and customer language
Selling countries and a trademark search route
steps: Run the category, product and buyer audits.
Decide the naming brief's type mix on purpose from the budget and category.
Generate in 3 briefs (full product story, an altered detail, an unrelated domain) at volume.
Score the long list with no sevens and legal and language screen the survivors.
Build believability mock-ups for the top 2 to 3.
On sign-off, deliver nomenclature, a positioning line and a short story.
Track recall and correct category association at 90 to 120 days.

test.method: Run the full P6 sequence and track the P6 step 13 instrument post-launch.
test.measure: Recall and correct category association at 90 to 120 days.

title: Run the short-form name screen for a product, SKU or collection name
hypothesis: If every new product, SKU or collection name passes the 7-point short screen (positioning, shopping-list, bartender, sound, generic risk, protectable, modular), then product-level naming stays fast without skipping the checks that matter most at that level.

signal.check: New SKU or collection names are chosen quickly with no short screen against search, ambiguity, or fit with the parent naming pattern.

risk.note: A quick check before a new SKU name ships.

prerequisites: Brand name already settled
steps: Check the name begins the positioning (the benefit or job is visible) or a subtitle carries the category word.
Run the shopping-list test: given the brand plus this name, does a shopper know exactly what arrives?
Run the bartender test: spoken aloud, is it ambiguous with another tier or SKU?
Check the sound, the generic risk, and that it is protectable and positive in every market.
Check it fits the parent's naming pattern so the next SKU can follow it.

test.method: Run the 7-point screen for each new SKU or collection name before it ships.
test.measure: Number of checklist rows passed.
test.read_point: Before the new SKU name is finalised

title: Check if a new product is the same job or a different job before stretching the brand name
hypothesis: If we check whether a proposed new SKU serves the same job-to-be-done as the current name or a different one, then we avoid weakening the parent name's meaning by stretching it onto an unrelated job.

signal.check: A new SKU or product line is being added under the existing brand name with no check of whether it serves the same job-to-be-done as the current product.

expected_effect.size: named historical share-loss cases only (Protein 21 fell from 13 percent to 2 percent share; Pall Mall fell from 14.4 percent to 3.8 percent)

risk.note: A launched extension that weakens the parent name is hard to reverse once shipped.

steps: Write the job-to-be-done the current brand name means to shoppers today.
Write the job-to-be-done the new product would serve.
If they match (a new flavour or format), the name can stretch; if not, run R79's house-name-vs-new-name decision instead.

test.method: Score the new product's job-to-be-done against the parent name's current meaning with the team.
test.measure: Match or mismatch on job-to-be-done.

title: Run the shopping-list and bartender test before any brand-name extension
hypothesis: If we test whether a shopper can name 1 clear product from the brand name alone, and whether it is ambiguous spoken aloud, then a diffuse or confusing extension gets caught before launch.

signal.check: A new SKU or tier is about to launch under the existing name with no shopping-list or bartender test run first.

risk.note: A quick test before launch.

steps: Ask 5 to 10 people: given only the brand name, what single product comes to mind?
Ask the same people to order the brand name aloud and see if it is ambiguous between tiers.
If ambiguous, give the new tier its own sayable name instead of forcing it under the same one.

test.method: Run both tests with 5 to 10 people unfamiliar with the extension plan.
test.measure: Share who name 1 clear product without hesitation.

title: Try a reverse line extension before creating a new SKU
hypothesis: If we promote a new use occasion for the identical product and pack instead of launching a new SKU, then growth comes with no added inventory or MOQ risk, because the product, name and package all stay the same.

signal.check: A new SKU is being planned to reach a new use occasion or audience, when the same product could instead be repositioned for that occasion with no new SKU.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases only (Johnson's baby shampoo promoted to adults, Arm and Hammer in the fridge)

risk.note: A messaging change with no new SKU risk.

steps: Identify the new use occasion or audience the proposed SKU targets.
Check if the identical existing product and pack could serve that occasion with new messaging alone.
Test the reverse extension messaging before committing to a new SKU.

test.method: A/B the new-occasion messaging for the existing product against the current single-use messaging.
test.measure: units_per_order and new-occasion attributed sales.

title: Decide house name vs new name using the 5 rules of the road plus a stage gate
hypothesis: If we weigh expected volume, competition, ad support, significance and distribution together, and pass a stage gate on size of prize, MOQ, margin, lead time and an anchor customer, then fewer new products launch under the wrong name or before they are truly ready.

signal.check: A genuine new product is being greenlit with no weighed decision on house name vs new name, and no stage gate on size of prize, MOQ, margin, lead time, or an anchor customer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 operator's practice cites a hero SKU revenue bar of 10 million dollars in his category before the next flavour

risk.note: A launched product with the wrong architecture is costly to unwind.

prerequisites: Sales data for the hero SKU
MOQ and margin figures from sourcing
steps: Weigh the 5 rules of the road together: expected volume, competition, ad budget, significance, distribution.
Check the hero SKU has reached the brand's own revenue bar before diverting attention.
Run the stage gate: size of prize, MOQ, margin, lead time, channel strategy, and a committed anchor customer.
Choose monolithic, endorsed, or new name architecture based on the outcome.
If the house name is used, plan the reorder-curve monitoring for 6 or more months.

test.method: Complete the stage gate checklist before committing to a manufacturer.
test.measure: Number of gate criteria met before go decision.

title: Do not expect a famous name to give a different product a free ride
hypothesis: If we budget real, separate launch support for a new product under a famous name instead of assuming the name alone will sell it, then the launch avoids underperforming on borrowed brand equity that does not automatically transfer.

signal.check: A new product's launch budget assumes the brand's existing fame will carry it, with no dedicated launch spend or plan of its own.

risk.note: A budgeting check before launch.

steps: Check whether the new product's launch plan includes dedicated budget, or only relies on the parent name's fame.
Add a real, separate launch support budget if none exists.
Track the new product's own sell-through independent of the parent line.

test.method: Compare sell-through of the new product against a launch with dedicated support versus none.
test.measure: units_per_order in the first 90 days.

title: Watch the reorder curve, not the launch flash, for 6 or more months after any extension
hypothesis: If we track sell-through and reorders for 6 or more months after a line extension instead of judging it on the first order flash, then a stalling extension gets caught before more inventory is committed.

signal.check: A recent line extension's success is being judged only on the initial trade or first-order volume, with no tracked reorder curve.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source's own arithmetic example (about 35 dollars of stock per US supermarket booking 1 million dollars in first orders) is 1980s era, not a general figure

risk.note: A monitoring habit.

prerequisites: Sell-in and sell-through data by SKU
steps: Set up a monthly reorder tracker for every new extension.
Track sell-in versus sell-through separately, not combined.
Flag any extension whose reorders stall after month 2 or 3 for withdrawal or rename before further inventory is committed.

test.method: Track sell-in versus sell-through monthly for 6 months post-launch.
test.measure: Reorder rate trend over 6 months.

title: Default a small brand to one master brand; split a sub-brand only when needed
hypothesis: If a small brand stays under 1 master brand name until a genuinely different audience or price tier needs distance, then design and marketing spend is not split across multiple identities before it is needed.
does_not_apply_when: A genuinely different audience or price tier needs real distance from the parent brand

signal.check: The store is considering a sub-brand or second brand name for a new line that serves the same core audience and price tier as the parent.

risk.note: A naming architecture decision made before launch is easy to keep simple.

steps: Ask whether the new line serves a genuinely different audience or price tier than the parent.
If not, keep it under the master brand with the parent-vs-product ownership split.
If yes, weigh the extra design and marketing cost of a real sub-brand against the distance it buys.

test.method: Review the architecture decision with the founder before any new sub-brand design work starts.
test.measure: Whether the decision matches the genuinely-different-audience test.

title: Cover a new competitive threat with a separate brand rather than stretching the flagship
hypothesis: If a genuine new sub-category threat is covered with a separate brand instead of stretching the flagship name onto it, then the flagship position stays intact while still contesting the new space.
does_not_apply_when: The threat is small enough that a line extension under the existing name is sufficient

signal.check: A new competitive sub-category threat is being answered by stretching the existing flagship brand name onto a very different product.

risk.note: Launching a second brand is a major cash and attention commitment.

prerequisites: A confirmed, real competitive threat in a new sub-category
steps: Confirm the threat is a genuinely new sub-category, not a line extension opportunity.
Weigh the cost of a separate brand against the risk of diluting the flagship name.
If proceeding, run the naming project (BRD-086) for the new, separate brand.

test.method: Track flagship brand perception and the new brand's traction separately post-launch.
test.measure: Flagship brand equity score and new brand's own sales.
test.read_point: 6 to 12 months after the new brand launches

title: Decide to rename only for a legal trigger, real friction, or a name that cannot hold the position
hypothesis: If a rename is only approved for a legal problem, measurable friction, or a name that cannot hold the intended position, then the brand avoids an expensive rename driven by taste alone.

signal.check: A rename is being discussed with no legal trigger, no measured friction data (spelling errors, search misses, recall gaps), and no container-fit problem, just a preference for something new.

risk.note: A decision gate before a costly rename.

prerequisites: Search-term misspelling data
Support mentions of name confusion
steps: Check for a real legal trigger (a challenge or a blocked market).
Check friction data: search-term misspellings, branded search share, support mentions of confusion.
Check whether the name can hold the position the brand wants to move into.
If none of these apply, do not rename; fix the positioning line instead.

test.method: Score the rename proposal against the 3 valid triggers before approving any rename work.
test.measure: Whether at least 1 valid trigger is documented.

title: Weigh company stage before renaming: cheap and low-risk early, needs a strong reason once equity is deep
hypothesis: If we weigh how much brand equity already exists before deciding to rename, then an early-stage brand renames cheaply while a brand with real accumulated equity is protected from an unjustified switch.

signal.check: A rename decision is being made with no assessment of how much recognition, search equity, or customer trust the current name already holds.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 practitioner's own account, not independently verified

risk.note: A rename decision at the wrong stage risks losing real accumulated equity.

prerequisites: A valid rename trigger from BRD-096
steps: Estimate the brand's accumulated equity: branded search volume, repeat customer recognition, review history under the current name.
If equity is low (early stage), proceed with the rename more freely once a trigger exists.
If equity is high, require a compelling, documented reason beyond the trigger before proceeding.

test.method: Score equity against a simple checklist (branded search volume, review count under the name, years in market) before the rename decision.
test.measure: Equity score and the documented reason to proceed.
test.read_point: Before the rename decision is finalised

title: Launch a rename with an explicit story and a 6 to 9 month extra resource budget
hypothesis: If a rename ships with an explicit we were here, now we're going this way story and a 6 to 9 month extra resource budget, then customers are reassured the product has not changed and the transition does not stall for lack of resources.

signal.check: A rename is planned with no explicit customer-facing story and no dedicated extra budget for redirects, listings, packaging, and announcements.

expected_effect.size: 1 practitioner reports a rename executed in about 6 weeks with 6 to 9 months of extra resources budgeted

risk.note: A poorly resourced rename can confuse or lose customers permanently.

prerequisites: A finalised, cleared new name from the naming project
steps: Write the explicit story: we were here, now we're going this way, here is the benefit to you.
Reassure customers the product itself has not changed.
Budget 6 to 9 months of extra resources for redirects, listings, packaging, and announcements.
Position the new name against the future, not the past.
Track recall and correct category association at 90 to 120 days post-launch.

test.method: Track branded search continuity and support confusion tickets through the transition window.
test.measure: Branded search retention and confusion-related support volume.
test.read_point: 90 to 120 days after the rename launches

title: Audit brand equity first in a rebrand and decide what to keep before deciding what to change
hypothesis: If we audit every existing brand asset for real equity before a rebrand and decide keep, refine, or replace based on that equity, then the rebrand does not throw away recognition it already earned.

signal.check: A rebrand is beginning with no audit of which existing assets (logo, colours, name, packaging) already carry real customer recognition.

risk.note: Replacing an asset that already carries equity is a costly, hard-to-reverse mistake.

steps: List every current brand asset: logo, colours, type, name, packaging elements.
For each, assess real customer recognition (not internal taste) using reviews, UGC, and repeat-buyer feedback.
Mark each asset keep, refine, or replace based on that recognition, not on what the team is tired of.

test.method: Show a sample of customers the current assets and ask what they recognise without prompting.
test.measure: Recognition rate per asset.
test.read_point: Before the rebrand creative direction is locked

title: Expect a rebrand to force catalogue cuts of products that no longer fit
hypothesis: If we plan for catalogue cuts as part of a rebrand instead of treating it as only a visual refresh, then the sharpened position does not stay contradicted by lingering off-brand SKUs.

signal.check: A rebrand is underway or planned with no review of which current SKUs still fit the sharpened position.

risk.note: Discontinuing a SKU affects existing customers and inventory; plan a wind-down, not an abrupt cut.

prerequisites: A sharpened positioning statement from the rebrand
steps: Review every current SKU against the new positioning statement.
Flag SKUs that clearly no longer fit the sharpened position.
Plan a wind-down (sell through existing stock, communicate the change) rather than an abrupt discontinuation.

test.method: Review the SKU list against the new position with the founder.
test.measure: Number of SKUs flagged for wind-down.

title: Decide which SKUs get brand-building spotlight and which stay workhorse listings
hypothesis: If we deliberately choose which SKUs get full brand-building investment and which stay simple workhorse listings, then identity budget concentrates where it can actually move revenue instead of spreading evenly and thinly.

signal.check: Identity and creative budget is being spread evenly across every SKU in the catalogue, with no deliberate spotlight versus workhorse split.

risk.note: A budget allocation decision.

prerequisites: Sales and margin by SKU
steps: Rank SKUs by revenue and margin contribution.
Pick the top few as spotlight SKUs that get full brand-building creative investment.
Keep the rest as workhorse listings with a simpler, template-based treatment.

test.method: Compare identity budget allocation against SKU revenue and margin ranking.
test.measure: Share of identity budget spent on spotlight SKUs versus their revenue share.

title: Choose which product format goes to DTC, marketplace and retail before building each identity kit
hypothesis: If we decide which pack size or format serves DTC, which serves marketplace, and which serves retail before building identity kits for each, then design spend does not go to waste on a format later found to not fit its channel.

signal.check: The store is building identity or packaging kits for multiple channels before deciding which specific format or pack size actually goes to each channel.

risk.note: A planning decision before production commitment.

prerequisites: Channel sales mix and margin by format
steps: List every channel the brand sells through (DTC, marketplace, retail).
Decide which product format or pack size fits each channel's economics and shopper expectation.
Build the identity kit for each format only after this decision is made.

test.method: Review the channel-format assignment against margin and sell-through data before kit production.
test.measure: Margin by channel-format pairing.

title: Run the line-extension checklist before approving any new SKU
hypothesis: If every new SKU proposal passes the 8-point line-extension checklist (shopping-list test, same-or-different job, reverse extension considered, 5 rules weighed, stage gate, hero bar, reorder plan, parent-product split written), then fewer SKUs launch that later strain the brand or the balance sheet.

signal.check: A new SKU is being approved with no structured run through the line extension and architecture checklist.

risk.note: A review step before commitment.

prerequisites: A proposed new SKU
steps: Run the shopping-list test on the current name.
Classify same job or different job for the new SKU.
Confirm a reverse extension was considered first.
Weigh the 5 rules of the road together.
Complete the stage gate: size of prize, MOQ, margin, lead time, channel, anchor customer.
Check the hero SKU has reached its own revenue bar.
Write the parent-vs-product ownership split and the reorder-curve monitoring plan.

test.method: Complete the checklist with the founder before committing to a manufacturer.
test.measure: Number of checklist rows passed out of 8.

title: Treat a logo refresh alone as an incomplete brand change
hypothesis: If a brand refresh also updates the PDP template, packaging insert and shipping confirmation email, not only the logo, then the brand actually changes for the customer, because a logo swap alone leaves every other touchpoint unchanged.

signal.check: A planned brand refresh scopes only the logo, with no update planned for the PDP template, packaging insert, or shipping confirmation email.

risk.note: A scoping change before work begins.

steps: List every customer touchpoint: logo, PDP template, packaging insert, shipping and order emails.
Confirm the refresh plan updates more than just the logo.
Keep the logo as long as the name stays the same, unless a real trigger (R84) exists; do not over-invest in redesigning it repeatedly.

test.method: Review the refresh scope document for touchpoint coverage before work begins.
test.measure: Number of touchpoints included beyond the logo.

title: Audit every brand element against navigation, reassurance and engagement jobs
hypothesis: If we check every identity element (logo, colour, packaging, copy) against whether it helps the brand stand out, validate the choice, or build identification, then gaps in the system become specific and fixable instead of vague.

signal.check: An identity audit has never checked elements against the 3 customer jobs of standing out, validating the choice, and building identification.

risk.note: An audit exercise.

steps: List every core identity element: logo, colour, packaging, key copy lines.
Score each element on navigation (does it stand out), reassurance (does it validate the choice), and engagement (does it build identification).
Flag any element scoring weak on all 3 for redesign priority.

test.method: Run the 3-job scoring with 2 or more reviewers.
test.measure: Number of elements flagged weak on all 3 jobs.

title: Design marks for shape-first, colour-second, words-last recognition at small sizes
hypothesis: If the mark is cleaned until shape and colour alone identify it at favicon and thumbnail size, then the brand is recognisable even before words are legible, because the mind reads shape first, colour second, and words last.

signal.check: The current logo relies on the wordmark or fine detail to be recognisable, and fails to register at favicon or thumbnail size with shape and colour alone.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a perception claim, no controlled study cited

risk.note: A design iteration; earlier logo can be kept during testing.

steps: Shrink the current mark to favicon and app-icon size.
Ask if shape and colour alone still identify the brand without reading any text.
If not, simplify the mark's shape until it does, before any colour or type refinement.

test.method: Show the shrunk mark to people unfamiliar with recent changes and ask what brand it is.
test.measure: Recognition rate at small size.

title: Match the mark type to what the brand can actually afford to teach
hypothesis: If an unknown brand chooses a pictorial, descriptive, wordmark or letterform mark instead of an abstract mark or mascot, then the mark carries meaning from day 1 without needing years of paid education spend.
does_not_apply_when: The brand has an ongoing budget dedicated to teaching an abstract mark's meaning over years

signal.check: A new, unknown brand is choosing an abstract mark or a mascot with no dedicated multi-year budget to teach its meaning.

risk.note: Choosing the wrong mark type can waste design spend that needs redoing later.

steps: Classify the proposed mark as pictorial, descriptive, wordmark, letterform, abstract, or mascot.
Check whether a dedicated multi-year teaching budget exists for an abstract mark or mascot.
If no such budget exists, choose a pictorial, descriptive, wordmark, or letterform mark instead.

test.method: Review the mark type choice against the marketing budget plan.
test.measure: Whether the chosen type matches the available teaching budget.

title: Score every logo candidate on 9 functional criteria before arguing aesthetics
hypothesis: If we score every logo candidate on bold, recognisable, consistent, persona, protectable, enduring, cross-media, black and white, and colour before debating taste, then the approval process stops being purely subjective.

signal.check: Logo approval discussions are based on personal taste with no structured scoring against the 9 functional criteria.

risk.note: A scoring exercise before final approval.

prerequisites: Logo candidates
steps: Score each candidate 1 to 5 on all 9 criteria: bold, recognisable, consistent, persona, protectable, enduring, cross-media, black and white, colour.
Discuss and resolve any candidate that fails more than 1 criterion before aesthetics are debated.
Only compare finalists on taste once all pass the functional score.

test.method: Run the 9-criteria scoring sheet with the decision-making group.
test.measure: Number of candidates passing all 9 criteria.

title: Check every symbol and colour choice against its real cultural reading in each selling market
hypothesis: If we check every candidate symbol, motif, or colour against its actual cultural reading in each selling market, then the brand avoids an unintended offensive or unlucky association that undermines trust.

signal.check: A symbol, motif, or colour choice for the mark or packaging has not been checked against its cultural reading in every market the brand sells into.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named cases only (a clover leaf dropped for its Irish reading; black connoting death in China)

risk.note: An uncaught wrong-culture reading can cause real reputational damage before it is fixed.

prerequisites: List of every selling country and market
steps: Decide the feeling the symbol or colour should evoke first.
Rule out category cliches.
Check each candidate's actual cultural reading in every selling market with a web check.
Drop any candidate with a mismatched or negative reading in any market.

test.method: Run a web check on symbol and colour readings for every selling market before finalising.
test.measure: Number of candidates dropped for a mismatched reading.
test.read_point: Before the mark or packaging symbol is finalised

title: Explore 3 genuinely distinct creative directions before any custom design work
hypothesis: If we build 3 genuinely distinct mood boards or stylescapes and merge the best elements, then the final identity direction is chosen from real options instead of the first idea anyone liked.

signal.check: Identity design work jumped straight to 1 direction, with no 3 distinct options built and scored against the written values first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 single-operator practices, not a tested optimum

risk.note: An exploration phase before commitment; skip only when time or budget truly does not allow it.

prerequisites: A written brand strategy and values (BRD-065)
steps: Build 3 genuinely distinct mood boards or stylescapes across key touchpoints.
Score each on team resonance and fit to the written values.
Ask which elements to borrow across directions.
Merge into 1 locked direction rather than picking 1 outright.

test.method: Present all 3 directions to the decision group and score against the values checklist.
test.measure: Score spread and elements merged into the final direction.

title: Anchor the palette on 1 core colour plus a small accent set, checked on print and screen
hypothesis: If the palette has 1 memorable anchor colour and a small accent set validated on both print and screen, then the brand reads consistently across packaging and site instead of a flat palette with no hierarchy.

signal.check: The current palette has multiple colours treated as equals with no anchor, or was approved on screen only with no print check.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no accessibility threshold given by the source

risk.note: A palette refinement, reversible.

steps: Pick 1 memorable colour as the anchor.
Choose a small set of accent colours that support, not compete with, the anchor.
Review swatches across multiple sessions on both print proofs and screen.
Add a contrast check against WCAG guidance since no source in this playbook gives a threshold.

test.method: Review the palette on both a printed proof and a screen mockup.
test.measure: Consistency of the anchor colour appearance across both media.

title: Assign typography by job and test pairings on real sample pages before committing
hypothesis: If typefaces are assigned by the job the copy does (header, body, technical, decorative) and tested on real pages with images and buttons, then the type system holds up in practice, not just on a specimen sheet.

signal.check: Typography was chosen from a font specimen alone, with no test on real sample pages containing actual images and buttons.

risk.note: A design refinement step.

steps: Assign a typeface to each job: header, body, technical or spec copy, and any decorative face.
Test the pairing in a specimen first.
Then test on at least 2 real sample pages with real images and buttons.
Restrict any decorative face to selective use to avoid dilution.

test.method: Review the 2 real sample pages with the design team before committing to the type system.
test.measure: Legibility and consistency across the sample pages.
test.read_point: Before the type system is locked

title: Write photography rules with reference images; use real photos where accuracy matters
hypothesis: If photography is briefed with a short list of explicit constraints and reference images, and real product photos are used wherever colour, size or texture matters, then shot selection and UGC curation stay consistent and accurate.

signal.check: Photography or UGC selection has no written constraint list with reference images, and generated or heavily graded images are used where product colour or texture accuracy matters.

risk.note: Using inaccurate product imagery risks returns and complaints once the real product arrives.

steps: Write 3 to 5 explicit photography constraints (light, tone, scene, people) with reference images.
Check every shot or UGC selection against the written constraints.
Replace any generated or heavily graded image with a colour-accurate real product photo wherever accuracy matters (packaging, PDP hero, size or texture claims).

test.method: Audit current PDP and packaging imagery against the written constraints and the real-photo rule.
test.measure: Number of images replaced for accuracy.
test.read_point: One-time audit, then on every new shoot

title: Put the identity's best execution on the one touchpoint that decides the purchase
hypothesis: If identity budget concentrates on the single touchpoint that actually decides the purchase (packaging for a physical product, the PDP for a site-first brand), then limited design resources move the needle instead of spreading thin.

signal.check: Identity effort is spread evenly across every touchpoint with no named decisive touchpoint getting priority investment.

risk.note: A prioritisation decision.

steps: Name the 1 touchpoint that actually decides the purchase (packaging, PDP, menu, interface).
Direct the best design execution and review time to that touchpoint first.
Revisit which touchpoint is decisive as the business or channel mix changes.

test.method: Compare design review time spent on the decisive touchpoint versus others.
test.measure: Share of design hours on the decisive touchpoint.

title: Apply the locked asset kit to the decisive touchpoint first as the proof point
hypothesis: If the locked identity kit is applied to the decisive touchpoint first, then any problem with the direction shows up early, because a mismatch there means revisiting the creative direction, not just the layout.

signal.check: The identity kit is being rolled out to secondary touchpoints before the single decisive touchpoint has a first proof built and reviewed.

risk.note: A sequencing decision.

prerequisites: Decisive touchpoint named (BRD-114)
Locked identity kit
steps: Apply the identity kit to the decisive touchpoint (label and pack for a physical product; sitemap then 2 placeholder pages for a site-first brand).
Review the first proof; if it feels off, revisit the creative direction, not the layout.
Only roll out to secondary touchpoints after the first proof passes review.

test.method: Review the first proof with the founder and at least 1 outside reader.
test.measure: Pass or fail on the first-proof review.

title: Design the launch identity to scale: write what the parent owns and what each product owns
hypothesis: If the launch identity kit clearly separates what the parent brand owns from what each product owns, then new SKUs can reuse the kit without a full redesign each time.

signal.check: The current identity kit has no written split between parent-owned elements (values, type, palette, seal) and product-owned elements (flavour name, accent), so every new SKU needs a fresh design pass.

risk.note: A documentation exercise.

prerequisites: A locked identity kit
steps: List every identity element and mark it as parent-owned or product-owned.
Write the rule for how a new SKU applies its product-owned elements onto the parent kit.
Test the split by mocking up 1 hypothetical new SKU using only the written rule.

test.method: Have someone outside the original design team build a mock new-SKU pack using only the written split.
test.measure: Whether they can complete it without needing new parent-level decisions.

title: Define brand coherence as one voice and quality, not rigid rules that block creativity
hypothesis: If coherence is defined as one voice, one strategy and uniform quality rather than a rigid rulebook, then the team can adapt creatively without breaking the brand, because over-enforcement kills the creativity the brand needs.

signal.check: Brand guidelines are being enforced so rigidly that new creative ideas are rejected for minor deviations, or so loosely that touchpoints read as different companies.

risk.note: A governance adjustment.

prerequisites: Brand guidelines document
steps: Review recent creative rejections for whether they broke the voice and strategy, or just a minor visual rule.
If a contained alter-ego visual layer would let a team experiment without breaking the core system, name and define it separately.
Update guidelines to focus enforcement on voice, strategy and quality, not every visual detail.

test.method: Compare creative rejection reasons before and after the guideline adjustment.
test.measure: Share of rejections tied to voice or strategy versus minor visual rules.

title: Set a default brand voice until a real voice sheet exists
hypothesis: If we set a default voice (professional not corporate, friendly not fake, no jargon, specs available for research-heavy buyers) before a full voice sheet exists, then copy stays consistent even before the fuller document is built.

signal.check: No brand voice sheet exists yet, and copywriters are each choosing their own tone with no shared default.

risk.note: A written default, easy to update once a full voice sheet exists.

steps: Write the default voice: professional not corporate, friendly not fake, no jargon or buzzwords.
Add the rule that technical specs stay available for research-heavy buyers, not deleted for tone.
Apply the reading-level rule (below tenth grade) alongside the voice default.
Share the default with every copywriter until the full voice sheet (BRD-127) is built.

test.method: Review a sample of recent copy against the default voice statement.
test.measure: Consistency of tone across samples.
test.read_point: After the default is shared, on the next batch of copy

title: Keep every asset on message: nomenclature, taglines, and key messages consistent everywhere
hypothesis: If nomenclature, taglines, descriptors and key messages stay identical across site, PDP, ads, email, support scripts and packaging, then customers can guess the whole brand from any 1 touchpoint, because inconsistent language across assets reads as multiple companies.

signal.check: More than 1 person writes brand copy, and no shared reference exists for nomenclature, taglines, or key messages, so wording drifts between site, ads, email and support.

risk.note: A documentation and process fix.

steps: Write a shared reference sheet: nomenclature, taglines, descriptors, key messages (1 big idea, up to 3), vocabulary to use and avoid.
Share the sheet with everyone who writes brand copy, including support.
Spot-check site, PDP, ads, email and support scripts for drift from the sheet.

test.method: Spot-check 5 assets across different channels for wording consistency.
test.measure: Number of inconsistencies found.
test.read_point: Monthly for the first quarter after the sheet ships

title: Make every ad or PDP one a stranger can infer the brand's position from alone
hypothesis: If a stranger can infer the brand's position from an ad or PDP alone, then the execution is doing the strategy's job, because clever creative that obscures the position fails even if it entertains.

signal.check: A recent ad or PDP is clever or stylish but a stranger cannot say what the brand's position is after seeing it.

risk.note: A creative review step.

prerequisites: A written positioning statement
steps: Show the ad or PDP to someone unfamiliar with the brand for 5 seconds.
Ask them to state what the brand stands for and what makes it different.
If they cannot, simplify the creative until it restates the strategy clearly.

test.method: Run the 5-second stranger test on every major new ad or PDP before it ships.
test.measure: Share of test viewers who correctly infer the position.

title: Package the identity as a 4-part brand book: logo, visual language, language rules, expressions
hypothesis: If the identity is packaged as 1 document with logo rules, visual language, language rules, and brand expressions, then a new designer, writer, or agent can work from it without re-deciding basics.

signal.check: Identity decisions exist scattered across files, chats, and 1 person's memory, with no single packaged brand book.

risk.note: A documentation project.

prerequisites: A locked identity kit and finalised strategy
steps: Write the logo usage section: variants, clear space, minimum size, misuse examples.
Write the visual language section: type by job, colour values, photography constraints.
Write the language rules section with ready messaging samples for PDP, ad, email and support.
Write a brand expressions section labelled as thought starters, not final.

test.method: Have someone outside the core team use only the brand book to build 1 new asset.
test.measure: Whether they can complete it without asking a basic question already answered in the book.
test.read_point: After the brand book is drafted

title: Measure a rebrand by shipped artifacts, not strategy documents, and budget the last 10 percent
hypothesis: If rebrand progress is tracked by shipped artifacts (guidelines, site, packaging, content capability, product) instead of strategy documents alone, then the project is not declared done before it actually changes what customers see.

signal.check: A rebrand's progress reports cite completed strategy documents as done, with no tracking of what has actually shipped to customers.

expected_effect.size: 1 case reports about 4 months to first deliverables, with the last 10 percent taking the most time

risk.note: A reporting change.

steps: List the concrete shipped artifacts a rebrand must produce: guidelines, live site, packaging, content capability, next product.
Track progress against shipped artifacts, not documents.
Budget disproportionate time and resources for the last 10 percent of rollout.

test.method: Report rebrand status monthly against the shipped-artifact list.
test.measure: Number of artifacts shipped versus planned.

title: Keep name, price, symbols and colour fixed across markets, adapt only taste and ritual
hypothesis: If we keep name, product, price, function, symbols, colour and sound fixed across markets and only adapt taste, humour, aspiration and ritual meaning, then expansion into a new market stays recognisably the same brand while still fitting local culture.

signal.check: Entry into a second selling market is changing core elements (name, price structure, symbols, colour) instead of only adapting taste, humour, and ritual meaning.

risk.note: Changing fixed elements per market risks brand fragmentation.

prerequisites: A native expert or reviewer for the new market
steps: List which elements are fixed (name, product, price, function, symbols, colour, sound) and confirm they stay the same in the new market.
List which elements can adapt (taste, humour, aspiration, ritual meaning).
Include a native expert in the review and test adapted elements before launch.

test.method: Have a native expert review the adaptation plan before launch in the new market.
test.measure: Number of fixed elements accidentally changed, caught before launch.

title: Only invest in a mascot if it carries real brand meaning and has a redraw budget
hypothesis: If a mascot proposal is only approved when it expresses real brand attributes, carries a voice, and has a dedicated redraw budget, then the store avoids sinking money into a character that ages badly and gets abandoned.

signal.check: A mascot or character is being proposed with no clear connection to real brand attributes, no defined voice, and no budget set aside for periodic redrawing.

risk.note: A gate before spend commits; the mascot itself, once launched, is harder to retire cleanly.

steps: Write which specific brand attribute the mascot expresses.
Define the mascot's voice in 1 to 2 sentences.
Confirm a redraw budget exists for future refreshes.
Reject the proposal if any of the 3 is missing.

test.method: Review the mascot proposal against the 3-part gate before approving design spend.
test.measure: Whether all 3 gate items are documented.

title: Disclose commercial relationships in content and write the crisis plan before it is needed
hypothesis: If sponsored or gifted content discloses the relationship where the reader meets it, and a crisis plan exists before a crisis happens, then the brand avoids both a disclosure violation and a scramble during a real incident.

signal.check: Sponsored, gifted, or affiliate content is not disclosed where the reader first sees it, or no written crisis plan (who declares, first statements) exists yet.

risk.note: Non-disclosure carries regulatory risk; an absent crisis plan risks a slow, damaging response during a real incident.

prerequisites: Current disclosure rules for each selling country from a web check
steps: Add disclosure language where the reader meets the content, not buried in a bio.
Do not delete negative comments; respond instead.
Write who declares a crisis and draft the first 3 statements in advance.
Check current disclosure rules per selling country with a web check.

test.method: Audit recent sponsored content for disclosure placement.
test.measure: Share of sponsored content with proper disclosure.

title: Walk the full funnel and mark each touchpoint functional or experiential
hypothesis: If we walk the whole funnel (search result, PDP, cart, checkout, shipping email, unboxing, support) and mark each touchpoint functional or experiential, then gaps beyond the single decisive touchpoint get found and fixed too.

signal.check: Brand consistency review has only ever covered the PDP and ads, with no check of cart, checkout, shipping email, unboxing, or support against the brand promise.

risk.note: An audit exercise.

steps: List every step of the funnel: search result, PDP, cart, checkout, shipping email, unboxing, support.
Mark each touchpoint functional (it just needs to work) or experiential (it should carry the brand).
Flag any experiential touchpoint that currently has no connection to the brand promise.

test.method: Run the full-funnel walk with a team member unfamiliar with recent brand changes.
test.measure: Number of touchpoints flagged with no brand connection.

title: Write the returns and exchange policy as a brand trust signal, not just an ops page
hypothesis: If the returns and exchange policy is written to match the brand's promise and tone, then it reinforces trust instead of contradicting it, because a policy that reads as cold or restrictive breaks the brand's other claims.

signal.check: The returns or exchange policy page reads as a plain legal or operations document with no connection to the brand's voice or promise.

risk.note: A copy rewrite of an existing page.

prerequisites: Brand voice default or voice sheet
steps: Read the current returns and exchange policy for tone.
Check the policy's actual terms match the brand's stated promise; do not just reword a policy that contradicts it.
Rewrite the page in the brand's voice, keeping all legal terms accurate.

test.method: A/B the rewritten returns page against the current version for perceived trust.
test.measure: Review mentions of the returns experience.

title: Apply the identity kit to marketplace brand pages with the same voice and visual rules as the site
hypothesis: If the marketplace brand page and buy-box content follow the same identity kit and voice rules as the site, then shoppers see 1 consistent brand across every channel, not a weaker, off-brand version on marketplaces.

signal.check: The Amazon A+ content, Flipkart brand store, or other marketplace brand page uses different visuals, tone, or messaging than the main site.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A content update on the marketplace page.

prerequisites: A locked identity kit and voice sheet
steps: Audit the current marketplace brand page against the site's identity kit and voice.
Update imagery, colour, and copy to match the kit.
Coordinate account-level mechanics with the team handling marketplace deployment.

test.method: Compare marketplace page conversion before and after the identity update.
test.measure: cvr_overall on the marketplace listing.

title: Design the hero and buy button for mobile thumb reach with local trust signals
hypothesis: If the hero and buy button are placed for thumb reach on mobile, with local trust signals like cash-on-delivery or payment badges added for the relevant market, then mobile-first shoppers convert with fewer taps and less hesitation.

signal.check: The buy button and key trust badges sit outside easy thumb reach on mobile, and no market-specific trust signal (COD badge, local payment logos, festival timing) is shown.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no library source, verify against brand data before use

risk.note: A layout and content change, reversible.

prerequisites: Mobile analytics on tap patterns
steps: Check the buy button position against typical mobile thumb-reach zones.
Add the local trust signal relevant to the market: COD and payment-trust badges for India, or the local equivalents for other markets.
Test around local demand timing (festival season, holidays) where relevant.

test.method: A/B the thumb-optimised layout with local trust signals against the current layout.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart and cvr_checkout_to_order on mobile.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 mobile sessions per arm

title: Run the identity system audit checklist before locking any new identity kit
hypothesis: If a new identity kit passes the full 16-point identity system audit (strategy first, small-size test, 9 criteria, cultural reading, cliche check, palette, type, photography, coherence, flexibility, decisive touchpoint, sellout, equity kept), then it launches with fewer avoidable gaps.

signal.check: A new or refreshed identity kit is about to launch with no structured run through the identity system audit checklist.

risk.note: A review step before launch.

prerequisites: A drafted identity kit
steps: Confirm strategy was written before visuals.
Run the small-size test and the 9 functional mark criteria.
Check cultural readings and category cliches.
Review the palette structure and typography testing.
Confirm photography rules and the real-photo rule are followed.
Check touchpoint coherence and flexibility for the next SKU.
Confirm equity was kept where it already worked.

test.method: Complete checklist 5.3 with a second reviewer before the kit is locked.
test.measure: Number of rows passed out of 16.
test.read_point: Before the identity kit is finalised

title: Run the brand guideline completeness checklist before calling guidelines finished
hypothesis: If brand guidelines are checked against the full completeness list (positioning, values, worldview, logo rules, visual language, language rules, voice sheet, claims register, architecture rule, disclosure, governance) before shipping, then a new hire or agent has no gaps to guess at.

signal.check: Brand guidelines exist but have never been checked against a completeness list, and gaps (missing voice sheet, no claims register, no disclosure section) are only found when someone asks a question they can't be answered.

risk.note: A review step.

prerequisites: A drafted brand guidelines document
steps: Check each section exists: positioning, values, worldview, logo usage, visual language, language rules, voice sheet, claims register, architecture rule, market variants, disclosure and crisis, governance.
Mark any missing section and assign an owner to write it.
Confirm the guidelines document itself reads below tenth grade.

test.method: Complete checklist 5.4 against the guidelines document.
test.measure: Number of sections present out of the full list.

title: Run the PDP and ad brand-consistency check before any asset ships
hypothesis: If every PDP, hero, or ad passes the 15-point brand-consistency check (position inferable, promise present, voice compliance, claims verified, no competitor assets, disclosure) before shipping, then off-brand or risky assets get caught before spend, not after.

signal.check: New PDPs, heroes, or ads ship with no structured brand-consistency review, relying only on 1 person's final look.

risk.note: A pre-launch review step.

prerequisites: A written positioning statement and voice sheet
steps: Show the asset to someone unfamiliar for 5 seconds and check the position is inferable.
Check the promise, voice compliance, and claims against the brand record.
Check for competitor marks, category cliches, fake scarcity, and disclosure gaps.
Compare the story against packaging and email for drift.
Fix or reject the asset before it ships if any row fails.

test.method: Complete checklist 5.5 for every major new PDP, hero, or ad.
test.measure: Number of rows passed out of 15.

title: Run a compressed identity and guideline sprint for a small brand with no agency
hypothesis: If a small brand with no agency runs a compressed 5 to 6 week sequence (positioning, brief, naming, identity, guidelines) instead of trying to do everything at once, then a complete, usable brand foundation gets built without a full agency budget.

signal.check: A small brand needs a full positioning, name, identity and guideline set, with no agency budget and no clear plan for sequencing the work.

expected_effect.size: unknown; not independently tested at small scale by the source, only 1 close case

risk.note: A staged plan; each week's output is versioned before moving on.

prerequisites: 1 or 2 people who can dedicate 5 to 6 weeks
steps: Week 1: run the positioning program using reviews, support tickets and search terms as a proxy for interviews.
Week 1 to 2: run the brand strategy workshop in a single working document, skipping a paid facilitator but getting 1 outside reader.
Week 2 to 3: run the compressed naming process with 3 lenses, a solo generation routine, and legal checks before any finalist is shown.
Week 3 to 5: build the identity with a wordmark or simple mark, 3 mood boards, and a first proof on the decisive touchpoint.
Week 5 to 6: write a 6 to 10 page guideline document plus the voice sheet and claims register.
Default to 1 master brand and skip abstract marks, mascots, and multi-market adaptation until genuinely needed.

test.method: Check off each week's deliverable against the plan and get founder sign-off at each stage.
test.measure: Weeks completed on schedule and deliverables signed off.

title: Run the full identity system build sequence for marks, colour, type and packaging
hypothesis: If the identity build follows the full sequence (equity audit, references, 3 directions, mark, typography, colour, photography, first proof, parent-product split) in order, then the resulting kit holds together instead of being assembled piecemeal.

signal.check: Identity elements (mark, colour, type, photography) are being decided independently by different people with no shared sequence or equity audit first.

risk.note: A build project; earlier assets stay usable until the new kit passes review.

prerequisites: The written brand brief (BRD-065)
The decisive touchpoint named (BRD-114)
steps: Audit existing assets for equity: keep, refine, or replace.
Gather visual references broadly, including for the decisive touchpoint.
Build and merge 3 distinct creative directions.
Decide the mark type, sketch in volume, and check cultural readings.
Vectorise the mark and clear the 9 functional criteria.
Assign typography by job and test on real sample pages.
Set the anchor colour and accents, checked on print and screen.
Write photography rules and assemble the full asset kit, then run the first proof on the decisive touchpoint.

test.method: Run checklist 5.3 on the completed kit before it ships.
test.measure: Checklist pass rate.

title: Run the full rebrand sequence for a business that already sells
hypothesis: If a rebrand for an already-selling business follows Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver in sequence with named owners, then the project produces real artifacts on a realistic timeline instead of stalling in open-ended discussion.

signal.check: A rebrand project for an existing business has no clear phase structure, owners, or artifact list, and risks running indefinitely on strategy discussion.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 case reports about 4 months to first deliverables

risk.note: A staged project; the logo and name audit happens first, so most work can revert to visuals while keeping the strategy.

prerequisites: Business goals in writing
Several weeks for research
steps: Discover: assemble the team plus an outside facilitator; gather data; run interviews; build personas; map the XY map.
Define: synthesise into named themes, decide what to discontinue, write how-might-we challenges.
Develop: run the identity build with the website or decisive touchpoint as the forcing function.
Deliver: ship guidelines, site, packaging, and content capability, budgeting extra time for the last 10 percent.

test.method: Track artifacts shipped per phase against the plan.
test.measure: Artifacts delivered per phase versus planned.
test.read_point: At the end of each phase

title: Run the full brand guidelines and voice sheet build once strategy and identity are settled
hypothesis: If the guideline build follows the full sequence (strategy page, logo usage, visual language, language rules, voice sheet, claims register, governance, market variants) in order, then the resulting document is genuinely complete instead of missing a section someone later needs.

signal.check: Brand guidelines are being drafted ad hoc, with sections added as someone happens to ask for them rather than following a complete structure.

risk.note: A documentation project.

prerequisites: Brand brief (BRD-065)
Identity kit (BRD-134)
steps: Write the strategy page: positioning, promise, values, worldview, tension, enemy.
Write logo usage and the visual language section.
Write language rules with ready messaging samples.
Write the voice sheet: poles, reading level, banned words, before-and-after rewrites.
Write the claims register and the governance section: approvers, disclosure, crisis lines.
Write market variants if selling into more than 1 country.
Run checklist 5.4 against the finished document.

test.method: Run checklist 5.4 and get founder sign-off.
test.measure: Checklist pass rate.

title: Weight order data, repeat rate and search terms over survey answers when they disagree
hypothesis: If we weight what customers actually do (orders, repeat rate, search terms) over what they say in a survey when the two disagree, then product, stocking and ad decisions rest on more reliable signal, because stated preference and revealed behaviour can diverge.

signal.check: A product, stocking, or ad decision is being made from survey or focus group answers alone, with no check against order data, repeat rate, or search terms.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the underlying neuroscience claim is disputed and should not be quoted externally

risk.note: A decision-input change, not a live asset.

prerequisites: Order, repeat rate, and search term data
steps: When survey or interview answers conflict with order data, repeat rate, or search terms, treat the behavioural data as the stronger signal.
Check any high comprehension score in name or copy testing is not being mistaken for real differentiation.
Document which data source drove the final decision.

test.method: Compare survey-stated preference against actual repeat purchase behaviour for the same segment.
test.measure: Correlation or divergence between stated and revealed preference.
test.read_point: After the next research and behavioural data cycle

title: Never quote the 90 percent unconscious or the over-50-percent decision figure on a client page
hypothesis: If we remove the 90 percent unconscious and over-50-percent point-of-sale figures from any client-facing material, then the brand avoids repeating a disputed, unmeasured claim as fact.

signal.check: Marketing or strategy material cites the 90 percent unconscious or the over-50-percent point-of-sale decision figure as an established fact.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the figures are unsourced or have a disputed method

risk.note: Repeating a disputed statistic risks credibility if challenged publicly.

steps: Search all current client-facing material for either figure.
Remove or replace with a properly sourced, current statistic if one exists.
Run a web check on post-2008 critiques of the source before using any of its figures again.

test.method: Audit current materials for the 2 disputed figures.
test.measure: Number of instances found and removed.

title: Test a distinctive signature moment for recall in a commodity-like, hard-to-differentiate category
hypothesis: If a commodity-like product tests a distinctive, repeated packaging quirk or signature moment, then it may build recall faster than a features list, but only if repeated consistently over time.
does_not_apply_when: The product already has strong feature-based differentiation

signal.check: The product competes in a category where features are hard to differentiate, and no distinctive, repeatable signature moment exists in packaging or content.

expected_effect.size: unknown; small-sample or client-reported cases only (Andrex puppy, Blendtec's Will It Blend)

risk.note: A test, not a full commitment; drop if it does not build recall over time.

steps: Identify 1 candidate signature moment (a packaging quirk, an unboxing detail, a repeated content format).
Repeat it consistently across at least 3 to 6 months of content and packaging.
Test brand recall with and without exposure to the signature moment.

test.method: Survey a small panel exposed versus not exposed to the signature moment for recall.
test.measure: Recall rate difference between groups.
test.read_point: After 3 to 6 months of consistent repetition

title: Test a designed first-use ritual or replenishment cue for repeat-purchase categories
hypothesis: If a repeat-purchase product adds a designed first-use sequence or replenishment cue, then repeat rate may improve, because an attached ritual can make a product stickier and a ritual can be engineered, not only discovered.

signal.check: A repeat-purchase product has no designed first-use sequence, unboxing order, or replenishment cue beyond basic instructions.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases only (Corona and lime, Guinness's timed pour, Oreo dunking), no controlled test given

risk.note: A packaging and onboarding addition, easy to test and revert.

steps: Design 1 specific first-use sequence or replenishment cue tied to the product (an order of use, a timing detail, a small ritual step).
Add it to packaging inserts or onboarding emails.
Compare repeat rate for customers exposed to the ritual versus those who are not.

test.method: A/B the ritual-style onboarding against the current plain instructions.
test.measure: repeat_rate_90d for each group.

title: Prioritise POV demo content over static feature shots for PDP video and UGC
hypothesis: If PDP video and UGC prioritise first-person point-of-view demos over static feature shots, then conversion may improve, because watching someone use a product may sell by imitation rather than only information.

signal.check: The PDP and ad creative library is mostly static feature shots, with no first-person point-of-view demo or unboxing content.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the mechanism (mirror neuron claim) is unproven at brand scale

risk.note: A creative test.

steps: Produce 1 POV demo or unboxing video for a top PDP.
Place it above the fold alongside or instead of the static feature shot.
Compare PDP-to-cart conversion for sessions that view the video versus those that see only static images.

test.method: A/B the POV video against the static image set on the same PDP.
test.measure: cvr_pdp_to_cart.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Test packaging and PDP colour choices for recall and price perception with a standard A/B test
hypothesis: If packaging or PDP colour choices are tested with a standard A/B method instead of chosen on instinct, then the store gets real evidence for a claim that colour can shift recall and price perception.

signal.check: A major colour decision for packaging, the PDP hero, or site theming was made on instinct with no A/B test of the alternatives.

expected_effect.size: unknown; the cited effect sizes (a Tiffany-blue test, a Heinz green ketchup sales run) are single-brand cases, not general figures

risk.note: A design test.

steps: Identify 2 candidate colour options for the packaging or PDP hero.
Run a standard A/B test of the 2 options on the PDP or ad creative.
Measure conversion and any price perception signal (add-to-cart rate at the current price).

test.method: A/B the 2 colour variants on the PDP hero or packaging image.
test.measure: cvr_overall and aov.
test.read_point: After 2 weeks or 1,000 sessions per arm

title: Run the smashable-logo recognition test only for an established brand, not a new one
hypothesis: If an established brand tests recognition from a packaging fragment with the logo covered, then it learns whether recognition depends only on the logo, but this test does not apply to a new or low-awareness brand with no code yet to be free of.
does_not_apply_when: The brand is new or not yet recognised beyond the logo (a first collection has no code to be free of)

signal.check: An established brand's recognition has never been tested at the packaging or asset level with the logo covered.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited case (Silk Cut) is not independently verified

risk.note: A test, not a redesign commitment.

prerequisites: An established brand with a recognisable visual code beyond the logo
steps: Cover the logo on a packaging or ad fragment.
Show it to people familiar with the category and ask if they can identify the brand.
If recognition is low, this is not a requirement for a new brand; use it only as an aspiration for later.

test.method: Show the logo-covered fragment to 10 or more people familiar with the category.
test.measure: Correct identification rate.
test.read_point: When testing an established brand's visual equity

title: Test congruent sensory pairings before adding a scent, sound or texture element
hypothesis: If a proposed scent, sound, or texture addition is tested for congruence with the existing visual before scaling it, then only pairings that score above either element alone get adopted, avoiding a mismatched addition that could hurt perception.

signal.check: A scent insert, notification sound, or texture change is being added to packaging or media with no test of whether it pairs well with the existing visual.
