expected_effect.size: unknown; a small commissioned study (20 subjects, 9-point scale), treat as a panel read, not a finding

risk.note: A small panel test before a packaging or media commitment.

prerequisites: The candidate sensory element and the current visual
steps: Present the visual alone to a small panel and record pleasantness.
Present the sensory element alone and record pleasantness.
Present them together, plus a deliberately mismatched pairing, and record both.
Adopt only a congruent pairing that scores above either element alone.

test.method: Run the 4-step panel test with at least 10 to 20 people.
test.measure: Pleasantness score for visual alone, element alone, congruent pair, and mismatched pair.

title: Test packaging weight and touch for a quality signal independent of function
hypothesis: If packaging weight and touch are tested for perceived quality independent of the actual product function, then a premium claim can be backed by a felt cue, not just a visual one.

signal.check: Packaging weight and material feel have never been tested for perceived quality against the store's premium claim.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited case (a lighter remote judged broken by 100 consumers)

risk.note: A packaging test, reversible before a full production run.

steps: Test 2 packaging weight or material options with a small consumer panel.
Ask panel members to rate perceived quality for each option, without other context.
Choose the option that best matches the store's stated premium claim.

test.method: Run a blind touch test with 10 or more consumers comparing 2 packaging options.
test.measure: Perceived quality score per option.

title: Test brand recall by creative variant before using a sexual or shock hook
lever: sexual or shock creative recall test
hypothesis: If any sexual or shock ad hook is tested for brand recall by variant before scaling, then the store avoids a hook that drives attention but suppresses recall of the brand itself.

signal.check: An ad or PDP image uses sexual or shock content to drive attention, with no test of whether viewers actually remember the brand afterward.

expected_effect.size: 1 cited eye-tracking study of 400 subjects reports recall falling to 9.8 percent versus about 20 percent for men, and 10.85 percent versus 22.3 percent for women, with sexual or shock creative

risk.note: Sexual or shock creative carries reputational and platform-policy risk beyond the recall question.

steps: Identify any current or proposed creative using sexual or shock content.
Test brand recall (not just clicks) for that creative against a non-sexual, non-shock variant.
Drop the sexual or shock variant if it underperforms on recall, even if it wins on clicks.

test.method: Survey exposed viewers on brand recall for both variants.
test.measure: other:brand_recall_score per variant.
test.read_point: After the ad set reaches sufficient reach for a recall survey, typically 10,000-plus impressions per variant

title: Check any co-brand or sponsorship placement for narrative fit before running it
hypothesis: If a sponsorship or co-brand placement is checked for whether the brand is load-bearing in the story, not passive wallpaper, then the placement lifts recall instead of being suppressed by a stronger co-brand or an unwanted association.

signal.check: A sponsorship, collab, or shared-media placement is planned with no check of whether the brand plays a real, load-bearing role in the story, or what association appearing there teaches.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited case study (an American Idol screen-time study) with about 400 subjects

risk.note: A weak or unwanted association from a placement can be hard to undo once public.

steps: Ask whether the brand is genuinely load-bearing in the sponsorship or placement's story, not just a background logo.
Ask what association appearing next to this partner or content teaches the audience.
Apply a brand-fit veto regardless of the deal's reach or ROI if the association is wrong.

test.method: Review the placement brief against the narrative-fit and association questions before signing.
test.measure: Whether both questions have a clear, positive answer.
test.read_point: Before the sponsorship or placement is confirmed

title: Keep every low-stock or urgency badge tied to the real stock file, never fabricated
hypothesis: If every low-stock or selling-fast badge is generated from the real stock file, then the store avoids the trust and marketplace-policy risk of a fabricated urgency counter.

signal.check: A low-stock, selling-fast, or limited-quantity badge appears on the PDP with no link to the real, current stock file.

risk.note: A fabricated stock counter breaks the no-invented-claims rule and risks a marketplace policy strike.

prerequisites: Real-time or regularly updated stock data
steps: Audit every urgency or low-stock badge currently shown on the site.
Connect each badge to the real, current stock file, not a static or manually set message.
Remove any badge that cannot be tied to real stock data.

test.method: Spot-check live badges against the actual stock count.
test.measure: Number of badges matching real stock data.
test.read_point: One-time audit, then on every new badge

title: Run the 5 steps of marketing in order instead of skipping straight to spreading the word
hypothesis: If the team runs invent, narrow, tell, spread, and persist in order instead of jumping straight to promotion, then acquisition efforts rest on a real product story instead of pushing a message with nothing behind it.

signal.check: The team is focused on step 4 (spreading the word through ads and content) with no clear step 1 through 3 (a real story, a narrow served audience, a matching narrative) done first.

risk.note: A planning check.

steps: Write what is worth making and the story worth telling about it.
Name the few people it particularly benefits.
Write the story to match their existing narrative.
Only after steps 1 to 3, design the conditions for those people to tell others.
Commit to showing up regularly and generously for years, not a single campaign.

test.method: Review the current marketing plan against the 5 steps and flag any skipped.
test.measure: Number of steps completed before spend increases.

title: Build products and messages from the market's own lock, not an internal change story
hypothesis: If the roadmap and positioning start from a real customer lock instead of a grandiose internal change story, then resources go to a fit the market actually wants, because reverse-engineering a story to justify what is already made wastes effort.

signal.check: A new product or campaign is being justified with an internal change narrative that was written after the product was already decided, not from a real customer need.

risk.note: A planning discipline.

prerequisites: Customer language from reviews or support
steps: Write the real customer lock (the specific need or frustration) before writing the product or campaign story.
Check whether the current plan was reverse-engineered from an existing product to justify it.
Reject a grandiose, unresourceable change story in favour of a lock the team can actually address.

test.method: Review the next 3 product or campaign briefs for a documented customer lock.
test.measure: Share of briefs with a real customer lock documented before the solution.

title: Own a permission asset instead of relying only on platform reach
hypothesis: If the brand builds a real owned permission asset (email, SMS, community), then it is not entirely dependent on rented platform reach, because a platform audience can disappear with an algorithm change.

signal.check: Most audience reach comes from platform followers or ad reach, with no growing, engaged email or SMS list of its own.

risk.note: A channel investment, easy to adjust.

steps: Add a clear, low-friction email or SMS capture point to every high-traffic touchpoint.
Move engaged social followers toward the owned list with a real incentive.
Test whether people would notice or ask where the brand went if it stopped posting; that is the real permission test.

test.method: Track list growth rate and engagement before and after adding capture points.
test.measure: list_size and flow_revenue_share.

title: Judge organic content by revenue and owned-audience growth, not views or followers
hypothesis: If organic content is judged by revenue and owned-audience growth instead of views or follower count, then the team stops chasing vanity reach that does not convert.

signal.check: Content success is reported and celebrated using views or follower counts, with no revenue or list-growth metric attached.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named example of 40 million views generating about 200 dollars of sales

risk.note: A reporting change.

steps: Replace views and follower count as the headline metric in content reports.
Add revenue attributed and owned-list growth per content piece.
Review the last quarter's top content by the new metric, not the old one.

test.method: Re-rank the last quarter's content by revenue and list growth instead of views.
test.measure: Correlation between view rank and revenue rank.

title: Set the give-and-ask rule per brand: soft asks in organic, hard CTAs in paid
hypothesis: If organic content defaults to a soft ask (a mention, a link in bio) while hard CTAs live in paid ads, then organic reach is protected while paid still drives direct conversion, unless the store's one-touch purchase path makes a lighter organic CTA the better fit.
does_not_apply_when: The store's purchase path is one-touch and light organic CTAs cost real, measurable sales

signal.check: Every organic post carries a hard sales CTA with no distinction from paid ad messaging, or the reverse: no path to purchase exists anywhere in organic content.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a documented rule, not a general lift figure

risk.note: A content policy, easy to adjust.

steps: Write the default rule: no hard CTA in organic, ask in paid, link in bio.
Check whether the store's one-touch purchase path is an exception that needs a lighter organic CTA.
Record the choice and track paid performance before and after organic ramps to judge it.

test.method: Compare paid performance before and after organic volume increases under the chosen rule.
test.measure: Paid conversion rate and organic engagement.
test.read_point: After 60 days of the rule being applied

title: Give the founder an early-face role with 1 to 3 content themes and a planned handover point
hypothesis: If the founder appears as the early face of the brand with only 1 to 3 content themes and a planned handover point, then founder-led content builds trust without becoming an unmanageable or unbounded commitment.
does_not_apply_when: The founder has decided to remain the permanent public face indefinitely, which is also a valid choice

signal.check: Founder content is unfocused across many themes with no tracked link to customer acquisition, and no discussion of a future handover point exists.

risk.note: A content focus decision.

steps: Pick 1 to 3 themes the founder will consistently cover.
Track which customers arrive via founder content specifically.
Decide and document either a handover date or the decision to stay the face indefinitely.
Apply the same guideline discipline to the founder's personal brand as to the company brand.

test.method: Tag new customers by whether they arrived via founder content.
test.measure: other:founder_attributed_customers as a share of total.

title: Document the brand's day-one journey on video as a marketing and negotiating asset
hypothesis: If the founder documents the brand's early journey on simple video from day one, then the store builds a content archive that later becomes both marketing material and negotiating currency with partners who lack production capability.

signal.check: No video or photo archive of the brand's early journey exists, and the founder has not started casual, regular documentation.

risk.note: A habit, not a live change.

steps: Start recording short, casual video clips of key moments (production, first sale, first setback) using just a phone.
Store the clips in an organised, dated archive.
Reuse archive footage later in founder story content and partner pitches.

test.method: Check the archive folder for content monthly.
test.measure: Number of clips added per month.

title: Pick 1 platform and 1 content format and go all in
hypothesis: If the team commits to 1 platform and 1 content format instead of spreading thin across many, then content quality and consistency improve, because dabbling across platforms rarely builds real traction on any of them.

signal.check: Content effort is spread thin across 3 or more platforms and formats with no single platform getting sustained, consistent focus.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 2 single-operator opinions agree, not a controlled test

risk.note: A focus decision.

prerequisites: A defined buyer segment
steps: Pick the 1 platform and 1 format the team can sustain consistently, based on fit with the buyer, not follower count.
Publish 3 to 4 niche pieces per 1 broader piece, adjusting the ratio based on view-to-buyer data.
Pause effort on other platforms until this 1 shows traction.

test.method: Compare engagement and conversion from the focused platform against the prior spread-thin approach.
test.measure: Engagement and conversion rate on the focused platform.

title: Identify and over-invest in the customers who already advocate for the brand
hypothesis: If the store identifies its existing superusers and over-invests attention in them, then advocacy compounds, because fixed resources mean not every customer can get the same treatment.

signal.check: No process exists to identify which customers already advocate for the brand (repeat reviewers, frequent UGC posters, referral sources), and all customers get the same generic treatment.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 named case (a daily creator for a year became a major driver and was hired)

risk.note: A segmentation and outreach effort.

prerequisites: Review, UGC, and referral data
steps: Identify the top 20 to 50 customers by reviews, UGC posts, or referrals.
Reach out with a specific, meaningful gesture (early access, recognition, a direct relationship).
Track whether their advocacy increases after the extra attention.

test.method: Compare advocacy activity (reviews, UGC, referrals) for the identified superusers before and after outreach.
test.measure: other:referral_share_rate for the superuser group.

title: Seed a launch through a few respected insiders in a high-trust community
hypothesis: If a launch is seeded through a small number of respected insiders in a high-trust community instead of broad advertising alone, then the message spreads through an existing trust network rather than starting from zero.

signal.check: A new launch relies only on paid ads or broad announcements, with no seeding through a small number of trusted community figures first.

expected_effect.size: unknown; illustrative headcounts only (about 3 at TED, about 15 in a theatre), not a formula

risk.note: An outreach effort.

prerequisites: Identified high-trust communities relevant to the product
steps: Identify 1 high-trust community relevant to the product (a running club, a hobbyist forum, a local group).
Find 3 to 5 respected insiders within that community.
Seed the launch with them first, before or alongside broader promotion.

test.method: Track whether the seeded community shows early adoption before wider promotion starts.
test.measure: Early sales or sign-ups attributable to the seeded community.
test.read_point: In the first 2 weeks after seeding

title: Limit the founder's daily focus to a short priority list and say no to most requests
hypothesis: If the founder keeps a short daily task list and declines most incoming requests, then scarce founder time goes to brand-moving work instead of being consumed by low-value asks.

signal.check: The founder's day is filled reactively with requests and small tasks, with no short, deliberate daily priority list.

expected_effect.size: unknown; a threshold table cites 3 tasks a day and saying no to about 97 percent of requests with no card or measured result behind it

risk.note: A time-management habit.

steps: Write no more than 3 priority tasks each morning.
Default to declining requests that do not serve those 3 tasks.
Review at the end of the week how much time went to the priority list versus reactive requests.

test.method: Track daily task completion against the 3-item list for 2 weeks.
test.measure: Share of days the 3 priority tasks were completed.

title: Run the full audience-building and content system for the brand
hypothesis: If the audience-building system runs as a full sequence (remarkable test, platform choice, give-and-ask rule, calendar, capture, founder plan, permission, revenue judging, persistence) instead of ad hoc posting, then organic content compounds into a real owned audience.

signal.check: Organic content posting happens with no documented system covering platform choice, the give-and-ask rule, a content calendar ratio, or a permission-channel goal.

risk.note: A system build; individual pieces (BRD-149 to BRD-159) can be adopted independently.

prerequisites: A chosen platform and format
The voice sheet
A permission channel
steps: Run the remarkable test: write the sentence a customer would say to a friend, or design an artifact that gives one.
Pick 1 platform and 1 sustainable format.
Set the give-and-ask rule and record the choice.
Set the 3-to-4 niche-to-broad calendar ratio, adjusted on data.
Set up 1 low-friction capture tool for content ideas.
Write the founder content plan with 1 to 3 themes.
Move every engaged viewer toward email or SMS.
Judge the system by revenue and owned-audience growth, and hold it for years unless a real signal says otherwise.

test.method: Track list_size and content-attributed revenue monthly against the pre-system baseline.
test.measure: list_size and other:content_revenue_attributed.

title: Hold the basic brand strategy for years; change the creative only when results say so
hypothesis: If creative is refreshed only when a real signal (the accountant, a measured decline) says so, not when the internal team is bored, then a working position is not abandoned too early.

signal.check: A creative refresh, tagline retirement, or channel cut is being proposed mainly because the internal team is tired of it, with no data showing it has stopped working.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical cases of abandoning a working position too early (Mailgram's late switch to next-day delivery)

risk.note: A decision discipline.

steps: Before any creative refresh, check performance data for a real, measured decline.
If no decline exists, treat internal boredom as insufficient reason to change.
Reserve full strategy changes for a failed test, a legal problem, or the runway running out (see BRD-166).

test.method: Review the last 3 creative refresh decisions for whether they were data-driven or boredom-driven.
test.measure: Share of refreshes backed by a real performance signal.

title: Treat consistency, not personal authenticity, as the customer-facing promise
hypothesis: If the brand delivers the same promised experience regardless of a bad day or a founder's mood, then customers get what they were promised every time, because consistency is the professional standard, while chasing constant personal authenticity can break the promise.

signal.check: Customer-facing tone or service quality shifts noticeably with the founder's or team's mood or energy on a given day.

risk.note: A standards discussion, not a live change.

prerequisites: Voice sheet or default voice (BRD-118)
steps: Document the promised tone and service standard regardless of internal mood.
Check recent customer-facing content or support interactions for consistency against that standard.
Address any drift as a training or workflow issue, not as a call for more authenticity.

test.method: Sample support interactions or posts across different weeks for tone consistency.
test.measure: Consistency score across samples.

title: Classify every ad line as performance or brand, and stop killing brand creative on ROAS alone
hypothesis: If every ad line is classified as performance (judged on ROAS, CAC) or brand (judged on branded search lift, repeat rate), then brand-building creative is not killed early for lacking a short-term ROAS it was never meant to deliver.

signal.check: All ad spend, including clearly brand-building creative, is being judged on ROAS or CAC alone, with no separate brand-lift metric tracked.

risk.note: A reporting and budget classification change.

steps: Tag every current ad line as performance or brand.
For performance lines, keep judging on ROAS and CAC.
For brand lines, set branded search lift and repeat rate as the judging metric instead, and do not kill them on ROAS alone.

test.method: Review ad spend allocation and kill decisions against the classification for 1 quarter.
test.measure: Number of brand-tagged lines killed on ROAS alone (should trend to zero).

title: Track position movement with the same instrument over time
hypothesis: If unaided awareness, attribute scores, category association, and the reorder curve are tracked with the same instrument over time, then real position movement becomes visible, instead of guessing from anecdote.

signal.check: No repeatable tracking instrument exists for unaided awareness, attribute scores, or category association, so position movement after a positioning or naming program cannot be measured.

expected_effect.size: 1 named case moved from last to first on 2 attributes in 15 months; another case's unaided awareness almost tripled in about a year

risk.note: A measurement build.

prerequisites: A research budget or a proxy (search terms, review mentions)
steps: Set the baseline: unaided awareness, per-attribute scores, correct category association, and the reorder curve, using a proxy if a research budget is not available.
Re-run the identical instrument 12 to 15 months later for a repositioning, or 90 to 120 days after a name launch.
Report movement, not just the current snapshot.

test.method: Repeat the same tracking instrument at the scheduled interval.
test.measure: Change in awareness, attribute scores, and category association versus baseline.
test.read_point: 12 to 15 months after a repositioning, or 90 to 120 days after a name launch

title: Confirm the funnel and lifetime value are visible before buying ads to build a position
hypothesis: If the store can see lifetime value and the funnel clearly before increasing acquisition spend on a new position, then budget is not committed blind to a funnel that cannot support it.

signal.check: Acquisition spend is being increased to support a new brand position with no clear, current view of lifetime value or the conversion funnel.

risk.note: A pre-spend check.

prerequisites: LTV and funnel reporting
steps: Pull current lifetime value and funnel conversion data before approving new acquisition spend for a position.
If the funnel cannot be seen clearly, fix reporting first (hand to the measurement domain) before committing spend.
Set the acquisition budget only once the funnel and LTV are visible.

test.method: Review LTV and funnel reporting readiness before each new acquisition budget increase.
test.measure: Whether LTV and funnel data were available and reviewed before the spend decision.

title: Overspend in 1 market or channel first, confirm the position lands, then repeat it identically
hypothesis: If a limited budget concentrates on 1 market, segment, or channel first instead of spreading thin everywhere, then the position has a real chance to land somewhere before the identical claim repeats elsewhere.

signal.check: A limited acquisition or positioning budget is being spread evenly across many markets, segments, or channels at once, with no market confirmed as established yet.

expected_effect.size: unknown; named historical rollout cases only (geographic, demographic, chronologic, distribution)

risk.note: A budget allocation change, easy to adjust.

steps: Choose 1 rollout axis: geographic, demographic, a single cohort, or 1 distribution channel first.
Overspend in that 1 area rather than underspending broadly.
Confirm the position is established there (branded search share, repeat purchase) before adding the next market.
Repeat the identical claim in the next market rather than reinventing the message.
Schedule the next markets or channels on a calendar.

test.method: Track branded search share and repeat purchase in the first market before expanding budget to the next.
test.measure: Branded search share and repeat rate in the pilot market.
test.read_point: Before the next market or channel receives budget

title: Bring in a second person to challenge every major positioning or identity decision
hypothesis: If a second person or outside facilitator challenges every major positioning or identity decision, then the design lead's assumptions get tested before launch, because positioning is a game best played by two.
does_not_apply_when: The founder is working entirely alone with no access to a second reviewer of any kind

signal.check: Positioning or identity decisions are being made and approved by 1 person alone, with no outside challenge before launch.

risk.note: A process addition.

steps: Identify 1 person, inside or outside the team, who can act as a genuine challenger.
Share the draft positioning or identity decision with them before finalising it.
If truly working solo, substitute a structured written exercise (writing the counter-argument yourself) and expect less challenge than a real second person provides.

test.method: Track whether every major positioning or identity decision has documented outside input before launch.
test.measure: Share of decisions with a second reviewer's input recorded.

title: Check for real resources and stamina before starting a demanding brand initiative
hypothesis: If the team checks for real resources and stamina before starting a demanding rebrand or launch, then it either commits fully or quits early at the low-commitment point, rather than stalling mid-project.

signal.check: A demanding brand initiative (a rebrand, a major relaunch) is starting with no honest check of whether the team has the resources and stamina to get through its hardest stretch.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this is not every setback, only under-resourced or unprepared projects

risk.note: A pre-commitment check.

steps: Write the hardest stretch the initiative will require (budget gap, time, emotional toll).
Honestly assess whether the team has the resources and stamina for that stretch.
If not, quit at this early, low-commitment point rather than starting and stalling mid-project.

test.method: Review the readiness check with the founder before the initiative kicks off.
test.measure: Whether the check was documented before starting.

title: Separate decision quality from outcome when reviewing a positioning or naming bet
hypothesis: If retros judge whether the positioning or naming decision was reasoned well given what was known, not just whether it happened to work out, then the team learns the right lesson instead of over- or under-crediting luck.

signal.check: A retro on a positioning or naming decision judges it only by the outcome (it worked or it didn't), with no separate assessment of whether the decision process itself was sound.

risk.note: A retro process change.

steps: In the retro, separately score the decision process (was it well-reasoned given known information) and the outcome (did it work).
Note cases where a good decision had a bad outcome, or a bad decision got lucky.
Carry forward lessons about the process, not just about the outcome.

test.method: Run the 2-part scoring in the next 3 positioning or naming retros.
test.measure: Number of retros using the 2-part scoring.

title: Plan for an adoption chasm between early fans and the mass market
hypothesis: If the team plans for a real chasm between early adopters and the mass market, and identifies a genuine network effect or status ratchet as the bridge, then scaling from a niche community to a mass audience is approached realistically instead of assumed to happen from hype alone.

signal.check: A plan to scale from a strong niche community to a mass audience has no identified real bridge (a network effect, a status ratchet) beyond hoped-for word of mouth or hype.

expected_effect.size: unknown; scaling from niche to mass is described as genuinely hard and rarely done

risk.note: A planning exercise; the underlying scaling attempt itself carries real cost and risk.

steps: Name the store's current early-adopter base honestly.
Identify a real network effect or status ratchet that could carry the message beyond that base, not just hoped-for virality.
If no real bridge exists, plan to grow the niche further rather than assuming a jump to mass market.

test.method: Review the identified bridge mechanism with the team before committing to a mass-market scaling plan.
test.measure: Whether a specific, real bridge mechanism is documented.

title: Let taste-led originality happen only in the creative direction step, after customer research
hypothesis: If customer research and the ladder shape the brief first, and personal taste is only used to originate the creative direction and naming tension-zone candidates, then the brand gets both a researched foundation and distinctive creative, instead of picking 1 approach and dropping the other.

signal.check: The team is either skipping customer research entirely in favour of pure founder taste, or letting research and consensus dictate every creative choice with no room for a distinctive, taste-led direction.

risk.note: A sequencing rule for how the team works, not a live change.

prerequisites: Category ladder and customer language research (BRD-003)
steps: Complete the positioning and brand strategy research (ladder, customer language, worldview) before any creative direction work starts.
Once the strategy is set, allow taste-led, distinctive options into the 3-direction creative exploration (BRD-110) and the naming tension zone (BRD-073).
Test the resulting creative in market rather than defending it on taste alone.

test.method: Check that research was completed and documented before the creative direction brief was written.
test.measure: Whether research preceded creative work in the project timeline.

title: Treat a hit-driven, mass-reach plan as a named, budgeted exception, not the default
hypothesis: If a plan to chase a broad hit instead of a narrow, sustainable audience is named explicitly with its own playbook and budget, then the store does not drift into a mass-reach strategy by default without deciding to take on its higher risk.
does_not_apply_when: The store has deliberately chosen and budgeted for a hit-seeking strategy with founder sign-off

signal.check: Marketing plans assume broad, viral-style reach as the default growth path, with no explicit decision or budget set aside for that higher-risk approach versus the default smallest viable market strategy.

risk.note: A strategy classification exercise; the underlying hit-seeking spend itself carries real risk.

steps: Check whether the current growth plan assumes a smallest viable market or a broad hit.
If a hit-driven approach is intended, write it down explicitly with its own budget and get founder sign-off.
Default back to the smallest viable market approach (BRD-011) if no such explicit decision exists.

test.method: Review the current growth plan for an explicit strategy type declaration.
test.measure: Whether the plan states smallest-viable-market or hit-seeking, with budget attached if the latter.

title: Run a causal or holdout test before crediting any channel for a sales change
hypothesis: If a channel or campaign is credited for a sales change only after a holdout or causal test confirms it, then budget decisions rest on more than attribution and self-reported survey data, because sales tracking alone cannot tell which half of spend worked.

signal.check: A channel, campaign or price change is being credited for a sales move using only aggregate sales data or a survey, with no holdout group or causal test.

expected_effect.size: unknown; no source gives a number for this habit

risk.note: A measurement discipline change, not a live spend change.

prerequisites: A channel or campaign whose effect is in question
steps: Pick a channel, campaign or price change whose sales effect is unclear.
Hold out a comparable group, region or time window from the change.
Compare the held-out group's sales to the exposed group's sales.
Credit the channel only if the causal test shows a real gap.
Stop crediting a channel from attribution or survey data alone.

test.method: Run a geo, time-based or audience holdout test alongside the next attribution claim.
test.measure: Gap between exposed and held-out group sales.

title: Run a blind branded-versus-unbranded test before blaming the product
hypothesis: If a blind, unbranded version of the product is tested against the branded version, then a low score or a complaint gets diagnosed correctly, because a brand can lift or drag perceived quality independent of the product itself, and the source's own taste study found preference reversed once the brand was revealed.

signal.check: A product change or a negative review is being blamed on the product itself with no test that separates brand perception from actual product performance.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited study found preference flipped from the unbranded to the branded condition

risk.note: A research exercise.

prerequisites: Enough product volume to run an unbranded and a branded taste, use or unboxing test
steps: Prepare an unbranded version of the product or its packaging for testing.
Have a panel evaluate the unbranded version and record their reaction.
Have a separate or the same panel evaluate the branded version.
Compare the 2 results to see whether the brand is lifting or dragging perception.
Fix the product if both score low, or fix the brand story if only the branded version underperforms.

test.method: Run a blind panel test comparing unbranded and branded versions of the same product.
test.measure: Score difference between unbranded and branded conditions.
test.read_point: After the panel completes both conditions

title: Track emotional association strength as a brand equity metric, not just recall
hypothesis: If brand equity is tracked as the strength of a positive emotional association, not only as unaided recall, then the brand can tell the difference between a name people remember and a name people actually feel good about, because recall alone can be neutral or even negative.

signal.check: Brand health reporting tracks recall or awareness only, with no read on whether the association carries a positive, negative or neutral emotional charge.

risk.note: A reporting addition.

prerequisites: An existing brand awareness or recall survey
steps: Add 1 question to the existing awareness survey asking how the respondent feels about the brand, not just whether they recognize it.
Score the emotional charge as positive, neutral or negative, not just present or absent.
Track the emotional-charge split over time alongside raw recall.
Flag a brand with high recall but a flat or negative emotional charge as a priority fix.
Repeat the combined measure at each future brand health check.

test.method: Add an emotional-charge question to the next brand awareness survey.
test.measure: Share of positive versus neutral or negative responses among those who recognize the brand.
test.read_point: At each brand health survey wave

title: Write an explicit ethical line before applying a persuasion technique
hypothesis: If the team writes an explicit ethical line for persuasion techniques (scarcity, fear, dark patterns) before applying any of them, then new tactics get checked against a standing rule instead of being approved case by case under launch pressure.

signal.check: A new persuasion tactic (urgency, fear-based copy, a dark pattern) is being approved without checking it against any written ethical standard.

risk.note: A governance document, not a live change.

prerequisites: None
steps: List the persuasion techniques the store currently uses or is considering (urgency, scarcity, social proof, fear appeals).
Write 1 explicit line the store will not cross for each technique (for example, never a fabricated stock count).
Circulate the line to everyone who writes copy or builds offers.
Check every new tactic against the line before it ships.
Revisit the line whenever a new tactic type is proposed.

test.method: Audit the last quarter's launched offers and copy against the written ethical line.
test.measure: Number of tactics that would have failed the line if it had existed sooner.

title: Test brand and message recall before and after ad exposure
hypothesis: If brand and message recall are tested before and after ad exposure, then creative effectiveness is judged on memory, not only on clicks or views, because a brand that is forgettable by default needs a direct recall check, not an assumption that distinctiveness happened automatically.

signal.check: Ad creative is being judged only on click-through or view counts, with no before-and-after recall check of the brand or key message.

risk.note: A measurement addition to existing creative testing.

prerequisites: An ad creative ready to test and a way to survey exposed versus unexposed viewers
steps: Survey a small group before they see the ad, asking if they can name or describe the brand and its core claim.
Show the ad to a comparable exposed group and an unexposed control group.
Survey both groups again afterward with the same recall question.
Compare the recall lift in the exposed group against the control group.
Use recall lift, not just CTR, to decide which creative to scale.

test.method: Run a pre/post recall survey alongside the next major creative test.
test.measure: Recall lift in the exposed group versus the unexposed control.
test.read_point: After the creative test window closes

title: Show product-in-use imagery before revealing price on the PDP
hypothesis: If a PDP or ad shows the product being used or enjoyed before the price is revealed, then the imitation response has a chance to build before the price triggers a rational counter-evaluation, because sequencing exposure before the price tag lets the emotional response register first.

signal.check: A PDP or ad layout shows price at the very top, before any product-in-use imagery, for a product where an emotional or aspirational response matters to the sale.

risk.note: A layout test.

prerequisites: A PDP or ad template that currently shows price early
steps: Identify the PDP or ad template currently showing price above or beside the first image.
Rebuild the layout so a product-in-use or lifestyle image appears before the price.
A/B test the reordered layout against the current price-first layout.
Measure PDP-to-cart conversion for both versions.
Roll out the winning sequence.

test.method: A/B test a product-in-use-first layout against a price-first layout on the same PDP.
test.measure: PDP-to-cart conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Build a designed anticipation moment into discovery or checkout
hypothesis: If a designed anticipation moment (a reveal animation, a countdown, a teaser) is added to product discovery or checkout, then engagement and completion improve, because a built anticipation moment gives the shopper a small dopamine-style reward loop instead of an instant, flat presentation.

signal.check: Product discovery or checkout presents the result instantly and flatly, with no designed anticipation or reveal moment.

risk.note: A UX addition, reversible if it adds friction instead of anticipation.

prerequisites: A discovery or checkout step that can host a brief anticipation moment
steps: Pick 1 step in discovery or checkout where a reveal or teaser could fit naturally.
Design a short anticipation moment (a countdown, a reveal animation, a teaser message).
A/B test the anticipation version against the current flat version.
Measure conversion and time-on-step for both.
Keep the version that lifts conversion without adding real friction.

test.method: A/B test a designed anticipation moment against the current flat step.
test.measure: Conversion rate and completion time at that step.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Attach the product to a ritual the customer already has
hypothesis: If the store identifies a daily or weekly ritual the customer already has and attaches product use to that specific moment, then repeat purchase improves, because riding an existing habit is cheaper than designing a brand-new one from scratch.

signal.check: Retention messaging talks about the product in isolation, with no attempt to identify or attach it to a ritual moment the customer already has in their day or week.

risk.note: A messaging and cue change.

prerequisites: Customer interview or review data describing when and how the product gets used
steps: Review customer language (reviews, support tickets, interviews) for a specific moment the product already fits into.
Identify the existing daily or weekly ritual that moment belongs to.
Write packaging, onboarding or reminder copy that names and attaches to that existing ritual.
Test the ritual-attached messaging against the current generic messaging.
Track repeat purchase for customers exposed to the ritual-attached messaging.

test.method: A/B test ritual-attached onboarding or reminder copy against current generic copy.
test.measure: 90-day repeat purchase rate.

title: Add a small ritual step that gives the shopper a sense of control
hypothesis: If checkout or configuration includes a small ritual-like step (a confirmation choice, a customization moment, a review-before-buy step) instead of a single frictionless click, then some shoppers convert better because a sense of control and involvement can outweigh the cost of 1 extra step.

signal.check: Checkout is a single, flat click-to-buy flow with no moment that gives the shopper a sense of choice or control over the purchase.

does_not_apply_when: A low-AOV, high-volume, impulse checkout where every extra step measurably lowers conversion.

expected_effect.size: unknown; this runs against general frictionless-checkout advice and should be tested carefully

risk.note: Adding a step can also reduce conversion; test before rolling out broadly.

prerequisites: A checkout or configuration flow that could host 1 additional control-giving step
steps: Identify 1 point in checkout or configuration where a small choice or confirmation ritual could fit.
Design the ritual step to feel like added control, not added friction (a customization pick, a review-and-confirm screen).
A/B test the ritual-added flow against the current frictionless flow.
Measure conversion and drop-off at that exact step for both.
Only keep the ritual step if it lifts or holds conversion.

test.method: A/B test a checkout flow with 1 added control-ritual step against the current frictionless flow.
test.measure: Cart-to-checkout conversion and step-level drop-off.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Prime price perception with imagery before the shopper sees the price
hypothesis: If imagery, color and context are used to prime a shopper's price expectation before they see the actual price, then willingness to pay is less dependent on the number alone, because visual and emotional cues can shift price perception independent of a discount.

signal.check: A PDP or ad shows the price with no preceding visual or contextual cue meant to shape the shopper's price expectation.

risk.note: A creative sequencing test.

prerequisites: A PDP or ad template that can be reordered
steps: Choose imagery, color or context (a face, a scene, a material close-up) that signals the intended price tier.
Place that priming element before the price is shown on the page or in the ad.
A/B test the primed sequence against the current unprimed sequence.
Measure AOV and conversion for both.
Roll out the sequence that lifts perceived value without misleading the shopper.

test.method: A/B test a price-primed layout against the current layout on the same PDP or ad.
test.measure: AOV and PDP-to-cart conversion.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Design replenishment reminders around craving cues, not plain low-stock notices
hypothesis: If a replenishment or reorder reminder uses sensory, craving-style imagery of the product in use instead of a plain informational low-stock notice, then reorder rate improves, because a warning-style message can activate wanting rather than caution the way a bland reminder does not.

signal.check: Replenishment or reorder emails and notifications are plain, informational stock-level messages with no sensory or craving-style imagery.

risk.note: A copy and creative change to an existing flow.

prerequisites: An existing replenishment or reorder email or notification flow
steps: Pull the current replenishment or reorder reminder copy and imagery.
Rewrite it around a sensory, craving-style depiction of the product in use, not a plain stock-level notice.
A/B test the craving-cue version against the current plain version.
Measure click rate and reorder rate for both.
Roll out the version that lifts reorder rate.

test.method: A/B test a craving-cue replenishment email against the current plain reminder.
test.measure: Click rate and reorder rate within the flow.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable send volume

title: Test an image-first hero layout against a text-first layout for recall
hypothesis: If a PDP or ad hero leads with a strong image before text, then brand and product recall improves, because recall works image-first, and a text-first layout asks the memory system to do more work than it naturally does.

signal.check: A PDP or ad hero leads with a headline or block of text before any strong product image.

risk.note: A layout test.

prerequisites: A PDP or ad template with a text-first hero layout
steps: Identify a PDP or ad hero currently leading with text before the main image.
Rebuild the hero to lead with a strong, clear product image, with text following.
A/B test the image-first layout against the current text-first layout.
Measure recall (via a quick survey) and click-through for both.
Roll out the layout that wins on recall.

test.method: A/B test an image-first hero against a text-first hero on the same page or ad.
test.measure: Recall lift and click-through rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Add explicit belonging signals to checkout, packaging and post-purchase emails
hypothesis: If checkout, packaging and post-purchase emails carry an explicit belonging signal (member-only language, an insider note, a name for the customer group), not just marketing pages, then repeat purchase improves, because belonging cues work best when they show up at the moments the customer is already emotionally engaged.

signal.check: Belonging or community language appears only on marketing pages, with no equivalent signal in checkout, packaging or post-purchase communication.

risk.note: A copy and packaging insert change.

prerequisites: A named customer group or community identity to reference
steps: Name the customer group in simple, ownable language (a member name, an insider label).
Add that language to the checkout confirmation, packaging insert and first post-purchase email.
Keep the tone consistent with the rest of the brand voice.
A/B test the belonging-signal version against the current neutral version.
Track repeat purchase for customers exposed to the belonging-signal touchpoints.

test.method: A/B test belonging-signal checkout and packaging copy against the current neutral copy.
test.measure: 90-day and 365-day repeat purchase rate.

title: Cultivate 1 deliberate unexplained detail instead of exhaustive explanation
hypothesis: If the brand story or PDP leaves 1 deliberate, unexplained detail (an unrevealed ingredient step, an untold origin fact) instead of explaining everything, then curiosity and engagement improve, because a small, sustained mystery keeps attention alive longer than a fully closed explanation.

signal.check: The brand story or PDP explains every detail of the product or process exhaustively, leaving no unresolved question for the shopper to be curious about.

risk.note: A copy edit.

prerequisites: A brand story or PDP with a genuinely interesting but omissible detail
steps: Identify 1 detail in the brand story or product process that is interesting but not essential for the purchase decision.
Remove or lightly tease that detail instead of fully explaining it.
Point to where curious customers can ask or find out more (a support channel, a future reveal).
A/B test the teased version against the fully explained version.
Measure engagement time and any follow-up questions or shares.

test.method: A/B test a page with 1 deliberately unexplained detail against the fully explained version.
test.measure: Page engagement time and follow-up questions or shares.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Build a consistent, repeated navigation pattern to raise familiarity switching cost
hypothesis: If the store keeps a consistent, repeated navigation and ordering pattern (an account dashboard, a saved reorder flow), then returning customers build a switching cost around familiarity with the store's own navigation, because relearning a competitor's layout is itself a real cost to the customer.

signal.check: The store's navigation, account area or reorder flow changes frequently or inconsistently, with no attempt to build a stable, familiar pattern returning customers can rely on.

risk.note: A navigation stability policy.

prerequisites: An account area or reorder flow used by repeat customers
steps: Document the current account, navigation and reorder flow structure.
Set a policy to keep that structure stable across redesigns unless a clear conversion problem forces a change.
When a change is needed, migrate gradually and communicate it to returning customers.
Track repeat purchase rate and account-area usage before and after any navigation change.
Treat navigation stability itself as a retention lever, not just a design preference.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate for the period before versus after a navigation change.
test.measure: 365-day repeat purchase rate around the change.
test.read_point: Before and after any planned navigation redesign

title: Add a small post-purchase commitment step to reinforce the buying decision
hypothesis: If a small, active commitment step follows purchase (a public choice, a short review request, a stated intention), then buyer's remorse and returns drop, because the extra step reinforces the decision through cognitive dissonance instead of leaving the purchase unreinforced.
does_not_apply_when: A low-involvement, low-AOV impulse purchase where an extra post-purchase step adds unnecessary friction.

signal.check: The post-purchase flow ends at the order confirmation with no small, active step that reinforces the customer's own decision.

risk.note: A post-purchase flow addition.

prerequisites: A post-purchase email or on-site confirmation flow
steps: Design 1 small, active step after purchase (a short 'why I chose this' prompt, a public share option, a quick intention-setting question).
Add the step to the order confirmation or first post-purchase email.
A/B test the commitment-step flow against the current flow with no such step.
Track return and refund rate for both groups.
Keep the step only if it measurably reduces returns without hurting the post-purchase experience.

test.method: A/B test a post-purchase commitment step against the standard confirmation flow.
test.measure: Return rate and refund rate.
test.read_point: Within the standard return window after purchase

title: Test a superstition or luck-themed merchandising angle for a limited drop
hypothesis: If a limited edition or seasonal drop tests a superstition or luck-themed angle (a lucky number, color or timing) adapted to the specific market's own associations, then it can lift interest for that drop, because superstition and ritual are real, measurable purchase drivers in the right cultural context.
does_not_apply_when: The chosen number, color or symbol carries a negative association in the target market; check per market before using.

signal.check: A seasonal or limited-edition drop uses no market-appropriate luck, number or color theme, despite the category or occasion supporting one.

risk.note: A themed limited-edition test.

prerequisites: A limited or seasonal drop opportunity
Knowledge of the target market's own lucky and unlucky associations
steps: Research the target market's own lucky and unlucky numbers, colors or timing associations.
Design 1 limited-edition or seasonal drop around a genuinely positive association for that market.
Avoid any number, color or symbol carrying a negative association in that market.
Run the themed drop against a standard, untheme-d drop of similar scale.
Compare conversion and AOV between the 2.

test.method: Compare a luck-themed limited drop against a standard drop of similar size and timing.
test.measure: Conversion rate and AOV during the drop window.
test.read_point: During and immediately after the drop

title: Share the brand's origin story internally to keep the team engaged
hypothesis: If the founder or brand's origin story is shared with the team internally, not just used externally in marketing, then team motivation and brand fluency improve, because a team that knows and believes the brand's own story can carry it more consistently into their daily work.

signal.check: The brand's origin or founder story exists in marketing material but has never been shared or discussed with the internal team as a source of shared motivation.

risk.note: An internal communication habit.

prerequisites: A documented founder or brand origin story
steps: Write or record the brand's origin story in a form that can be shared internally.
Share it with new hires as part of onboarding.
Revisit and retell it at a team meeting or milestone at least once a year.
Ask the team to explain the story in their own words as a fluency check.
Update the story as the brand's own history grows.

test.method: Ask a sample of team members to summarize the brand's origin story before and after it is formally shared.
test.measure: Accuracy and consistency of team members' summaries.
test.read_point: At onboarding and again 6 months later

title: Test whether a fear-based warning or disclaimer increases interest instead of deterring it
hypothesis: If a fear-based warning, disclaimer or negative claim is tested for its actual effect on interest, not assumed to deter the behavior it targets, then the store avoids a warning that backfires, because at least 1 cited study found a warning label produced zero suppression of the targeted craving and instead activated it.

signal.check: A warning, disclaimer or negative-framed claim is being added to copy or packaging with no test of whether it actually reduces the targeted behavior or interest.

risk.note: A copy test.

prerequisites: A warning, disclaimer or negative claim planned or already in use
steps: Identify the warning, disclaimer or negative-framed claim currently in use or being planned.
Write down what behavior or outcome it is meant to deter or discourage.
Test the copy with a small group and ask about their resulting interest or intention, not just comprehension.
Check whether interest rose, fell or stayed flat after seeing the warning.
Rework or drop any warning that increases interest in the behavior it was meant to deter.

test.method: Survey intention or interest before and after exposure to the warning or disclaimer copy.
test.measure: Change in stated interest or intention after exposure.
test.read_point: Before finalizing any warning or disclaimer copy

title: Audit an established premium brand against the 10 traits shared by religions and strong brands
hypothesis: If an already-strong or aspiring premium brand is audited against the 10 traits it shares with strong belief systems (belonging, vision, us-versus-them, sensory appeal, storytelling, grandeur, evangelism, symbols, mystery, rituals), then gaps in loyalty-building structure get found, because these traits are what the source found strong brands and strong belief systems share in common.
does_not_apply_when: A new or low-trust brand with no organically earned traits yet; the checklist too early reads as inauthentic.

signal.check: An established or aspiring premium brand has never been audited against a structured belonging-and-ritual framework, relying only on ad-hoc brand exercises.

risk.note: A strategy audit exercise.

prerequisites: An already-established or clearly aspiring premium brand with some existing loyalty
steps: List the 10 traits: belonging, clear vision, power over enemies, sensory appeal, storytelling, grandeur, evangelism, symbols, mystery, rituals.
Score the brand's current state honestly on each trait.
Identify the 2 or 3 weakest traits as the priority to build.
Design 1 concrete initiative per weak trait (a community identity, a signature ritual, a story asset).
Re-score the brand against the same 10 traits after a defined period.

test.method: Score the brand on the 10-trait checklist now and again after 6 to 12 months of targeted work.
test.measure: Change in score on the weakest traits.
test.read_point: 6 to 12 months after the initial audit

title: Account for short-term reward bias when designing BNPL or installment offers
hypothesis: If BNPL, installment and immediate-discount offers are designed knowing buyers favor a smaller immediate reward over a better delayed one, then offer structure accounts for real buyer psychology, because a cited delayed-gratification study found the immediate, smaller option activated the emotional brain more strongly regardless of objective value.

signal.check: A BNPL, installment or discount offer is structured using only the rational total-cost math, with no account of the pull toward the smaller, immediate option.

risk.note: An offer-framing test.

prerequisites: An existing BNPL, installment or discount offer to test
steps: Review the current BNPL, installment or discount offer copy for how it frames the immediate versus delayed choice.
Rewrite the immediate option to feel like the natural, easy default, since buyers lean toward it regardless of total cost.
Keep the delayed or full-payment option available but not the default framing.
A/B test the reframed offer against the current framing.
Measure checkout completion and AOV for both.

test.method: A/B test the reframed BNPL or installment offer against the current framing at checkout.
test.measure: Checkout-to-order conversion and AOV.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Use a verifiable origin story on packaging as a price-positioning lever
hypothesis: If a specific, verifiable origin or sourcing story is used on packaging or the PDP, then the store can justify a higher price than a commodity, generic-origin framing would support, because a documented origin case showed a plain commodity item reach a large price increase once a credible origin story was attached to it.

signal.check: The PDP or packaging describes the product generically, with no specific, verifiable origin or sourcing detail, even though a genuine one exists.

risk.note: Any origin claim must be genuinely verifiable; do not invent a sourcing story.

prerequisites: A genuine, verifiable origin or sourcing fact about the product
steps: Document a specific, verifiable fact about the product's origin, sourcing or production method.
Write the fact into packaging and PDP copy as a concrete detail, not a vague claim.
Test the origin-story version against the current generic description.
Measure AOV and conversion for both.
Only keep the claim if it can be substantiated on request.

test.method: A/B test PDP or packaging copy with the origin story against the current generic copy.
test.measure: AOV and conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Test a signature sound for negative association before scaling it
hypothesis: If a signature sound (a notification tone, an unboxing sound, a jingle) is tested for negative association before it is paired consistently with the visual brand, and re-audited periodically, then the brand avoids the failure mode where overexposure turns a once-neutral sound into a negative cue that drags down the visual brand alongside it.

signal.check: A signature sound is used consistently across the brand with no periodic check for whether it still reads as positive or has gone negative through overexposure.

risk.note: A periodic audit.

prerequisites: An existing or candidate signature sound
steps: Before scaling a candidate signature sound, test it alone and paired with the brand image for sentiment.
Only pair the sound with the visual brand if the combination scores above either element alone.
Re-test sentiment for the sound periodically once it is in wide use.
If sentiment for the combination drops below the visual-alone baseline, retire or refresh the sound.
Document the sentiment check as a recurring brand-asset review, not a one-time decision.

test.method: Rate sentiment for the sound alone, the visual alone and the combination, repeated every 12 months.
test.measure: Sentiment score for the combination versus the visual-alone baseline.
test.read_point: At launch and every 12 months after

title: Run NPS quarterly and segment results by historical customer value
hypothesis: If NPS is run quarterly and segmented by historical purchase value, not just reported as a single average, then the store can see whether its most valuable customers are actually the ones driving the score, because a blended average can hide a split between high-value promoters and low-value detractors.

signal.check: NPS is tracked as a single blended score with no breakdown by customer historical value or repeat status.

risk.note: A reporting addition to an existing survey.

prerequisites: An existing NPS survey and customer purchase history data
steps: Run the existing NPS survey on the usual quarterly cadence.
Join survey responses to each respondent's historical purchase value.
Segment the NPS score into at least a top-value and a bottom-value group.
Compare the segments instead of reporting only the blended average.
Flag any gap where high-value customers score lower than low-value ones for follow-up.

test.method: Segment the next 2 quarterly NPS waves by historical customer value.
test.measure: NPS score by value segment versus the blended average.

title: Run recurring research separately with complaining and non-complaining customers
hypothesis: If recurring customer research is run separately with customers who complained and customers who did not, then the store gets a fuller signal about what is actually broken, because a complaint sample and a silent sample give different information and averaging them together can hide both.

signal.check: Customer research (surveys, interviews) draws from a single mixed pool with no split between customers who filed a complaint and customers who did not.

risk.note: A research segmentation habit.

prerequisites: A support or complaint log and a way to run recurring customer research
steps: Pull a list of customers who filed a complaint in the last research period.
Pull a comparable list of customers who did not complain in the same period.
Run the same research questions with both groups, kept separate.
Compare the 2 groups' answers instead of blending them into 1 average.
Feed distinct findings from each group into separate fixes.

test.method: Run the next customer research wave split by complaint status instead of as 1 mixed pool.
test.measure: Difference in findings between the complaining and non-complaining groups.
test.read_point: At the next scheduled research wave

title: Cap the share of research budget spent on collecting more data
hypothesis: If the team caps the share of research and analytics budget spent on collecting more data once existing data already suggests an action, then more of the budget goes toward acting on findings instead of endlessly gathering more, because collecting data has no value until a decision is made from it.

signal.check: Research or analytics budget keeps growing toward collecting more data even though existing data already points to a clear next action.

risk.note: A budget allocation rule.

prerequisites: An existing research or analytics budget line
steps: Review the current research and analytics spend and separate it into collecting versus acting categories.
Check whether existing data already supports a clear action that has not been taken.
If so, redirect new spend toward implementing that action instead of collecting more data.
Set a rule requiring a stated action before approving further data-collection spend on the same question.
Review the collecting-versus-acting split each budget cycle.

test.method: Track the ratio of research spend spent on collecting versus acting over 2 budget cycles.
test.measure: Share of spend that produced a shipped action.

title: Frame a trial as give-then-ask-to-keep, not browse-and-choose
hypothesis: If a trial hands the product to the shopper first and asks a small payment to keep it, then more shoppers convert than under a browse-and-choose trial, because loss aversion is a stronger pull than an open choice.

signal.check: A trial or sample offer is framed as a browse-and-choose experience instead of a give-first, pay-to-keep offer.

expected_effect.size: roughly doubled conversion in 1 cited case, from about a third to about two thirds

risk.note: An offer-framing test, reversible if it does not lift conversion.

prerequisites: A low-cost product or sample that can be handed over before payment
steps: Pick a low-cost product or sample suited to a give-first offer.
Hand the product to the shopper or place it in their possession first.
Ask a small payment to keep it, framed as a loss if declined.
Compare conversion against the existing browse-and-choose offer.
Roll out the winning frame if it lifts conversion.

test.method: A/B test give-then-ask-to-keep against browse-and-choose on the same offer.
test.measure: Conversion rate difference between the 2 frames.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Target shoppers whose routine just broke for a habit-replacing product
hypothesis: If acquisition targets people whose routine just changed, such as a move, engagement or new job, for a product that replaces a habit, then conversion is easier than targeting people already settled into an incumbent, because a broken pattern has no established habit to unseat.

signal.check: A habit-replacing product is being marketed broadly instead of to people whose life context just changed and has no settled incumbent.

risk.note: A targeting and messaging change.

prerequisites: A product that replaces an existing habit or incumbent
steps: List the life-context triggers that break an incumbent habit for this category.
Build or select an audience segment tied to that recent life-context change.
Write creative that names the fresh-start moment, not just the product features.
Run this audience against the standard broad audience and compare CPA and conversion.
Shift budget toward the pattern-interrupt segment if it wins.

test.method: Split-test a fresh-start-triggered audience against a standard broad audience.
test.measure: CPA and conversion rate by audience.
test.read_point: After each audience reaches statistical comparability

title: Show the result without the method to build purchase-driving tension
hypothesis: If demo or inspiration content shows the result without revealing how it was done, then viewers feel the tension of wanting to know, and that tension drives more purchases than a fully explained demo, because unresolved curiosity is itself a motivator.

signal.check: Demo or inspiration video content explains the full method and result together, leaving no unresolved question for the viewer.

expected_effect.size: unknown; source cites over a billion views at zero distribution cost for 1 brand

risk.note: A content-format change.

prerequisites: A product with a visible before-and-after or demonstrable result
steps: Pick a product moment with a clear, visible result.
Script the content to show the result happening without narrating the full method.
Put the purchase link or call to action at the point the curiosity peaks.
Compare click-through and hook rate against a fully explained demo.
Scale the format that produces stronger engagement.

test.method: A/B test a withhold-the-method cut against a fully explained cut of the same demo.
test.measure: Hook rate and click-through rate.
test.read_point: After both cuts reach comparable impressions

title: Track branded search growth instead of chasing generic category SEO terms
hypothesis: If the store tracks growth in searches for its own name as a marketing goal, then effort shifts toward building a name worth searching for instead of an unwinnable generic-term SEO race, because most stores cannot outrank thousands of pages for a category term.

signal.check: SEO effort and reporting focus only on generic category-term rankings, with no tracking of branded search volume over time.

risk.note: A reporting and goal change, not a live change.

prerequisites: Access to search-console or equivalent branded-term volume data
steps: Pull the current monthly search volume for the store's own name.
Add branded search volume as a tracked marketing KPI alongside generic-term rankings.
Review branded search volume monthly against content, PR and campaign activity.
Deprioritize generic-term SEO spend where branded search is not moving.
Reinvest saved effort into activity that grows name recognition.

test.method: Track branded search volume before and after a quarter of name-building activity.
test.measure: Month-over-month change in branded search volume.

title: Retire an ad or tagline on audience exposure, not internal fatigue
hypothesis: If an ad or tagline is retired only once a minimum audience exposure count is reached, then creative is not killed early from internal team boredom, because the audience typically has not absorbed the message at the point the internal team gets tired of it.

signal.check: An ad or tagline is being retired because the internal team is tired of it, with no check of how many times the target audience has actually seen it.

risk.note: A decision-rule change.

prerequisites: Frequency or impression data for the creative in question
steps: Set a minimum frequency or impression threshold before any creative is eligible for retirement.
Check the creative's actual frequency against that threshold before killing it.
If under the threshold, let it keep running rather than replacing it on team sentiment.
Retire it only once the threshold is passed and performance has genuinely flattened.
Record the retirement reason to separate audience fatigue from team fatigue going forward.

test.method: Compare CTR and conversion at low, medium and high frequency bands for the same creative.
test.measure: Performance trend across frequency bands.

title: Show the storefront to an unfamiliar viewer for 5 seconds and ask what it recalls
hypothesis: If someone unfamiliar with the brand looks at the storefront, PDP or packaging for 5 seconds and says what it reminds them of, then a mismatch between the intended promise and the actual reading is caught before launch, because shoppers scan for pattern matches, not detailed reading.

signal.check: A storefront, PDP or packaging design has shipped with no outside, unfamiliar-viewer read on what it visually signals.

risk.note: A cheap pre-launch check.

prerequisites: A design draft and a person unfamiliar with the brand
steps: Show the storefront, PDP or packaging to someone who has never seen the brand.
Give them 5 seconds, then ask what it reminds them of and what kind of company they think it is.
Compare the answer to the intended promise and positioning.
Flag any answer that reads as generic, dated or untrustworthy.
Revise the typeface, photography style or layout that caused the mismatch.

test.method: Run the 5-second test with at least 3 to 5 unfamiliar viewers before a design ships.
test.measure: Share of viewers whose answer matches the intended promise.
test.read_point: Before launch or before a redesign is finalized

title: Audit the store's actual response to its last refund dispute or data incident
hypothesis: If the store reviews what it actually did on its last refund dispute, data incident or public complaint, then the real trust signal is found and fixed, because trust compounds from documented action, not from marketing statements about being trustworthy.

signal.check: The brand makes trust claims in copy without ever reviewing what it actually did the last time a customer had a bad experience.

risk.note: A review exercise, not a live change.

prerequisites: Records of at least 1 recent refund dispute, complaint or incident
steps: Pull the record of the store's most recent refund dispute, complaint or data incident.
Write down exactly what the store did, step by step, in response.
Compare that action against any trust claim currently made in copy.
Fix the gap in process first, then update the copy to match the real action.
Repeat this review after each significant incident going forward.

test.method: Review the action log against the stated trust claim for the next incident that occurs.
test.measure: Whether the documented action matches the stated claim.

title: Build the single definitive item for a narrow niche instead of a mass hit
hypothesis: If a marketplace or catalogue seller builds the one definitive item for a narrow niche and connects that niche's buyers to each other, then it captures a real, sustainable segment instead of losing to the long-tail trap of chasing a broad hit no single seller can own.

signal.check: A catalogue or marketplace assortment is spread thin trying to compete broadly, with no single SKU built to be the definitive choice for a specific niche.

risk.note: An assortment and positioning focus decision.

prerequisites: A defined niche with a real, identifiable community
steps: Identify a narrowly defined niche within the broader category the brand serves.
Build or position 1 SKU as the definitive item for that niche's specific need.
Find where that niche's buyers already gather and connect them to each other around the item.
Measure share of that niche, not share of the broad category.
Repeat the pattern in an adjacent niche once the first one is won.

test.method: Track niche-specific sales share and repeat purchase for the definitive SKU over 1 quarter.
test.measure: Niche market share and repeat rate.

title: Seed a new product in one tight community before a wider rollout
hypothesis: If a new product launches inside one tight community or region first and relies on visible peer status pressure to spread, then it crosses the local adoption chasm faster and cheaper than a broad, thin launch, because proximity-based social proof compounds within a small, connected group.

signal.check: A new product or store is launching broadly and thinly across many audiences at once, with no single tight community seeded first.

risk.note: A launch-sequencing decision.

prerequisites: A specific community, campus, region or group the product genuinely fits
steps: Identify a specific, contained community the product genuinely fits, such as a region, a campus or an interest group.
Concentrate the entire early launch budget and content in that one community.
Make product use or ownership visible within that community so peers see each other adopting it.
Track adoption within the community before expanding to the next one.
Repeat the identical approach in a second community once the first is proven.

test.method: Track adoption rate within the seeded community versus a broad-launch control group or a prior launch.
test.measure: Adoption rate and time to saturation within the community.
test.read_point: After the community-seeded launch window closes

title: Audit the funnel on 6 levers before scaling acquisition spend
hypothesis: If the funnel is audited on 6 levers (right people, promise match, decision-step count, support content, tension, referral ask) before scaling spend, then leaks get fixed before money is spent pushing more traffic through a broken path.

signal.check: Acquisition spend is being increased with no recent audit of whether the funnel itself attracts the right people, keeps its promise, and converts them.

risk.note: A review exercise before a spend decision.

prerequisites: Funnel stage data from ad to repeat purchase
steps: Map every funnel stage from first touch to repeat purchase.
Check whether the traffic source attracts people who match the entry promise.
Check whether the landing content actually delivers on that promise.
Count decision steps and remove any not earning their cost in trust or conversion.
Check for a tension-and-relief moment at the highest-drop-off step.
Check whether a successful buyer is handed an explicit way to tell others.
Only scale spend once the audit finds no major leak.

test.method: Run the 6-lever audit before the next acquisition budget increase.
test.measure: Number of leaks found and fixed versus funnel conversion rate after fixes.

title: Rewrite checkout and bundle copy that only appeals to rational long-term value
hypothesis: If checkout, bundle and promotion copy is audited for appeals to impulse, identity and urgency, not just rational long-term value, then conversion improves, because most buyers act on current urges and social identity more than a considered cost-benefit case.

signal.check: Checkout, bundle and promotion copy leans entirely on rational value math, such as cost per use or long-term savings, with no impulse, identity or urgency framing.

risk.note: A copy edit, reversible if it does not test well.

prerequisites: Existing checkout, bundle or promotion copy to audit
steps: Pull current checkout, bundle and promotion copy.
Flag any line that appeals only to rational, long-term value.
Rewrite flagged lines to add an impulse, identity or genuine urgency angle.
A/B test the rewritten copy against the original.
Keep whichever version lifts conversion or AOV without a false urgency claim.

test.method: A/B test rewritten checkout or bundle copy against the current rational-only version.
test.measure: Cart-to-checkout conversion and AOV.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Collect the specific objections that block non-buyers before writing new copy
