hypothesis: If the specific internal objections and narrative blocking non-buyers are collected from reviews, abandoned-cart surveys and support tickets before writing new acquisition copy, then the copy answers real blockers instead of guessed ones, because the actual reason someone doesn't buy is rarely the reason a team assumes.

signal.check: New acquisition or PDP copy is being written from internal assumptions about why people don't buy, with no review of actual objection data.

risk.note: A research step before a copy rewrite.

prerequisites: Reviews, abandoned-cart data or support tickets to mine
steps: Pull a sample of reviews, abandoned-cart survey responses and support tickets.
List the specific stated or implied objections that come up repeatedly.
Rank the objections by frequency.
Write or revise PDP and ad copy to directly answer the top objections.
Track conversion before and after the objection-informed rewrite.

test.method: A/B test objection-informed copy against the current copy.
test.measure: PDP-to-cart conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Write 2 versions of key messaging for early adopters and for the mass market
hypothesis: If a store writes 2 versions of its key claim, 1 for early adopters comfortable with a new category idea and 1 for the mass market that needs a familiar anchor first, then each segment converts better than a single blended message, because the 2 groups differ in how much explanation and reassurance they need before a new claim lands.

signal.check: A single messaging version is used for both early-adopter and mass-market audiences, with no adjustment for how much category education each needs.

risk.note: A copy variant test.

prerequisites: A product or claim that is genuinely new to at least part of the audience
steps: Identify which parts of the audience are early adopters versus mass-market shoppers for this category.
Write 1 message version that leads with the new, distinctive claim for early adopters.
Write a second version that anchors to something already familiar before introducing the new claim.
Route each audience to its matching version.
Compare conversion by audience and version.

test.method: A/B test the 2 messaging versions against their matching audience segments.
test.measure: Conversion rate by audience and message version.
test.read_point: After both segments reach a comparable sample size

title: Write copy for the buyer, not the end user, when the 2 differ
hypothesis: If the store identifies when the buyer and the end user are different people, such as a gift, a pet product or a kids' product, and writes copy primarily for the buyer's motivations, then conversion improves, because the buyer's decision, not the end user's experience, is what actually drives the purchase.
does_not_apply_when: A product where the buyer and end user are almost always the same person.

signal.check: PDP and ad copy is written entirely for the end user's experience even though the buyer and end user are frequently different people for this product.

risk.note: A copy rewrite test.

prerequisites: A product category where the buyer and end user are often different people
steps: Check purchase and support data for how often the buyer differs from the end user for this product.
If the split is meaningful, identify the buyer's own motivation (a gift-giver's status, a parent's safety concern, a pet owner's love).
Rewrite the PDP and ad copy to speak primarily to that buyer motivation, not just the end user's experience.
A/B test the buyer-focused copy against the current end-user-focused copy.
Measure conversion for both.

test.method: A/B test buyer-focused copy against end-user-focused copy on the same PDP.
test.measure: PDP-to-cart conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Emphasize uniqueness, not consensus, when marketing to a micro-tribe
hypothesis: If community or micro-tribe messaging emphasizes how few others share the belief or identity, not how many already agree, then belonging and engagement improve, because a cited study found people more enthusiastic about a shared belief when told fewer, not more, others held it.

signal.check: Community or brand messaging leans on how popular or widely shared the belief or product is, for a small, identity-driven micro-tribe audience.

risk.note: A messaging test.

prerequisites: An identifiable micro-tribe or niche community audience
steps: Identify a micro-tribe or niche community segment the brand serves.
Write 1 message version emphasizing broad popularity and consensus.
Write a second version emphasizing the group's own distinctiveness and how few others share it.
A/B test the 2 versions with the micro-tribe audience.
Keep the version that lifts engagement or conversion.

test.method: A/B test a uniqueness-framed message against a consensus-framed message with the same micro-tribe audience.
test.measure: Engagement or conversion rate by message version.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Diagnose non-purchase as an unstated fear, not a missing feature
hypothesis: If a shopper's non-purchase is diagnosed as an unstated fear (of misuse, judgment or waste) rather than a missing feature, and that fear is addressed directly in copy or a guarantee, then conversion improves, because adding more feature information does not resolve a fear-based objection.

signal.check: A product with good fit and strong reviews still underperforms on conversion, and the fix being tried is adding more feature detail rather than addressing a possible unstated fear.

risk.note: A diagnostic and copy exercise.

prerequisites: Reviews, support tickets or exit-survey data for a specific underperforming product
steps: Pick a product with good reviews but underperforming conversion.
Review support tickets, exit-survey responses and reviews for an unstated fear (buyer's remorse, judgment, misuse, waste).
Name the specific fear in plain language.
Address that fear directly in copy or with a guarantee, instead of adding more feature detail.
A/B test the fear-addressing copy against the current feature-focused copy.

test.method: A/B test fear-addressing copy against the current feature-focused copy on the same PDP.
test.measure: PDP-to-cart conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Add an offline or human element online competitors cannot copy
hypothesis: If the purchase or unboxing experience includes an offline or human element (a handwritten note, a real phone call, a physical extra) that a pure online competitor cannot easily copy, then trust and repeat purchase improve, because a genuine human touch is a differentiator commodity ecommerce competitors struggle to replicate at scale.

signal.check: The entire purchase and post-purchase experience is fully automated with no offline or human touch that a pure online competitor could not easily replicate.

risk.note: An operational addition, cost and scale need checking.

prerequisites: Order volume low enough to sustain a genuine human touch, or a plan to scale it
steps: Identify 1 point in the order or post-purchase journey where a human or offline touch fits naturally.
Design the touch to be genuine and specific, not templated (a handwritten note, a real call for a high-value order).
Test the added touch on a subset of orders against the standard automated flow.
Measure repeat purchase and review sentiment for both groups.
Scale the touch only if it holds up at higher volume without losing its genuineness.

test.method: A/B test orders that receive the human touch against orders that receive the standard automated flow.
test.measure: 90-day repeat purchase rate and review sentiment.

title: Write down why a non-buyer segment's decision is actually reasonable
hypothesis: If the team writes down the reasons a non-buying segment's decision not to buy is actually reasonable from their own point of view, then messaging and product decisions improve, because dismissing non-buyers as simply wrong hides real, fixable objections.

signal.check: Non-buyers are being discussed internally as simply wrong or uninformed, with no written exercise considering why their decision makes sense from their own point of view.

risk.note: An internal exercise.

prerequisites: A defined non-buyer segment (visited but did not purchase, or churned)
steps: Pick a specific non-buyer segment (site visitors who did not convert, or churned customers).
Write down, from that segment's own point of view, why not buying was a reasonable decision.
Identify which of those reasons the store could actually address.
Prioritize 1 or 2 fixes based on the exercise.
Test the fix and track conversion for that segment.

test.method: Run the empathy exercise, then A/B test the resulting fix against no change for the same segment.
test.measure: Conversion rate for the targeted non-buyer segment.
test.read_point: After the fix has run for a comparable sample size

title: Normalize a big ask for a high-status cohort as what people like them do
hypothesis: If a high-status customer cohort's large spend, referral or public gesture is normalized as what people like them already do, cultivated deliberately over time, then it outperforms treating the same ask as an unusual favor, because peer-status pressure among an already-connected cohort can drive outsized results beyond the format's own design.

signal.check: A premium tier, big-ticket upsell or major ask is presented as an unusual, one-off favor rather than as a normalized behavior within a defined high-status cohort.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 cited case raised over $100 million in a single night

risk.note: A framing and cultivation strategy for an existing high-value cohort.

prerequisites: An identifiable high-status or high-value customer cohort with some existing connection to each other
steps: Identify the store's existing high-status or highest-value customer cohort.
Find or create a setting where members of that cohort see each other's behavior (an event, a shared community, a leaderboard).
Frame the big ask (a top-tier purchase, a large referral, a public gesture) as what members of that cohort already do, not as an unusual favor.
Cultivate the norm over multiple touchpoints, not a single pitch.
Track the cohort's upgrade or big-ask rate over time.

test.method: Track the high-status cohort's big-ask conversion rate before and after the norm-building framing is introduced.
test.measure: Cohort upgrade or big-ask conversion rate.

title: Design a referral mechanic where the product genuinely improves as friends join
hypothesis: If a referral or sharing mechanic is designed so the product or service genuinely gets better once a friend joins (a shared saving, a shared feature, a shared list), not just a discount code, then referral spread compounds faster, because a real network effect gives the sharer a selfish reason to recruit, not just a favor to the brand.

signal.check: The current referral mechanic is a simple discount code with no genuine improvement in the product or service once a referred friend joins.

risk.note: Requires a real product or service mechanic, not just a marketing wrapper.

prerequisites: A product or service where a shared feature, saving or list is technically feasible
steps: Identify a feature, saving or benefit that could genuinely improve when a friend also joins (a shared discount tier, a shared list, a group benefit).
Build the mechanic so both the referrer and the referred friend see the improvement, not just a 1-time code.
Launch the network-effect mechanic alongside or in place of the current referral code.
Track referral rate and the resulting group's retention.
Iterate the shared-benefit design based on uptake.

test.method: Compare referral rate for the network-effect mechanic against the current discount-code referral program.
test.measure: Referral rate and referred-cohort retention.

title: Write a 5-part launch or reposition plan: truth, assertions, alternatives, people, money
hypothesis: If a store launch or reposition is planned in 5 explicit sections (truth about the market, assertions about what will happen, alternatives if an assertion misses, people involved, money required), written in that order, then the plan surfaces real risk and flexibility instead of a vague mission statement everyone quietly disagrees with.

signal.check: A store launch or major reposition is being planned from a vague mission statement with no written truth section, no stated fallback if an assertion is wrong, and no explicit money plan.

risk.note: A planning document.

prerequisites: A launch or reposition decision underway
steps: Write the Truth section: the market as it is, with data, no positions taken.
Write the Assertions section: what the store will do and what response it expects, accepting some will be wrong.
Write the Alternatives section: what happens if an assertion misses, and how flexible the product or supply chain is.
Write the People section: the team and customers' attitudes, abilities and track record.
Write the Money section last: capital needed, spend plan, cash flow and margins.
Get the team to agree on the Truth section before moving to the rest.

test.method: Compare launch outcomes for launches planned with the 5-part structure against past launches planned without it.
test.measure: Whether the launch stayed on the plan's alternatives when an assertion missed.
test.read_point: After the launch's first review milestone

title: Justify any price difference between segments with a story, not silent mechanics
hypothesis: If a store offers different prices to different segments (member pricing, regional pricing, loyalty pricing) and explicitly justifies the difference with a story the customer accepts, then trust is protected, because silently varying price mechanics without an accepted reason risks a customer feeling deceived if they discover it.

signal.check: Different prices are shown to different customer segments with no visible or stated reason a customer would accept if they compared notes with another segment.

risk.note: Undisclosed price variation risks a trust incident if discovered.

prerequisites: An existing or planned segment-based pricing structure
steps: List every segment-based price difference currently in place (member, regional, loyalty, first-time).
For each, write the story or reason a customer in the higher-priced segment would accept if they saw it.
State that reason somewhere the customer can see it, not just internally.
Remove or redesign any price difference with no acceptable story.
Monitor support tickets and reviews for price-fairness complaints after the change.

test.method: Track price-fairness complaints in support tickets and reviews before and after adding the stated reason.
test.measure: Volume of price-fairness complaints.

title: Budget for community management specifically for the post-launch lull
hypothesis: If community management is planned and budgeted specifically for the period after launch excitement fades, then engagement does not collapse when organic momentum drops, because a community left to sustain itself after the initial spike typically declines without deliberate maintenance.

signal.check: Community or launch-excitement content planning stops at the launch window, with no specific plan or owner for the weeks after initial excitement fades.

risk.note: A resourcing and planning decision.

prerequisites: An active community or launch-driven audience
steps: Identify the expected date the initial launch excitement will taper off.
Name an owner and a content or engagement plan specifically for the weeks after that point.
Budget time or spend for that post-launch period, not just the launch window itself.
Track engagement through the transition to see if the plan holds the level.
Adjust the post-launch plan based on what actually sustains engagement.

test.method: Track community engagement week over week through the launch and post-launch period.
test.measure: Engagement level in the weeks after launch excitement typically fades.

title: Anchor a company-wide position on 1 attribute that spans the whole range
hypothesis: If a company-wide, not product-line, position is anchored on 1 attribute that spans every product the store sells, then the corporate story stays credible, because vague platforms like diversification or our-people-are-our-asset create a credibility gap a smaller company cannot close.

signal.check: The company's own about page or corporate positioning claims a vague platform, such as diversification or our people, instead of 1 attribute that spans every product line.

risk.note: A messaging change to the about page and corporate copy.

prerequisites: A product range with more than 1 distinct line or category
steps: List every product line or category the company sells.
Find 1 attribute genuinely true of every line, not just the flagship one.
Write the corporate about page and messaging around that 1 attribute.
Drop vague platforms like diversification or our-people-are-our-asset from corporate copy.
Check every new product line against the attribute before it launches.

test.method: Ask 5 people unfamiliar with the brand what the company stands for after reading the about page.
test.measure: Whether answers converge on the intended single attribute.

title: Score the brand and every competitor 1 to 10 on real category attributes
hypothesis: If the brand and every named competitor are scored 1 to 10 on the category's real attributes by real prospects, then the position gets built on the attribute the brand already wins, not the ones it is trying to fix, because a hidden strength is often more ownable than a fixed weakness.

signal.check: Positioning work is based on where the brand wants to improve rather than on a scored comparison against every named competitor across real category attributes.

risk.note: A research exercise before a positioning decision.

prerequisites: A list of real category attributes and named competitors
Access to real prospects or customers for scoring
steps: List the attributes that plausibly matter to the buying decision in this category.
Have real prospects score the brand and every named competitor 1 to 10 on each attribute.
Look for the attribute where the brand ranks first, even if it ranks last elsewhere.
Build the position and copy around that winning attribute.
Repeat the same scoring 12 to 15 months later to confirm the position moved.

test.method: Run the attribute scoring survey now and again 12 to 15 months after the position ships.
test.measure: Change in the brand's rank on the chosen attribute.
test.read_point: 12 to 15 months after the position launches

title: Diagnose which messaging era the category is in before writing a positioning claim
hypothesis: If the category is first diagnosed as being in a product-feature era, an image era or a mind-share positioning era, then the store leads with the right kind of claim (a feature claim, an image claim, or a position claim), instead of defaulting to a features pitch in a category where features no longer differentiate.

signal.check: The category is treated as still in a features-first era by default, with no check of whether competitors have already moved to image or positioning-based claims.

risk.note: A diagnostic step before writing new positioning copy.

prerequisites: A view of how top competitors currently message in this category
steps: Review the top competitors' current homepage and ad claims in this category.
Classify the category's dominant messaging as feature-led, image-led or position-led.
Check whether the store's own current claim matches or lags that era.
Rewrite the lead claim to match or move ahead of the category's current era.
Recheck the category's messaging era periodically as competitors shift.

test.method: Compare the store's own claim style against a review of the top 5 competitors' current claims.
test.measure: Whether the store's claim matches, lags or leads the category's dominant era.
test.read_point: Before the next major positioning or homepage rewrite

title: As category leader, reinforce the original claim instead of saying we're number 1
hypothesis: If a category-leading brand reinforces the original claim that earned its position, or sells the category itself, instead of running we're-number-1 ads, then leadership perception holds, because a we're-number-1 claim reads as insecure to those who already know and does not transfer belief to those who do not.

signal.check: A category-leading brand's advertising states its rank (we're number 1, the leading brand) instead of reinforcing the specific claim or category behavior that earned the leadership.

risk.note: A messaging change for an already-leading brand.

prerequisites: A brand that genuinely holds the leading position in its category
steps: Identify the original claim or behavior that earned the brand's leading position.
Check current advertising for a we're-number-1 or leading-brand style claim.
Replace that claim with a reinforcement of the original earned claim, or a category-wide message that positions competitors as followers.
A/B test the reinforced claim against the rank-based claim.
Track brand perception and conversion for both.

test.method: A/B test reinforced-claim creative against rank-based creative for the leading brand.
test.measure: Brand perception survey score and conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Give a hero product feature its own distinct, brandable name
hypothesis: If a hero product feature is given its own distinct, brandable name instead of a generic spec label, then the store can own that feature in the prospect's mind, because a named feature is easier to remember, repeat and defend than a generic technical description competitors can copy in wording.

signal.check: A genuinely differentiating product feature is described only with a generic technical or spec label, with no distinct, brandable name of its own.

risk.note: A naming exercise for 1 feature.

prerequisites: A genuinely differentiating hero feature with no name of its own
steps: Identify the 1 hero feature that most differentiates the product.
Generate several candidate names for that feature, screened for the same naming qualities used for a brand name.
Check trademark and domain availability for the leading candidate.
Use the named feature consistently across PDP, packaging and ads.
Track recall of the named feature versus the prior generic label.

test.method: Survey customers on whether they recall the named feature before and after the rename.
test.measure: Feature recall rate.
test.read_point: 3 to 6 months after the named feature ships

title: Watch for sales outrunning a product's real mind-share position
hypothesis: If a product's sales are checked against whether a real mind-share position actually backs them, then a short-term hit driven by novelty or trend, not positioning, is caught early, because a star product with no real position behind its sales typically declines fast once novelty fades.

signal.check: A product is selling well with no clear, ownable position behind it, and no one has checked whether the sales trend is durable or trend-driven.

risk.note: A diagnostic review.

prerequisites: A fast-selling product with an unclear or undefined position
steps: Identify any product whose sales are rising quickly with no clear stated position.
Check whether repeat purchase and brand-name search are rising alongside sales, or only the initial sales spike.
If only the spike is real, invest in building an actual position before assuming the trend continues.
Track sales alongside repeat rate and branded search over the following months.
Flag the product for a positioning investment if the gap between sales and position persists.

test.method: Track sales, repeat rate and branded search for the product over the following 2 quarters.
test.measure: Whether sales hold once novelty-driven traffic fades.
test.read_point: 2 quarters after the initial sales spike

title: Reposition a drifted brand by retracing its original founding mission
hypothesis: If an established brand that has drifted is repositioned by retracing its original founding mission and restating it simply, then the reposition feels earned rather than invented, because a simple, true restatement of the founding purpose is easier for both the team and customers to believe than a newly manufactured complex positioning.

signal.check: An established brand's positioning has drifted from its founding purpose, and a reposition is being planned by inventing a new complex story instead of retracing the original mission.

risk.note: A strategy exercise before a reposition.

prerequisites: Access to the brand's own founding documents, early marketing or founder account
steps: Pull the brand's earliest founding materials, first marketing or founder's own account of why it started.
Restate that original mission in 1 simple sentence.
Compare the current positioning against that simple restatement.
Where they diverge, decide whether to return to the original mission or state explicitly why it changed.
Use the simplified original mission as the anchor for the new positioning work.

test.method: Test the retraced-mission positioning statement against the current drifted statement with a small customer or prospect panel.
test.measure: Which statement customers find more credible or memorable.

title: Confirm a trend is durable, not a fad, before committing brand resources
hypothesis: If a trend is checked for steady growth across multiple periods before committing brand resources, instead of reacting to a single spike, then the store avoids over-investing in a fad that reverses quickly.

signal.check: Brand or product resources are being committed to a trend based on a single period's spike, with no check of whether the trend has grown steadily across multiple periods.

risk.note: A due-diligence step before a resourcing decision.

prerequisites: At least 2 to 3 periods of data on the trend in question
steps: Pull search, sales or social data for the trend across at least the last 2 to 3 periods.
Check whether growth is steady and broadening, or a single spike already flattening.
Commit meaningful brand resources only to a trend showing steady, broadening growth.
For a single-spike pattern, test with a small, reversible commitment instead.
Review the classification again before increasing the commitment.

test.method: Track the trend's growth pattern for 1 additional period before increasing commitment.
test.measure: Whether growth continues, flattens or reverses.
test.read_point: 1 additional reporting period after the initial spike

title: Find the pack space that is regulatorily fixed before budgeting design effort
hypothesis: If the team first identifies the percentage of pack space that is fixed by regulation, such as a barcode, mandated text or origin, and spends design effort only on the remaining space, then design budget is not wasted fighting constraints that cannot move.

signal.check: Packaging design time is being spent debating mandated, non-negotiable elements instead of concentrating on the space actually available for brand expression.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source cites roughly 35 percent of a can as untouchable

risk.note: A scoping exercise before a design pass.

prerequisites: A physical, regulated packaged product
steps: List every mandated element on the package, such as barcode, legal text, origin and size disclosures.
Calculate the share of total pack space those elements occupy.
Brief the design team only on the remaining, genuinely controllable space.
Resolve QA-versus-design conflicts over mandated elements before design starts, not during review.
Revisit the split whenever packaging regulation changes.

test.method: Compare design review cycle time before and after the controllable-space brief is used.
test.measure: Number of design revision rounds caused by mandated-element conflicts.

title: Model the full retail margin stack before setting a shelf price
hypothesis: If shelf price is set only after modeling the retailer's cut, distribution cost and a separate trade-spend budget, then the brand avoids committing to a retail account it cannot actually afford to service at the gross margin it needs.

signal.check: A shelf price or retail buyer pitch is being prepared with no explicit model of retailer margin, distribution cost and trade-spend budget.

expected_effect.size: target 50 percent or more after retailer margin and distribution costs, per 1 source's rule of thumb

risk.note: A pricing model; wrong inputs can misprice a retail launch before it starts.

prerequisites: Cost of goods, retailer margin ask and distribution cost estimates
steps: Set the proposed shelf price.
Subtract the retailer's expected margin cut to find the sell-in price.
Subtract distribution and shipping cost from the sell-in price to find true margin over cost of goods.
Separately budget a trade-spend percentage for promotions and activation.
Confirm the resulting gross margin meets the store's own minimum before proceeding.

test.method: Run the full margin model against the actual retailer's quoted terms before signing.
test.measure: Resulting gross margin percentage against the store's minimum threshold.
test.read_point: Before any retail buyer agreement is signed

title: Weigh direct distribution against a distributor before committing a route
hypothesis: If direct distribution and a third-party distributor are weighed explicitly on margin kept versus reach gained before committing, then the store picks the route that fits its actual supply-chain capacity instead of defaulting to whichever route was easiest to start.

signal.check: A distribution route, direct versus distributor, is being chosen by default or convenience, with no explicit comparison of margin kept against reach and risk.

expected_effect.size: distributors typically take roughly 15 to 25 percent margin for reach, per 1 source

risk.note: A distribution contract can be hard to unwind once volume depends on it.

prerequisites: A defined product ready for wholesale or retail distribution
steps: List the margin a distributor would take versus the margin kept under direct distribution.
List the supply-chain, warehousing and staffing cost direct distribution would add.
List the accounts and reach a distributor already services that direct distribution cannot reach quickly.
Weigh the 2 routes against the store's actual current supply-chain capacity.
Choose the route and document the reasoning before signing any distribution agreement.

test.method: Track fulfilment cost and reach for the chosen route over 1 quarter against the rejected route's estimated numbers.
test.measure: Realized margin and reach versus the pre-decision estimate.
test.read_point: 1 quarter after the route is live

title: Win 1 anchor account yourself before handing it to a distributor or broker
hypothesis: If the brand proves demand with 1 paying anchor account before approaching a distributor or broker, then the distributor takes the brand seriously with real proof instead of being asked to prove demand it has no incentive to chase for an unproven brand.

signal.check: The brand is approaching a distributor or broker to find its first retail or wholesale customer instead of selling to 1 account directly first.

risk.note: A sales-sequencing decision.

prerequisites: A product ready to sell into a wholesale or retail account
steps: Identify 1 realistic anchor account to sell to directly, without a broker.
Pitch and close that account using the founder's own relationships and effort.
Prove sell-through and reorder demand at that 1 account.
Approach a distributor or broker only with that proven account as evidence.
Hand the proven account to the distributor or broker once the relationship scales beyond founder capacity.

test.method: Track time to first distributor meeting with versus without a proven anchor account in hand.
test.measure: Whether the distributor pitch converts faster with proof attached.
test.read_point: At the next distributor or broker pitch

title: Enter a major retail account only once supply chain can survive the volume
hypothesis: If a major retail account is only entered once supply chain and unit economics can survive the requested volume, then a bad first sell-through does not permanently damage the brand's shelf position, because retailers rarely give a second chance after a failed launch.

signal.check: A major retail account is being pursued or accepted with no explicit check that production, supply chain and unit economics can survive the requested volume.

risk.note: A failed first sell-through into a major account is very hard to recover from.

prerequisites: A retail account offer or opportunity of meaningful scale
steps: Estimate the volume the retail account would require at expected velocity.
Check current production capacity and lead time against that volume.
Check unit economics still hold at that volume and price.
If capacity or economics fall short, delay entry or negotiate a smaller initial commitment.
Only proceed once the store can survive the volume without breaking margin or stocking out.

test.method: Model worst-case sell-through velocity against production lead time before signing.
test.measure: Whether modeled worst-case demand stays inside production capacity.

title: Pitch differentiation before data, then pitch proven sales after data
hypothesis: If the first retail buyer pitch leads with differentiation and incrementality and the second pitch leads with proven store-level sales, then each pitch uses the evidence actually available at that stage instead of overselling unproven numbers or underselling a proven track record.

signal.check: A retail buyer pitch is using the same structure regardless of whether store-level sales data exists yet.

risk.note: A pitch-structure change.

prerequisites: A retail buyer meeting scheduled
steps: Before any store-level sales data exists, build the pitch around category differentiation and the incrementality the brand brings.
Include any existing DTC audience size that could be redirected into the retailer's stores.
Once store-level sales data exists, rebuild the pitch to lead with proven per-store sales.
Frame the retailer's current lack of the product as a missed-incrementality gap.
Send the founder to early pitches rather than delegating to a broker.

test.method: Track meeting-to-commitment conversion rate for pitches before versus after store-level data exists.
test.measure: Retail buyer conversion rate by pitch stage.
test.read_point: After a set of retail buyer pitches at each stage

title: Put each SKU or format in the channel where that purchase already happens
hypothesis: If each SKU or format is placed in the channel where that type of purchase already happens (a daily-use item in grocery, an impulse add-on in DTC or marketplace), instead of trying to train a new purchase behavior in the wrong channel, then conversion improves, because shoppers rarely change where they already shop for a given item type.

signal.check: A SKU or format is being pushed into a channel where that type of purchase does not already happen, with no channel-fit check against existing shopper behavior.

risk.note: A channel allocation decision.

prerequisites: Multiple SKUs or formats and multiple sales channels
steps: List each SKU or format and the channel it currently sells through.
Research where shoppers already buy that type of product (grocery, DTC, Amazon, in-store).
Reallocate marketing and distribution effort toward the channel that matches existing purchase behavior for each SKU.
Track conversion and sell-through by channel after reallocation.
Stop trying to train a new purchase behavior in a channel that does not fit.

test.method: Compare conversion and sell-through for a SKU in its matched channel versus a mismatched channel.
test.measure: Conversion rate and AOV by channel.
test.read_point: After 1 quarter in the reallocated channel

title: Treat a stockout on a daily-use SKU as an operational failure, not a flex
hypothesis: If a stockout on a daily-use or subscription SKU is treated as a demand-planning failure that risks permanent customer substitution, and scarcity messaging is reserved only for genuine limited-edition drops, then the brand avoids losing daily-use customers to a competitor during a stockout.

signal.check: A stockout on a daily-use or subscription SKU is being treated as a positive demand signal or ignored, with no urgency to fix the underlying demand-planning gap.

risk.note: A customer lost to a competitor during a stockout may not return.

prerequisites: A daily-use or subscription SKU with any stockout history
steps: Classify each SKU as daily-use/subscription or limited-edition/drop-based.
For daily-use SKUs, set a demand-planning alert well before projected stockout.
Treat any daily-use stockout as a required root-cause review, not a marketing win.
Reserve scarcity or sold-out messaging only for genuine limited-edition drops.
Track repeat rate for customers who experienced a daily-use stockout versus those who did not.

test.method: Compare repeat purchase rate for customers who hit a stockout on a daily-use SKU against those who did not.
test.measure: 90-day repeat purchase rate.

title: Run demand planning as 1 integrated model, not a reorder-by-feel habit
hypothesis: If demand planning combines pipeline, velocity, cash, inventory and lead time into 1 model instead of separate, feel-based reorder decisions, then stockouts and overstock both drop, because misjudging any 1 input alone can still produce a costly surprise even when the others look fine.

signal.check: Reorder and production decisions are made from a single input (last month's sales, or a gut feel) with no combined model of pipeline, velocity, cash and lead time.

risk.note: A planning process change; early misses are likely while the model calibrates.

prerequisites: Sales velocity, current inventory, supplier lead time and cash position data
steps: Pull current sales velocity, inventory on hand, supplier lead time and available cash into 1 view.
Set a reorder trigger point that accounts for all 4 inputs together, not just 1.
Recalculate the model at a fixed cadence (weekly or monthly) rather than reacting ad hoc.
Track actual stockouts and overstock against the model's predictions.
Refine the model's assumptions each cycle based on the gap between prediction and reality.

test.method: Compare stockout and overstock incidents in the 2 quarters before and after adopting the integrated model.
test.measure: Number of stockout and overstock incidents.

title: Choose custom formulation over white-label only when owning the IP matters
hypothesis: If custom formulation is chosen over white-label only when owning the formula's IP genuinely matters for a future acquisition or licensing story, then the brand avoids spending extra time and capital on ownership it does not actually need, since white-label is a legitimate, faster, cheaper strategy when the brand itself is the real moat.

signal.check: A new product's formulation strategy (custom versus white-label) is being decided without asking whether owning the formula IP is actually needed for the brand's future plans.

risk.note: A strategic decision made before committing manufacturing spend.

prerequisites: A new product formulation decision underway
steps: Ask whether owning the exact formula matters for a future acquisition, licensing deal or defensible claim.
If yes, budget the extra time and capital for custom formulation with an outside formulator.
If no, use white-label and put the saved time and capital into brand-building instead.
Document the reasoning so the decision is not revisited without new information.
Revisit the decision only if the brand's future plans genuinely change.

test.method: Compare time-to-launch and cost for the chosen path against the rejected path's estimate.
test.measure: Time to launch and total formulation cost.

title: Set a key spec meaningfully above category norms using real usage data
hypothesis: If a key ingredient or spec is set meaningfully above category norms using real usage-window data, and the resulting gap is used as the headline differentiation claim, then the store earns a genuine, defensible claim instead of a marketing-only differentiation that competitors can dismiss.

signal.check: The product's headline spec matches the category norm, with no attempt to set it meaningfully higher based on real usage data and use that gap as the claim.

risk.note: Changing a core spec may require reformulation or re-engineering.

prerequisites: Real usage-window or usage-context data for the product category
steps: Gather real usage-window data for the category (how long, how often, under what conditions the product is used).
Calculate the spec level that would meaningfully out-deliver the category norm for that usage window.
Set the product's spec at that level, verified with real testing, not just marketing copy.
Use the resulting gap versus category norms as the headline differentiation claim.
Track whether the claim moves conversion and whether competitors respond.

test.method: A/B test PDP copy leading with the data-grounded spec claim against the current generic claim.
test.measure: Conversion rate and AOV.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Build a multi-format product line that cross-sells across channels
hypothesis: If the store runs more than 1 product format at different price and margin points that cross-sell into each other across channels, then a customer discovered through 1 format can be converted through another, because each format can serve a different discovery or purchase context while reinforcing the same brand.

signal.check: The store sells only 1 product format, with no lower-commitment or higher-margin companion format designed to cross-sell customers discovered elsewhere.

risk.note: A new-format launch carries its own production and inventory risk.

prerequisites: A hero product format with an established core customer
steps: Identify a lower-commitment or higher-margin companion format for the same core customer (a sample size, a single-use format, a different channel-fit format).
Launch the companion format in the channel where it naturally fits (a sample at an event, a single-use pack on a marketplace).
Track how many companion-format buyers later buy the core format, and vice versa.
Adjust channel and pricing for each format based on the cross-sell pattern.
Expand the halo only once cross-sell between the first 2 formats is proven.

test.method: Track the share of companion-format buyers who convert to the core format within 90 days.
test.measure: Cross-format conversion rate.
test.read_point: 90 days after the companion format launches

title: Split influencer spend into a brand-credibility tier and a revenue tier, with a brand-fit veto
hypothesis: If influencer or athlete spend is split into a small brand-credibility tier where low direct ROI is tolerated and a larger revenue tier judged on ROI, and every partner is screened with a hard brand-fit veto regardless of ROI, then the program builds both credibility and revenue without a high-ROI but off-brand partner damaging the store's position.

signal.check: Influencer or ambassador spend is judged only on direct ROI, with no separate brand-credibility tier and no brand-fit veto applied regardless of ROI.

risk.note: A budget-allocation and screening policy.

prerequisites: An existing or planned influencer or ambassador program
steps: Split the influencer budget into a small brand-credibility tier (a few elite, highly aligned partners) and a larger volume tier judged on revenue.
Set a brand-fit veto: reject any partner who does not visually or tonally fit the brand, no matter how strong their expected ROI.
Track the credibility tier on brand lift and community signals, not direct ROI.
Track the volume tier on ROI and CAC as usual.
Review both tiers separately at each budget cycle.

test.method: Track brand-lift and community engagement for the credibility tier separately from ROI for the volume tier.
test.measure: Brand lift for the credibility tier; ROAS and NCPA for the volume tier.

title: Default collabs to non-competitive brands serving the same ICP
hypothesis: If a brand collaboration defaults to a non-competitive brand serving the same ideal customer, and a same-category exception requires real personal trust and a genuinely different demographic, then the collab reaches new relevant customers without training them to compare the store against a direct competitor.

signal.check: A brand collaboration is being considered or run with no explicit check of whether the partner competes in the same category, or whether it reaches the same ideal customer from a different angle.

risk.note: A screening step before a partnership agreement.

prerequisites: A candidate brand collaboration under consideration
steps: Check whether the candidate partner would ever plausibly enter the store's own category, or vice versa.
Default to no partnership if the categories overlap.
Confirm the partner reaches the same ideal customer from a different angle before proceeding.
If a same-category exception is being considered, require a documented, genuine personal trust relationship and a materially different demographic.
Underwrite time and capital costs of the collab only after the category-overlap screen passes.

test.method: Track new-customer quality (repeat rate, AOV) from a screened collab against an unscreened past collab.
test.measure: New-customer repeat rate and AOV from the collab audience.

title: Offer produced content as negotiating currency to partners who lack it
hypothesis: If the brand offers its own produced content (photo, video) as negotiating currency to partners, athletes or collaborators who lack production capability, instead of or alongside cash, then partnership costs drop, because content production is often worth more to a resource-constrained partner than an equivalent cash amount.

signal.check: Every partnership or collaboration negotiation defaults to a cash-only offer, with no consideration of produced content as an alternative or supplementary currency.

risk.note: A negotiation-tactic change.

prerequisites: An in-house or affordable content production capability
steps: Identify a partner, athlete or collaborator with limited content production capability of their own.
Offer produced content (photos, video, edited assets) as part or all of the partnership value.
Estimate the market value of that content to make the offer concrete.
Track whether the content-inclusive offer closes deals faster or at lower cash cost.
Build a standing content-package offer for future partnership negotiations.

test.method: Compare deal-closure rate and cash cost for content-inclusive offers against cash-only offers.
test.measure: Closure rate and cash cost per partnership.
test.read_point: After a set of comparable partnership negotiations

title: Buy expert practitioner time for a specific capability gap instead of a full hire
hypothesis: If a specific capability gap (such as pitching a major retail buyer) is filled by paying for expert practitioner time rather than hiring a full-time senior person, then the team gets the needed judgment quickly and cheaply, because a 1-time or occasional expert session can close a narrow gap without the cost and time of a permanent hire.

signal.check: A specific, narrow capability gap is being addressed by starting a lengthy senior hiring process instead of buying 1 or a few expert practitioner sessions first.

risk.note: A short-term spend instead of a long-term hiring commitment.

prerequisites: A defined, narrow capability gap and access to a paid expert or mentor network
steps: Define the specific capability gap narrowly (for example, pitching a specific type of retail buyer).
Find and pay for 1 or a few sessions with a practitioner who has genuinely done that task before.
Bring the relevant team members to the session so the knowledge spreads.
Apply the session's guidance to the immediate task at hand.
Only pursue a full-time hire if the gap keeps recurring after the expert session.

test.method: Compare outcome quality (pitch success, decision quality) for the task before and after the expert session.
test.measure: Task outcome quality.
test.read_point: Immediately after applying the expert's guidance

title: Hire generalists early, then narrow specialists as revenue scales
hypothesis: If early hires are generalists who do a bit of everything and specialists are hired only once revenue crosses a meaningful threshold, then the team stays lean and flexible early and gains deep expertise exactly where it starts to matter, instead of over-hiring specialists a small team cannot yet fully use.

signal.check: An early-stage store is hiring narrow specialists before it has enough scale or revenue to keep them fully utilized, or a scaling store is still relying only on generalists past the point specialization would help.

risk.note: A hiring-sequence policy.

prerequisites: A revenue trajectory and hiring plan
steps: Set a rough revenue threshold at which the store will start hiring narrow specialists instead of generalists.
Below that threshold, hire generalists who can cover multiple functions.
At and above the threshold, hire the best specialist for each critical function (content, paid media, creative direction, demand planning) one at a time.
Review the threshold periodically as the store's own economics become clearer.
Avoid hiring a specialist role before the store has enough volume to use it fully.

test.method: Review team utilization and output quality before and after crossing the specialist-hiring threshold.
test.measure: Output quality and role utilization by function.

title: Screen hires for lean execution autonomy, not resume pedigree
hypothesis: If candidates are screened for autonomous execution at a lean company, using specific probes about what they owned end-to-end and how large their prior support team was, instead of resume pedigree alone, then the store avoids hiring someone who cannot function without the large support structure a bigger company gave them.

signal.check: Hiring decisions are made mostly on brand-name company experience or title, with no specific probe into how autonomously the candidate actually worked or how large their support team was.

risk.note: An interview-process addition.

prerequisites: An open role at a lean, fast-moving store
steps: Add 1 interview question asking what the candidate owned end-to-end without a team at their prior role.
Ask how large their support team was at their most recent fast-growing company, and at what stage they joined it.
Ask what they would say if asked why they'd leave in 3 months, even after being told they're doing great; note if they dodge it.
Weigh autonomy and directness of these answers alongside, not instead of, relevant experience.
Track new-hire performance against these interview signals after 90 days.

test.method: Track 90-day performance for hires screened with the autonomy questions against prior hires screened without them.
test.measure: 90-day performance review outcome.

title: Treat decision and response speed as the small brand's real competitive edge
hypothesis: If the team deliberately pushes decision and response timelines down (from a week to a few days) and uses response speed as a screen for partners and hires, then the store competes on speed instead of trying to out-resource better-capitalized incumbents, because speed compounds across many small decisions over time.

signal.check: Internal decisions and external responses (to investors, partners, vendors) routinely take a week or more with no deliberate push to shorten the cycle.

risk.note: An operating-pace policy.

prerequisites: None
steps: Track how long the last 5 to 10 meaningful decisions took from question to answer.
Set a target to cut that cycle time meaningfully, for example from a week to 3 or 4 days.
Use how quickly a partner, vendor or candidate responds as part of how the store evaluates them.
Remove approval steps that add delay without adding real judgment.
Track decision cycle time over time as an operating metric.

test.method: Track average decision cycle time before and after the deliberate speed push.
test.measure: Average days from question to decision.

title: Reduce first-production-run risk with a lower-MOQ format choice
hypothesis: If a lower-minimum-order-quantity format (such as a sleeve label instead of a fully printed container) is chosen for a first production run, then cash risk on unproven demand drops, because a lower MOQ format lets the store test real demand before committing capital to a large, fully customized run.

signal.check: A first production run is being committed at a high minimum order quantity for a fully custom format, with no lower-MOQ alternative considered for validating demand first.

risk.note: A format choice, not a large capital commitment.

prerequisites: A new product entering its first production run
steps: Ask the manufacturer for the MOQ difference between a fully custom format and a lower-MOQ alternative (such as a sleeve label or simpler packaging).
Choose the lower-MOQ format for the first run if the difference is meaningful.
Validate real demand at that smaller scale before committing to the fully custom format.
Move to the fully custom format only once demand is proven.
Track cash tied up in the first run against the demand it actually validated.

test.method: Compare cash tied up and demand validated for a lower-MOQ first run against a full-MOQ commitment.
test.measure: Cash conversion days and sell-through rate on the first run.
test.read_point: After the first run sells through or stalls

title: Use units and dollars per store per week as the real retail KPI
hypothesis: If retail performance is tracked as units and dollars per store per week, not just door count, then the store can tell whether a retail account is actually working, because a high door count with low per-store velocity is a warning sign the retailer will notice before the brand does.

signal.check: Retail success is being reported and celebrated as a door count with no per-store velocity metric tracked alongside it.

risk.note: A reporting change.

prerequisites: Point-of-sale or retailer-reported sell-through data by store
steps: Pull sell-through data by individual store, not just aggregate retailer sales.
Calculate units and dollars sold per store per week.
Set a minimum velocity threshold below which an account is flagged for review.
Run a 30-day review cycle: change 1 lever (price, promotion or placement) and re-measure velocity.
Report velocity per store alongside door count in every retail update.

test.method: Track units and dollars per store per week for each retail account on a rolling 30-day cycle.
test.measure: Change in per-store velocity after each lever change.

title: Design a limited collab as a deliberate bridge into a bigger retail channel
hypothesis: If a limited collaboration product is designed specifically as a bridge into a bigger retail or distribution channel the brand cannot reach alone, checked against whether it still fulfills the core mission, then the collab expands reach without diluting the brand's core positioning.

signal.check: A collaboration opportunity into a larger retail or distribution channel is being considered with no explicit check that it still fulfills the brand's core mission.

risk.note: A collab that misses the mission-fit check can dilute brand positioning.

prerequisites: An opportunity to collaborate with a partner that has access to a bigger channel
steps: Identify a channel the brand wants to reach but cannot access alone.
Find a partner with genuine access to that channel and a compatible audience.
Design the collab product and check it explicitly against the brand's core mission before proceeding.
Launch the collab as a limited, clearly branded bridge, not a permanent line extension.
Track how many customers from the new channel convert to the core brand afterward.

test.method: Track post-collab conversion of new-channel customers into the core brand's regular customer base.
test.measure: Conversion rate of collab-acquired customers to repeat core-brand customers.

title: Screen investors for operator experience and behavior, not just check size
hypothesis: If investors are screened for real operating experience and behavior, not just check size, and red flags surfacing during diligence are treated as disqualifying, then the store avoids capital that comes with limited-information, quarterly-only oversight and outsized influence over decisions the investor does not understand operationally.

signal.check: Fundraising or capital decisions are being made based mainly on check size or valuation, with no screen for the investor's own operating experience or behavior during diligence.

risk.note: An investor relationship is hard to undo once capital is accepted.

prerequisites: A fundraising process with more than 1 candidate investor
steps: For each candidate investor, ask about their own direct operating experience, not just their portfolio or fund size.
Expose the candidate investor to the founder's own network or a reference check before committing.
Note any red flag that surfaces (poor treatment of a reference, evasive answers, pressure tactics).
Prefer an investor who can engage with operating detail over one who will judge the business from limited quarterly information.
Disqualify a candidate investor if a real red flag surfaces, regardless of check size.

test.method: Track post-investment friction or disagreement rate for investors selected with versus without the screening process.
test.measure: Frequency and severity of founder-investor friction in the first year.

title: Default to sales as the single forcing metric for a defined stretch
hypothesis: If the team picks sales as the single forcing metric for a defined stretch of months while still tracking channel composition and margin alongside it, then internal debate over which metric matters gets resolved simply, because a single clear metric focuses effort while the paired margin check prevents it from masking a unit-economics problem.

signal.check: The team is debating which metric matters most for a growth phase with no single forcing metric chosen, or sales is used as the only metric with no margin or channel check alongside it.

risk.note: A focus decision, paired with a margin check to avoid masking problems.

prerequisites: A defined growth phase with internal disagreement on priority metrics
steps: Set sales as the single forcing metric for a defined stretch, such as 3 to 6 months.
Still track which channel drove each sale and the resulting margin, even while sales is the headline metric.
Review the paired margin and channel data monthly to catch any unit-economics problem sales alone would hide.
Communicate the single-metric focus clearly to the team to resolve competing priorities.
Revisit the choice of forcing metric at the end of the defined stretch.

test.method: Track sales growth alongside margin and channel composition through the defined stretch.
test.measure: Sales growth versus margin trend over the period.
test.read_point: At the end of the defined stretch

title: Manage every influencer or affiliate relationship with explicit KPIs
hypothesis: If every influencer, affiliate or broker relationship is managed with explicit KPIs and regular follow-up, not a set-and-forget arrangement, then the program surfaces its real performers faster, because consistency and accountability, not raw follower count, predict which partners actually drive results over time.

signal.check: Influencer, affiliate or broker relationships are set up once with no explicit KPI or regular follow-up cadence to check performance.

risk.note: A program-management process change.

prerequisites: An existing or planned influencer, affiliate or broker program
steps: Set an explicit KPI (posts per period, click volume, conversion, or consistency of output) for every partner in the program.
Set a regular follow-up cadence (weekly or monthly) to check each partner against their KPI.
Flag partners who consistently miss their KPI for a conversation or exit from the program.
Identify partners whose consistency, not just reach, is driving results and consider promoting them to a larger role.
Review the whole program's KPI coverage each quarter.

test.method: Track KPI adherence and resulting output for partners under the new management cadence against the prior set-and-forget approach.
test.measure: Share of partners meeting their KPI and resulting attributable revenue.

title: Score any rebrand or new line against the 9 brand ideals before approval
hypothesis: If any rebrand, new line, packaging system or partnership is scored against 9 ideals (vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability) before approval, then weak proposals get caught before launch, because a qualitative scorecard surfaces gaps a single taste-based approval would miss.

signal.check: A rebrand, new line, packaging system or partnership proposal is being approved on taste or gut feel with no structured check against a written set of brand ideals.

risk.note: A review checklist, not a live change.

prerequisites: A rebrand, new line or partnership proposal ready for review
steps: List the 9 ideals: vision, meaning, authenticity, coherence, flexibility, commitment, value, differentiation, sustainability.
Score the proposal on each ideal, qualitatively, with a brief note for each.
Flag any ideal scoring notably weak as a required revision, not an automatic rejection.
Revise the proposal against the flagged ideals before final approval.
Keep the scorecard on file to compare against future proposals.

test.method: Apply the 9-ideal scorecard to the next 3 major brand proposals before approval.
test.measure: Number of weak ideals caught and revised before launch.
test.read_point: Before each major brand decision ships

title: Verify perception, behavior and performance separately before promising a rebrand's ROI
hypothesis: If a rebrand or identity project is checked for a real change in perception, then behavior, then business performance as 3 separate, verifiable links, instead of promising a revenue outcome from identity work alone, then leadership gets an honest read on what the work actually moved, because each link can succeed or fail independently.

signal.check: A rebrand or identity project is being sold internally on a promised revenue outcome with no plan to check perception change, behavior change and performance change as separate steps.

risk.note: A measurement framework for an already-planned project.

prerequisites: A rebrand or identity project underway or planned
steps: Before launch, define how perception change will be measured (a brand survey, a sentiment check).
Define how behavior change will be measured (site visits, add-to-cart rate, repeat purchase).
Define how business performance will be measured (revenue, margin) separately from the first 2.
Report all 3 separately after launch, not blended into 1 headline number.
Use the pattern (which link succeeded or failed) to diagnose what to fix next.

test.method: Measure perception, behavior and performance separately before and after the rebrand launches.
test.measure: Change in each of the 3 measures.
test.read_point: 3 to 6 months after the rebrand ships

title: Cap any single page or pitch to 1 big idea and at most 3 key messages
hypothesis: If any single homepage, PDP, pitch or press release is capped to 1 big idea and at most 3 key supporting messages, then the audience retains more of what matters, because people at risk of information overload can only reliably hold a small number of messages at once.

signal.check: A homepage, PDP, pitch or press release is carrying more than 1 big idea or more than 3 key messages, with no cap applied before publishing.

risk.note: A copy-editing rule.

prerequisites: A page or pitch draft to audit
steps: List every distinct claim currently on the page or in the pitch.
Identify the single big idea the page is meant to carry.
Cut supporting claims down to the 3 that matter most.
Remove or move every remaining claim to a secondary page or appendix.
Test the capped version against the current uncapped version.

test.method: A/B test the capped page against the current uncapped version, or survey recall after each.
test.measure: Message recall and conversion rate.
test.read_point: After both versions reach a comparable sample size

title: Write the 3-way role split before signing a licensing deal
hypothesis: If a licensing deal explicitly writes out and agrees the 3 role splits (licensor sets strategy and polices trademarks, licensee develops and pays royalties, agent sources and negotiates deals), then disputes and gaps in execution drop, because an unwritten split leaves room for each party to assume the other covers a given duty.

signal.check: A licensing deal is being negotiated or signed with no written, agreed split of licensor, licensee and agent duties.

risk.note: A licensing agreement is a contract; get it right before signing.

prerequisites: A licensing deal under negotiation
steps: List the licensor's duties: strategy, approval of licensees/products/collateral, providing assets and a style guide, registering and policing trademarks.
List the licensee's duties: development, manufacturing, marketing, and reporting royalties.
List any agent's duties: sourcing deals, negotiating, administering royalties, policing the market.
Write the agreed split into the contract explicitly, not left implied.
Review the split at each contract renewal or renegotiation.

test.method: Review dispute or gap incidents for licensing deals with an explicit written split versus past deals without one.
test.measure: Number of role-related disputes or execution gaps.

title: Only display a certification badge the brand actually earned
hypothesis: If a certification or trust badge is displayed on a PDP only after it has been earned through an actual third-party or government test, then the badge functions as a real decision shortcut for the customer, because an implied certification the brand has not actually passed risks a trust-damaging discovery.

signal.check: A certification-style badge or trust mark appears on a PDP or packaging with no verification that the underlying test was actually passed.

risk.note: A false or implied certification claim is a real compliance and trust risk.

prerequisites: A list of every badge or certification mark currently displayed
steps: Audit every certification or trust badge currently displayed on the PDP or packaging.
Verify documentation exists proving the underlying test was actually passed for each one.
Remove any badge that cannot be verified.
Set a rule requiring verification before any new badge is added.
Re-audit badges whenever a certification's terms or the product formulation changes.

test.method: Audit all displayed badges against verification documents.
test.measure: Number of badges with missing or expired verification.
test.read_point: Immediately and at each product reformulation

title: Position a private-label or white-label line on story and value, not on looking cheap
hypothesis: If a private-label or white-label line is positioned on story and value rather than looking generic or cheap, then it can command a better price and perception, because it already sits inside a trusted branded storefront and can spend less on raw recognition and more on product story than a standalone brand would need to.

signal.check: A private-label or white-label line is packaged and priced as a generic, budget alternative with no distinct story or value narrative of its own.

risk.note: A repositioning and packaging investment.

prerequisites: An existing or planned private-label or white-label product line
steps: Choose a master-brand or sub-brand architecture for the private-label line, matching the store's own scale.
Write a genuine story or value narrative for the line, not a generic budget-alternative pitch.
Redesign packaging and PDP copy to carry that story, borrowing credibility from the store's own trusted environment.
A/B test the story-led positioning against the current generic positioning.
Track AOV and margin for the repositioned line.

test.method: A/B test story-led private-label packaging and copy against the current generic version.
test.measure: AOV and gross margin for the line.
test.read_point: After both variants reach a comparable sample size

title: Run the 5-step organic social process before producing content
hypothesis: If organic social content follows a 5-step process (define the objective, find the existing community, decide content on purpose, assign and train an owner, agree measurement in advance), then content stays purposeful and measurable, because skipping straight to posting without these steps leads to reactive, unmeasured content.

signal.check: Organic social content is being produced and posted with no defined objective, no identified existing community, and no measurement plan agreed in advance.

risk.note: A planning process, not a live change.

prerequisites: An existing or planned organic social presence
steps: Define the objective for the channel (customer service, engagement, driving sales, media outreach).
Identify where the target audience already gathers before pushing new content.
Decide what to say based on that objective, not reactive trend-chasing.
Assign and train whoever manages the channel, internally or externally.
Agree in advance how success will be measured, both quantitative and qualitative, and review it regularly.

test.method: Compare content output and measured results before and after adopting the 5-step process.
test.measure: Engagement quality and progress against the agreed measurement plan.

title: Audit a digital experience against 5 experience-design lenses
hypothesis: If a customer-facing digital experience is audited against 5 lenses (ubiquitous, social, semantic, sentient, human) instead of a single usability pass, then gaps a plain usability review would miss get caught, because each lens surfaces a different kind of failure a general review does not specifically probe.

signal.check: A digital experience (site, app, checkout flow) is reviewed only for basic usability, with no structured check against ubiquity, social connection, information relevance, contextual sensing and simple human interaction.

risk.note: A review exercise.

prerequisites: A digital experience ready for review
steps: List the 5 lenses: ubiquitous, social, semantic, sentient, human, as defined in the source's experience-design framework.
Score the current experience on each lens.
Identify the weakest 1 or 2 lenses as the priority fix.
Design and test a fix targeting the weakest lens.
Re-score after the fix ships.

test.method: Score the experience on the 5 lenses before and after a targeted fix.
test.measure: Change in score on the targeted lens.

title: Run the parts-of-speech distillation exercise on top naming candidates
hypothesis: If top naming candidates are split into their component meanings and reassigned across parts of speech (verb, adjective, adverb, noun) as a group discovery exercise, then hidden nuance and key messages surface that a plain up-or-down vote on the whole name would miss.

signal.check: Naming candidates are being voted on as whole words with no exercise breaking each candidate into its component meanings across different parts of speech.

risk.note: A group workshop exercise.

prerequisites: A shortlist of naming candidates
steps: Take each shortlisted naming candidate or its underlying descriptive phrase.
Split it into its component words or roots.
Reassign each component across different parts of speech (as a verb, an adjective, an adverb, a noun).
Discuss as a group what nuance or key message each variation surfaces.
Use the surfaced nuance to refine the finalist copy and messaging, not just the name itself.

test.method: Run the exercise on the current naming shortlist and compare resulting message clarity against the pre-exercise brief.
test.measure: Number of distinct nuances or messages surfaced per candidate.
test.read_point: During the naming shortlist review session

title: Budget legal protection into the cost of every major brand asset
hypothesis: If trademark filing and registration cost is budgeted as part of a brand asset's creation cost, not as an afterthought, then the store avoids launching a name, logo or tagline it cannot actually protect or that later needs an expensive rework.

signal.check: A new name, logo or tagline is being finalized and launched with no trademark filing budget included in the project's cost from the start.

risk.note: Skipping this budget risks a costly rename later if a conflict surfaces.

prerequisites: A new or updated brand asset (name, logo, tagline) in development
steps: Add a line item for trademark search and filing cost to every new brand asset project budget from the start.
Run the trademark search before the asset is finalized, not after launch.
File for registration in the store's primary markets once the asset is locked.
Track filing status and renewal dates going forward.
Treat legal protection cost as part of the asset's true cost when comparing naming or design options.

test.method: Review the last 3 brand asset launches for whether legal protection cost was budgeted from the start.
test.measure: Share of asset launches with legal protection budgeted upfront.
test.read_point: At each future brand asset project kickoff

title: Force clear high or low scores on naming or creative candidates, ban the middle
hypothesis: If reviewers are forced to score naming or creative candidates as clearly high or low, with middling scores banned, then the real signal in the review surfaces, because a cluster of noncommittal middle scores hides the specific quality or flaw that actually matters.

signal.check: Naming or creative candidates are being scored with a wide spread of noncommittal middle-range ratings, with no rule forcing reviewers to commit to a clear high or low.

risk.note: A scoring-rule change.

prerequisites: A candidate set (names, creative concepts) awaiting review scores
steps: Set a scoring scale that bans middle, noncommittal scores (a no-sevens rule on a 1-10 scale, or a forced high/low binary).
Ask each reviewer to score every candidate under that rule.
Review the resulting spread for genuine high and low signal instead of a flat middle cluster.
Use the forced scores to shortlist candidates, not the raw average alone.
Apply the same rule to future naming or creative reviews.

test.method: Compare the score spread from a no-sevens review against a past review using an unconstrained scale.
test.measure: Spread of scores and shortlist agreement among reviewers.
test.read_point: At the next naming or creative review

title: Run naming or creative ideation in individuals or 2-person teams, not large groups
hypothesis: If naming or creative ideation runs in individuals or 2-person teams instead of a 4-to-10-person brainstorm, then output quality improves, because peer pressure and a slow evaluation cascade tend to degrade group brainstorm output once the group passes a small size.

signal.check: Naming or creative ideation sessions are run as large group brainstorms of 4 or more people, with no individual or 2-person alternative tested.

risk.note: A process change to an ideation session.

prerequisites: A naming or creative project needing new candidates
steps: Split the ideation task among individuals or 2-person teams instead of 1 large group session.
Give each individual or pair the same or a slightly varied brief.
Collect each contributor's raw output separately before any group discussion.
Combine and evaluate the pooled output as a separate step.
Compare output volume and quality against a past large-group brainstorm on a similar task.

test.method: Run the next naming or creative task in small teams and compare output against the last large-group brainstorm.
test.measure: Number and quality of usable candidates produced.

title: Generate naming or creative candidates through 3 different information lenses
hypothesis: If naming or creative generation runs through 3 different information lenses (the full product brief, an altered or added detail, a completely unrelated domain), instead of 1 uniform brief, then the candidate space widens, because a differently informed brief structurally reaches ideas the other lenses cannot.

signal.check: Naming or creative generation uses only 1 uniform brief for every contributor, with no deliberate variation in what information each contributor works from.

risk.note: A briefing process change.

prerequisites: A naming or creative project with at least 2 to 3 contributors or generation passes
steps: Write the full, accurate product brief for 1 contributor or pass.
Write a second brief with 1 detail deliberately altered or added.
Write a third brief that withholds the category and instead frames the product from an unrelated angle.
Run generation separately under each brief.
Compare the resulting candidate sets for genuinely different territory.

test.method: Compare the candidate sets generated under the 3 lenses for overlap and distinctiveness.
test.measure: Share of candidates that are genuinely distinct between lenses.
test.read_point: After all 3 generation passes are complete

title: Separate idea generation from evaluation in every ideation session
hypothesis: If instant-rejection language is banned during ideation and judgment is held for a separate, scheduled pass, with contributors managed through encouragement rather than instant critique, then the team produces more distinctive ideas, because killing an idea the moment it surfaces shuts down the problem-solving instinct before it can develop.

signal.check: Ideation sessions mix generation and evaluation together, with ideas being rejected out loud the moment they are proposed.

risk.note: A facilitation-rule change.

prerequisites: A scheduled ideation session
steps: Set an explicit rule banning instant-rejection language during the ideation portion of a session.
Schedule a separate, later session or block for evaluating the ideas generated.
Coach facilitators to respond to a raw idea with encouragement or a reframing question, not immediate critique.
Run the evaluation pass against written criteria, not in-the-moment reactions.
Track whether more distinctive (not just more) ideas survive to the shortlist.

test.method: Compare the shortlist from a session using generation-evaluation separation against a past session without it.
test.measure: Number of genuinely distinctive ideas reaching the shortlist.

title: Run an approximate-thinking exercise to unlock half-baked ideas
