hypothesis: If contributors are asked to share deliberately unfinished, half-baked ideas along a bizarre-to-safe spectrum instead of only polished or self-censored ones, then the team's creative output spikes, because giving explicit permission to be unfinished removes the fear of instant judgment that normally suppresses distinctive ideas.

signal.check: Ideation sessions only accept polished, fully thought-out contributions, with no explicit permission or structure for sharing rough, unfinished ideas.

risk.note: A facilitation technique.

prerequisites: A scheduled ideation session
steps: Introduce a spectrum from bizarre or absurd at 1 end to safe and workable at the other.
Ask contributors to stop somewhere in the middle and share the unfinished idea as-is, not polished.
Explicitly state that half-baked, unfinished contributions are welcome and expected.
Collect the raw contributions before any evaluation happens.
Reset the framing if the team's output is landing only in the safe, forgettable zone.

test.method: Compare the range and novelty of ideas from a session using the approximate-thinking exercise against a standard brainstorm.
test.measure: Range of the bizarre-to-safe spectrum actually used and resulting idea novelty.

title: Spend a bounded 20 to 30 minutes in unrelated material before finalizing a direction
hypothesis: If someone spends a bounded 20 to 30 minutes in material completely unrelated to the product, looking only for a transferable connection, before finalizing a naming or creative direction, then a genuinely new angle is more likely to surface, because deliberately connecting unrelated material is a real, repeatable source of fresh perspective.

signal.check: A naming or creative direction is being finalized with no deliberate session spent in material unrelated to the product looking for a transferable idea.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 practitioner estimates a new angle roughly 30 percent of the time

risk.note: A bounded personal exercise.

prerequisites: A naming or creative project still open to new direction
steps: Set a 20 to 30 minute timer.
Read or browse material genuinely unrelated to the product's category.
Look only for a transferable connection, metaphor or angle, not a direct answer.
Write down any candidate connection immediately.
Check the connection against the real product facts before using it in a claim.

test.method: Run the bounded session before finalizing the next naming or creative direction and note whether it produced a usable angle.
test.measure: Whether a usable angle was found within the session.

title: Run a small tracking study 90 to 120 days after a name or rebrand launch
hypothesis: If a small tracking study runs 90 to 120 days after a name or rebrand launch, checking recall, category association and correct spelling or search, then the decision to hold or make a further change rests on real data instead of noisy early impressions.

signal.check: A name or rebrand has launched with no planned tracking study to check recall, category association and search behavior at a defined point after launch.

risk.note: A measurement step, not a live change.

prerequisites: A recently launched name or rebrand
steps: Schedule a small tracking study for 90 to 120 days after the name or rebrand launch.
Measure unaided and aided recall of the new name.
Check category association and correct spelling or search behavior.
Compare results to the pre-launch baseline where one exists.
Use the results to decide whether to hold the current direction or make a further change, rather than deciding on small-sample noise.

test.method: Run the tracking survey at 90 to 120 days and compare to the pre-launch baseline.
test.measure: Recall, category association and search accuracy.

title: Keep a cross-category idea archive that different projects feed into over time
hypothesis: If the store keeps 1 theme-based idea or name archive that different product or naming projects feed into over time, then future projects start with a running head start instead of from zero, because unrelated past assignments often turn out to hold a relevant candidate for a later, different project.

signal.check: Each new naming or creative project starts research and idea generation completely from scratch, with no shared archive of past raw material to draw from.

risk.note: A knowledge-management habit.

prerequisites: More than 1 naming or creative project over time
steps: Set up 1 shared archive organized by theme (not by individual product) for raw naming and creative material.
After each project, file the unused but interesting raw material into the relevant theme in the archive.
Check the archive first at the start of each new naming or creative project.
Track how often archived material contributes to a later project's shortlist.
Keep the archive organized as themes grow rather than letting it become an unsorted dump.

test.method: Track how many future naming or creative shortlists include a candidate sourced from the archive.
test.measure: Share of shortlisted candidates sourced from the archive.
test.read_point: At each new project's shortlist stage

title: Write the exact sentence a customer would say about the product to a friend
hypothesis: If the team writes the exact sentence a real customer would say about a candidate product or feature to a friend, then remarkability gets tested concretely, because a specific, non-generic sentence is evidence the product is worth a remark, while an inability to write one signals it needs redesign or a paid-acquisition plan instead of relying on word of mouth.

signal.check: A product or feature is assumed to be remarkable with no attempt to write the specific sentence a customer would actually say about it to a friend.

risk.note: A diagnostic writing exercise.

prerequisites: A candidate product or feature to test
steps: Pick the product or feature to test for remarkability.
Write the exact, specific sentence a real customer would say about it to a friend.
If no specific, non-generic sentence can be written, treat the product as not remarkable as defined here.
Either redesign the product or packaging to earn a genuine sentence, or plan to sell it through paid acquisition instead of organic word of mouth.
Re-run the test after any redesign.

test.method: Ask 5 real or prospective customers what they would tell a friend about the product and compare to the written sentence.
test.measure: Whether customer answers match a specific, non-generic sentence.
test.read_point: Before committing to an organic word-of-mouth strategy for the product

title: Test a candidate niche against 2 viability bounds before committing
hypothesis: If a candidate niche is checked against 2 bounds, too narrow to sustain the business even with total capture, and too broad to avoid being an interchangeable commodity, then the store avoids both under-sized and over-diluted target definitions.

signal.check: A target niche or segment has been chosen with no check against either a too-narrow or a too-broad failure bound.

risk.note: A sizing exercise before committing to a target.

prerequisites: A candidate niche or segment definition
steps: Estimate the total addressable size of the candidate niche.
Check whether even full capture of that niche could sustain the business at its current cost structure.
Check whether the niche is broad enough that the store would just be competing as an interchangeable commodity within it.
Narrow or broaden the definition until it clears both bounds.
Revisit the check whenever the cost structure or ambition changes.

test.method: Model revenue at full capture of the proposed niche against the store's fixed cost base.
test.measure: Whether modeled revenue at full capture clears the business's sustainability threshold.
test.read_point: Before committing marketing resources to the niche

title: Observe real customers directly instead of assuming their needs from your own taste
hypothesis: If the team practices practical empathy by observing real customers directly (support tickets, session recordings, in-person conversations) instead of assuming they understand needs because they would buy the product themselves, then product and copy decisions rest on real behavior instead of an untested personal assumption.

signal.check: Product or copy decisions are being made from the team's own personal taste or assumed preferences, with no direct observation of real customer behavior.

risk.note: A research habit.

prerequisites: Access to support tickets, session recordings or real customers to observe
steps: Before finalizing a product or copy decision, pull a sample of support tickets or session recordings relevant to it.
Watch or read for actual stated needs and behavior, not projected assumptions.
Where possible, talk directly with a few real customers instead of guessing on their behalf.
Adjust the decision based on what was actually observed, even if it differs from personal taste.
Make direct observation a required step before major product or copy decisions.

test.method: Compare a decision made from direct observation against 1 made from assumed preference on a similar past decision.
test.measure: Outcome (conversion, satisfaction) of the observation-informed decision.

title: Open educational video content with promise, proof, then path
hypothesis: If educational or informational video content opens with a concrete promise, then the fastest credible proof, then a short path outline, in that order, then viewers stay longer, because promise and proof answer why to stay while path answers what happens next, and reordering to path-first loses viewers before they know why to care.

signal.check: Educational or informational video content opens with an outline of what will be covered before establishing a concrete payoff or credible reason to keep watching.

risk.note: A script structure change.

prerequisites: Educational or informational video content in production
steps: Write the Promise: the concrete, specific thing the viewer will get.
Write the Proof: the fastest credible reason to believe it, placed as early as possible.
Write the Path: a short outline of what the video covers, in order.
Sequence the video Promise, then Proof, then Path, and ensure the video actually delivers on the stated Path.
A/B test the 3 Ps structure against the current opening structure.

test.method: A/B test videos opening with the 3 Ps structure against the current opening structure.
test.measure: Hook rate and hold rate.
test.read_point: After both variants reach comparable impressions

title: Publish 3 to 4 niche content pieces for every 1 broad content piece
hypothesis: If the content calendar defaults to 3 to 4 hyper-niche pieces for the exact buyer avatar per 1 broad, top-of-funnel piece, adjusting the ratio as buyer-relevant engagement shifts, then the channel grows reach without diluting buyer relevance.

signal.check: The content calendar has no deliberate niche-to-broad ratio, either publishing only niche content with no top-of-funnel reach piece, or the reverse.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source uses roughly 3:1 to 4:1 as a starting ratio

risk.note: A content-calendar policy.

prerequisites: A defined buyer avatar and an active content calendar
steps: Default every content piece to serve the exact buyer avatar.
Schedule 1 broad, top-of-funnel piece for every 3 to 4 niche pieces.
Track raw views for the broad piece and buyer-relevant engagement (comments, DMs, sales-attributed traffic) for the niche pieces separately.
Treat the ratio as adjustable, shifting toward broad if reach is needed or back toward niche if buyer relevance drops.
Review the ratio and its effect on both view volume and buyer engagement each month.

test.method: Track view volume and buyer-relevant engagement by content type over 1 month at the starting ratio.
test.measure: View volume for broad content versus engagement/conversion for niche content.

title: Run a 4-bucket ideation ritual so content never runs out of ideas
hypothesis: If content ideas are captured the instant they occur in 1 low-friction tool, mined weekly from recent real problems, occasionally mined from older lessons, and rarely supplemented with a manufactured stunt piece, then the content pipeline never runs dry, because each bucket draws from a different, renewable source of raw material.

signal.check: Content ideation has no structured capture system and relies on ad hoc inspiration, regularly running short on ideas.

risk.note: A process habit.

prerequisites: 1 low-friction capture tool (a notes app, a running document)
steps: Set up 1 low-friction tool to capture ideas the instant they occur, throughout the day.
Weekly, review the past week's real problems, decisions and client conversations for content topics.
Periodically mine older lessons or belief shifts valuable to someone earlier in the journey.
Occasionally add a higher-effort, manufactured stunt or challenge piece, used sparingly.
Multiply each captured idea across formats (a short clip, a post, a longer piece) instead of using it once.

test.method: Track the content calendar's fill rate and idea source mix before and after adopting the 4-bucket ritual.
test.measure: Share of calendar slots filled from each bucket, and whether the pipeline runs dry.

title: Build a named, teachable framework from your own top-performer data
hypothesis: If a large set of the store's own comparable top-performing executions is collected, every element in each is listed, and only what is common to nearly all is kept and packaged as a named framework, then the resulting method is teachable and repeatable, because it is derived from real, shared patterns rather than 1 person's intuition.

signal.check: The store relies on 1 person's intuition for a repeated task (content hooks, retention actions, pitch structure) with no attempt to derive a named, shared framework from its own top-performing examples.

risk.note: An internal knowledge-building exercise.

prerequisites: A large enough set of the store's own comparable executions (top content, top retention accounts, top pitches)
steps: Collect a large set of the store's own comparable top-performing executions for the task in question.
List every distinct element or action present in each example.
Cross out elements that do not recur across nearly all examples.
Isolate the small number of universal elements that remain.
Package the result memorably (an acronym or alliteration) and apply it going forward instead of re-deriving the decision each time.

test.method: Apply the derived framework to the next few executions and compare their performance against the prior ungoverned approach.
test.measure: Performance of executions built with the framework versus without it.
test.read_point: After a comparable number of executions under each approach

title: Interview your top-retention customer cohort to build a standard retention program
hypothesis: If a strict, low-churn or top-retention customer cohort is interviewed for every action each one takes to stay engaged, and only the actions shared by nearly all are kept, then the resulting standard retention program reflects real shared behavior instead of 1 customer's idiosyncratic habits.

signal.check: The store's retention or onboarding program was designed from assumption or 1 example customer, with no structured interview of its own top-retention cohort.

risk.note: A research exercise before a retention program redesign.

prerequisites: Customer data to identify a strict low-churn or top-retention cohort
steps: Define a strict low-churn or top-retention cohort from the customer base.
Interview each cohort member and ask them to list every action they take related to using or re-buying the product.
Cross out idiosyncratic, non-shared actions.
Keep only the actions shared by nearly all cohort members.
Turn the shared actions into the standard retention or onboarding program, not any single member's full playbook.

test.method: Roll out the derived retention program to a new cohort and compare 365-day repeat rate against the prior program.
test.measure: 365-day repeat purchase rate.
test.read_point: 365 days after the new program launches

title: Build long-form video from self-contained beats, each with its own hook
hypothesis: If a long-form video is structured as a sequence of self-contained beats (list, steps, story) and each beat is cut down with its own dedicated hook instead of reusing the parent video's intro, then the resulting short-form cuts perform better, because a cut without its own hook loses viewers who never saw the original context.

signal.check: Long-form video content is cut into shorts by reusing the parent video's original intro or hook, instead of writing a dedicated hook for each cut.

risk.note: A content-production process change.

prerequisites: An existing long-form video production process
steps: Structure the long-form video's outline as a sequence of self-contained beats (a list, a set of steps, or a story).
Let each beat run the length it needs rather than forcing a strict short-form time cap.
When cutting a beat into a short-form piece, write a dedicated hook for that cut instead of reusing the parent video's intro.
Publish the cuts to short-form platforms with their own hooks.
Compare hook rate for dedicated-hook cuts against any past cuts that reused the parent's intro.

test.method: A/B test short-form cuts with a dedicated hook against cuts reusing the parent video's intro.
test.measure: Hook rate and click-through rate.
test.read_point: After both sets of cuts reach comparable impressions

title: Use a low-cost agency for cadence accountability, then build in-house to beat it
hypothesis: If a brand-new content channel starts with a low-cost agency hired purely for posting-cadence accountability, while an in-house team is built in parallel, and the agency is cut only once in-house metrics beat it, then the channel gets off the ground without the founder needing to learn every publishing mechanic personally, while avoiding a premature full in-house build.

signal.check: A new content channel is stalling because no one internally knows the publishing mechanics, and no low-cost agency has been used to enforce cadence while an in-house capability is built.

risk.note: A staged staffing decision; budget for a short overlap period.

prerequisites: A new content channel the store wants to stand up from zero internal expertise
steps: Hire a low-cost agency whose main job is enforcing the store's own posting cadence for the new channel.
Focus the team's own time on making the content itself strong, not on learning publishing mechanics.
Once serious about the channel, hire or assign an in-house lead to manage the agency relationship and build an in-house team in parallel.
Budget for a short period of double-paying during the overlap.
Cut the agency once in-house output beats the agency's own metrics on the same scale.

test.method: Track in-house content metrics against the agency's metrics on the same scale during the overlap period.
test.measure: Cadence consistency and content performance, in-house versus agency.
test.read_point: During the planned overlap period before cutting the agency

title: Evaluate any brand association on influence strength, direction and reach
hypothesis: If a brand-shaping association (a spokesperson, a controversy, a viral moment, a stage or podcast appearance) is evaluated on 3 separate axes, strength of influence, direction toward or away from the brand, and reach, instead of on reach alone, then the store avoids treating a purely high-reach but reputationally negative moment as a win.

signal.check: A brand association opportunity (a sponsorship, a stage appearance, a viral moment) is being evaluated only on expected reach, with no check of its likely direction or strength of influence.

risk.note: A decision framework, not a live change.

prerequisites: A candidate association opportunity to evaluate
steps: For the candidate association, estimate its likely reach.
Separately estimate its likely direction, toward or away from the brand's intended perception.
Separately estimate its likely strength of influence on the audience.
Reject or reshape any opportunity with strong reach but a negative or uncertain direction.
Only proceed with associations that score acceptably on all 3 axes, not reach alone.

test.method: Score the last 3 association decisions retroactively on all 3 axes and compare to how they were originally judged.
test.measure: Whether reach-only judgments missed a direction or influence problem.

title: Shift from content volume to disproportionate polish once you know what performs
hypothesis: If a content channel shifts from ramping volume to disproportionate polish on fewer, higher-quality pieces once it has enough reps to know what performs, then results improve faster than continuing to add average volume, because a real quality gain can produce a much larger view or conversion gain than a proportional effort increase would suggest.

signal.check: A content channel keeps ramping raw volume even though the team already has enough data to know what a strong piece looks like.

expected_effect.size: unknown; 1 source claims a roughly 20 percent retention or CTR gain can produce a much larger view multiple

risk.note: A resourcing shift within an existing content budget.

prerequisites: Enough historical content performance data to know what a strong piece looks like
steps: Review historical content performance to confirm the team knows what a top-performing piece looks like.
Pick 1 upcoming piece to receive disproportionate extra time and polish instead of average effort.
Compare its resulting hook rate and CTR against the recent average of standard-effort pieces.
If the quality gain produces an outsized performance gain, shift more of the content budget toward fewer, higher-effort pieces.
Keep testing the volume-versus-polish balance as the channel matures.

test.method: Compare hook rate and CTR for a disproportionately polished piece against the recent average of standard pieces.
test.measure: Hook rate and CTR lift versus the standard-effort average.

title: Segment buyers by behavior and required treatment, not demographics
hypothesis: If buyers are segmented by behavior and the site or marketing treatment they actually need, not by demographics, and new research time is concentrated on the segments the team does not already understand, then research effort produces more usable insight than researching the customers already known by name.

signal.check: Customer segmentation for a research or redesign project is built on demographic labels, with no check of which segments the team already knows well versus poorly.

risk.note: A research prioritization step.

prerequisites: An upcoming brand or site research project
steps: List the distinct behavioral segments the store serves (not demographic labels).
For each segment, note what site or marketing treatment it actually needs.
Identify which segments the team already knows well by name and behavior.
Concentrate new research time and budget on the segments the team does not already understand.
Update personas or segment definitions based on the new research.

test.method: Compare research output quality for a previously under-researched segment against a well-known segment researched the same way.
test.measure: Number of new, actionable findings per segment.

title: Sequence a site redesign: sitemap, then 2 sample pages, then full build
hypothesis: If a site redesign is sequenced as a full sitemap first, then 2 placeholder-content sample pages to test components and aesthetic, then a full build and gradual rollout, then costly rework is avoided, because testing components and aesthetic on 2 pages first catches problems before they are built across the whole site.

signal.check: A major site redesign is starting full production before a complete sitemap exists or before any placeholder sample pages have tested the core components and aesthetic.

risk.note: A major redesign project; sequencing reduces but does not remove risk.

prerequisites: A planned major site redesign
steps: Build a full sitemap of every page and route the redesign will cover.
Build 2 key pages with placeholder content to test menus, typography, buttons, galleries and the overall aesthetic.
Get sign-off on the 2 sample pages before starting the rest of the build.
Build and roll out the rest of the site gradually, not all at once.
Revisit earlier pages as the team learns from later ones, rather than treating the first pages as untouchable.

test.method: Track design rework requests before versus after adopting the sitemap-then-sample-pages sequence on comparable redesign projects.
test.measure: Number of major rework requests during the build.
test.read_point: During and after the full site build

title: Let the customer's own aha moment decide which marketing channel gets investment
hypothesis: If research surfaces the specific moment customers say they connected with the brand, and that moment decides which marketing channel gets the incremental investment, then acquisition spend follows real customer behavior instead of a generic customer-centric statement with no specific channel implication.

signal.check: Marketing channel investment decisions are made with no reference to the specific moment customers themselves say they connected with the brand.

risk.note: A research-informed budget reallocation.

prerequisites: Customer research capable of surfacing a recurring connection moment
steps: Run customer research asking specifically when and how they felt they connected with the brand.
Identify the recurring aha moment across responses.
Map that moment to the channel or format most able to recreate or extend it (in-person events, unboxing content, a specific content format).
Shift incremental marketing investment toward that channel or format.
Track whether the shift improves conversion or engagement versus the prior allocation.

test.method: Compare conversion or engagement for the newly prioritized channel against its prior allocation level.
test.measure: Conversion or engagement rate for the aha-moment-matched channel.

title: Define brand attributes through 4 separate brainstorming lenses before positioning
hypothesis: If brand attributes are defined through 4 separate, sequential brainstorming lenses (values and beliefs, features and benefits, voice and tone, look and feel) before competitive positioning work, then the resulting attribute list is richer and more grounded, because each lens surfaces a different category of attribute a single open brainstorm tends to blend together.

signal.check: Brand attributes are being defined through 1 open, unstructured brainstorm instead of separate passes through values, features, voice and visual lenses.

risk.note: A workshop exercise before positioning work.

prerequisites: A small cross-functional team available for a structured session
steps: Run a focused brainstorm on values and beliefs only.
Run a separate focused brainstorm on features and benefits only.
Run a separate focused brainstorm on voice and tone only.
Run a separate focused brainstorm on look and feel only.
Group and prioritize the resulting word clusters into themes before starting competitive positioning work.

test.method: Compare the resulting attribute list's richness and usability against a past single, unstructured brainstorm.
test.measure: Number of distinct, usable attributes surfaced per lens versus a single open session.

title: Use drop-based stocking as a real operating form of exclusivity
hypothesis: If limited, drop-based release stocking is used as a real operating model for exclusivity, not just marketing language, and only when production and replenishment genuinely support it, then the exclusivity claim is credible, because a drop model backed by real limited production reads as authentic where a fabricated stock message does not.

signal.check: The brand talks about exclusivity or limited availability in marketing copy without an actual limited, drop-based stocking model behind the claim.

risk.note: A drop model constrains revenue timing and requires real production discipline.

prerequisites: Production and replenishment capacity that can genuinely support a limited-run model
steps: Confirm production and replenishment can genuinely support a limited, drop-based run without silently restocking behind the scenes.
Design 1 SKU or collection to launch as a real, limited drop.
Communicate the drop model plainly and let it actually sell out or end on schedule.
Track demand and sell-through for the drop against a standard, always-in-stock SKU.
Only expand the drop model to more SKUs if production can keep supporting it honestly.

test.method: Compare sell-through velocity and customer perception for a drop-based SKU against a standard, always-in-stock SKU.
test.measure: Sell-through velocity and perceived exclusivity in reviews or surveys.
test.read_point: After the drop's sales window closes

title: Change the brand's marketing vector only when entering a new category
hypothesis: If the brand's written marketing vector is changed only when entering a genuinely new category, never because 1 ad underperformed, then the brand avoids drifting its core positioning in reaction to normal short-term creative noise.

signal.check: The brand's core marketing vector or positioning is being revised in reaction to a single underperforming ad or campaign, rather than only at a genuine category-entry decision.

risk.note: A governance rule for when to revisit core positioning.

prerequisites: A written marketing vector or core positioning statement
steps: Write down the brand's current marketing vector explicitly.
Set a rule that the vector itself is revisited only when the brand is entering a genuinely new category or audience.
When an individual ad or campaign underperforms, diagnose and fix the creative within the existing vector instead of rewriting the vector.
Reserve a full vector review for a real category-entry decision.
Document any vector change with the category-entry reason attached.

test.method: Review the history of vector or positioning changes and check how many were triggered by a single underperforming ad versus a real category entry.
test.measure: Share of past vector changes triggered by single-ad underperformance.

title: Judge early-stage content or product work by craft, not early metrics
hypothesis: If early-stage content or product creation is judged against the team's own craft bar, not early metrics, view counts or revenue, then the team keeps investing through the period before traction typically appears, because real traction commonly lags sustained obsession by a long stretch.

signal.check: An early-stage content or product effort is being judged or abandoned based on flat early metrics, with no separate check of whether the craft itself is improving.

risk.note: A judgment-criteria change for early-stage work.

prerequisites: An early-stage content or product effort with limited traction so far
steps: Define what craft quality looks like for the specific effort (production value, writing clarity, product finish).
Track craft quality on a fixed cadence, separate from view counts or revenue.
Continue the effort as long as craft quality is genuinely improving, even if metrics are flat.
Reassess only if craft quality itself stalls over a defined period.
Avoid killing an improving-craft effort purely because early metrics have not caught up yet.

test.method: Track craft quality and metrics separately over several months for an early-stage effort.
test.measure: Craft quality trend versus metrics trend.
test.read_point: Every month during the early-stage period

title: Sketch a large volume of rough logo concepts before narrowing to a final mark
hypothesis: If a logo or symbol project sketches and discards a large volume of rough concepts by hand before narrowing, instead of searching for the final mark on a first attempt, then the resulting shortlist is stronger, because volume sketching surfaces options a single early attempt would never reach.

signal.check: A logo or symbol design project moves straight from a single early concept to refinement, with no volume sketching phase producing and discarding many rough ideas first.

risk.note: A creative-process step.

prerequisites: A locked creative direction and brand strategy to sketch within
steps: Lock the creative direction and core brand attributes before sketching begins.
Set aside dedicated time for volume sketching, by hand, with no expectation any single sketch is final.
Explore symbol and monogram or seal-format variety within the locked direction.
Screen out symbols carrying an unwanted cultural association as they come up.
Narrow to a small shortlist only after a genuinely large volume of rough concepts has been produced.

test.method: Compare the final shortlist's quality and diversity for a project using volume sketching against a past project that skipped straight to refinement.
test.measure: Number and distinctiveness of shortlisted concepts.
test.read_point: At the shortlist stage of the design project
